The mind, situated within the sense objects, having passed away, and established through its connection with the vital air,
revolves within the center of the wheel, conjoined with the wind.
By means of the beautiful practice of the right [nostril], the tawny wind of the sun is led very slowly through the application of prāṇa and apāna;
it abides in the center of the leaf of that Supreme Self.
One should maintain the state of being absorbed in that; of this there is no doubt.
When that [breath] migrates from the middle of one petal to another, one should know that to be a *saṃkrānti* (transit); by those six [transits], there is the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*).
Likewise, at the equinox, the twelfth [transit], and during the transits into the zodiacal signs,
as well as during solar eclipses occurring every twelve years.
Through the conjunction of six months and days, the eclipse of the moon occurs;
the great yogi, established in samādhi, stands between the sun and the moon.
When one perceives oneself situated in the center of the lunar disc through a vision distinguished by the configuration of the inhalation, it is seen directly.
I know its grasping; one perceives it as fixed within the moon. The wheels of the moon and sun are the agents of creation and destruction.
It is obtained only through the successive lineage from the mouth of the Guru;
by means of which, one's own self, situated in the center of the wheel, proceeds toward dissolution.
By means of the application of the moon and the sun, there is no doubt that dharma and adharma, as well as liberation, knowledge, and even dispassion, are known.
One certainly perceives desire, anger, and greed as being situated in the *cakra* when [the breath] is located in the wind; one recognizes them in their conjunction on the left and right sides.
Situated between the prāṇa and apāna breaths, it is established at the tip of the nose;
for fire stands above, water below, and the wind blows across.
In the center, one should know the earth, and the all-pervading one is indeed the grandson (of the Self).
At the end of the elements is the equinox, whose movement pierces the head of the Suṣumnā.
O woman of excellent complexion, when the self becomes poised in the middle,
there is no doubt that one carries the supreme yoga of the equinox.
O Goddess of the Gods, listen to how deception occurs regarding all those marks which I have previously described.
One should know that the entire triple world, including the moon and sun and all things mobile and immobile, as well as the path, is devoid of a path within those very limits.
I shall describe the movement and the nature of that self:
therein, in the center, is a bull engaged in copulation and a crow.
One should always abide in the Rudra-measure, which is the great sound of the unstruck (anāhata);
sattva, rajas, and tamas constitute its three bonds.
By means of the movement of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, the three quarters are situated there;
one should know that Brahmā and the others are located below within their respective portions.
Earth, water, fire, and the fourth, which is established as air—
these indeed reside in the upper portion of the field, as do the four peaks.
Three and a half [units] are situated on the left, and again these same [units] on the right;
they are established in unstable forms through the differentiation of the movement of the channels (nāḍī).
These seven cubits, O Goddess, are the two heads of the Moon and the Sun;
that which is situated in the middle, O Goddess, produces the Unstruck Sound (anāhata).
Without sexual union, his breath does not exist, nor indeed his life;
therefore, with every effort, always remain established in sexual union.
One attains liberation through sexual union; sexual union increases longevity.
O Goddess, sexual union is proclaimed to be the bestower of all accomplishments.
O beautiful one, I shall fully explain the liberation of that God of gods, who remains established in primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as his own self-deception.
Birth occurs there in the middle, as well as at the times of the rising of the periods;
these three are declared to apply to the degrees of the feet of Taurus.
The causal principle situated there should be joined and led very gradually,
having contracted the seven cubits of the vital air that resides within the channels.
O lady of excellent complexion, there are two heads, four horns, three bonds, and the primordial nature; these are not found in the hundred faces of the Guru, nor in the Karaṇa.
By means of the sequential yoga, make that which consists of twenty-four principles abide on the left;
this is renowned as "contraction" (saṃkoca), and then it becomes "situated in the body" (piṇḍastha).
For in the heart, situated in the midst of space, there exists that which has the form of a lamp;
within the center of the heart, the sense organs and their objects are consumed by it.
Sāvitrī resides within his body, possessing a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction;
like a blazing fire that consumes both the dry and the moist, he burns away all Yakṣas.
Likewise, the lord of yogins established here burns away all karmas,
when he remains contracting everything in the form of fire.
Then it is declared that [the path] goes through all the paths,
to the east of the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) and to the north of the path of the gods (devayāna).
But she who is established in the three bodies as the vital energy (vāyu), the subtle part (kalā), and the warmth (ūṣmā), is led very slowly toward the Setubandha.
The first is named Ekāsaṃvaraṇī, and the second is Visarjanī;
the third is Kalā, and the one renowned by the name Anteṣṭi is at the end.
By relying on the Visarjanī and practicing it again and again, she is led through the yoga of binding; and she is the digit known as Saṃvaraṇī.
One should cause [the breath] to enter in reverse order, situated between the feet of the *anteṣṭi*,
bypassing the station of Brahmā and reaching the stations of Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara.
Śaṅkhinī and Dvārabheda, as well as Kuñcikā, pierce through the membrane;
that channel which is supremely subtle is renowned by the name Suṣumnā.
Having pierced through the crown of the head, the path is established there in the center;
by that path one must go to the very state that is free from affliction.
Having first and second entered the hollow interior of the bone,
and having diligently brought about dissolution by resorting to the third.
And this, O fair-complexioned one, is declared to be the deception of Time;
there, birth is not divided, nor is there any exhaustion of Time.
Having abandoned both dharma and adharma, one dissolves into the supreme state;
when dissolved in that place, the prāṇa and apāna breaths come to an end.
One neither hears the coming nor the going, nor the non-breath nor the breath itself; one does not hear sounds, being liberated and indeed free from mental agitation.
He does not perceive form, nor what its colors may be; his tongue is like new [metal], and he perceives neither cold nor heat to the touch.
The nose does not perceive even a foul odor;
the intellect perceives all this that is visible—the three worlds, including everything mobile and immobile.
When that external mental cognition no longer exists, then duality is not found;
for the self has become one, devoid of all sense organs.
Consciousness, the conscious, and the cognizer, as well as the non-decay of time—
this, O Goddess, is the Supreme Brahman, Nirvāṇa, the supreme imperishable.
The stainless place of liberation, residing within the mouth of the Guru, is known;
and the lord of practitioners effects entry into another city.
That which was described by the Goddess as the non-emission of the digits (kalās),
[is realized] by a measure of only one cubit, with the flower resting in the palm of the hand.
First, one should perform the binding with that which is the "concealer of the digits" (kalā-saṃvaraṇī);
then, the wind situated in the center of the flower should be led very slowly.
Seeing that flower move, one should practice twice as much;
when the movement of the flower occurs through an application of two cubits, [one has succeeded].
Success is achieved here without a doubt within the measure of five cubits;
and having seen the flower move, one should pierce it with "vajra-milk."
When the vajra-tree has been split apart, effect its dissolution into the body of another;
when it comes to reside upon a lotus in the center of that other's heart.
Then the elements differentiate themselves through their own five qualities:
one perceives form through the sense of sight and hears sound through the sense of hearing.
The vital air (vāyu) situated at the tip of the nose seizes the breath (prāṇa) in such a way that the conscious being perceives everything, including cold, heat, and touch itself.
In various places, the sense faculties and their objects spread forth;
whatever knowledge was previously described, all of that it certainly declares.
And the entry into another's body, O Goddess, has been described as very difficult to attain—
whether among bipeds, quadrupeds, or even those that are footless or possess a multitude of feet.
There is no doubt that he may transfer [his consciousness] through the power of this yoga;
furthermore, those men who are overcome by dispassion desire to depart [from the body].
I shall now fully explain how the immediate departure occurs,
so that through the yoga of contraction it first attains dissolution in the supreme state.
One shall transcend [birth], of this there is no doubt; rebirth is no longer found.
O Goddess, I have declared all that which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
"What else do you ask regarding the differentiation of self-awareness? Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, on the Differentiation of Self-Awareness, in the Guhya, the doctrine of the Supreme Lord.
The Goddess said:
Right here, in the center of Meru, resides the Mistress of the Kula,
renowned as the Tripurā-mantra, who is joined with the portions of the faces [beginning with] the letter *va*.
O Lord of Gods, you should explain the twenty-seven yoginīs as well as the five mudrās, their efficacy, and the procedure for worship.
In the Catuṣka and the Mahātantra, in the six Uttaratantras,
and in the midst of the Rudrayāmala, that which was previously mentioned was heard by me.
"O Lord, please speak further in detail regarding how this occurs.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"I shall tell you, without doubt, the lineage exactly as it has been established."
She is born from the splendor of Brahmā, from the splendor of Viṣṇu, and from the splendor of Rudra.
Tripurā is the Great Vidyā that bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
I shall now declare its extraction as it exists within the center of Meru.
Having extracted that which is the ornament at the end of the eyebrow of the left ear of Mālinī,
Lakulī is established there.
One should recognize that in each half [of the diagram], there is one seated on a seat with a staff held askance;
he is accompanied by Sarasvatī and has a cruel [expression] fixed upon his head.
And the Vāgbhava syllable, O Great Goddess, arises from the splendor of Brahman;
by the power of this seed-syllable, the Grandfather [Brahmā] takes the form of creation.
Having extracted the syllable *karālī* (KĀRĀLĪ) colored white, which is situated at the beginning of *rudra* (RU),
place it right there, joined with *bhairava* (BHAI) located in the left eye (VĀMA).
One should know that seat where Śukrabhairava is above and Pūtanā is situated— that which is located upon the head of Ambikā.
One should place this Kāmarāja, endowed with the Bindu, in its established position;
it is known as that which arises from the splendor of Viṣṇu and causes great agitation.
O Goddess, through the yoga of constant practice, one attains that which bestows great good fortune—
the Bhairava born of semen situated in the midst of water.
O Goddess of the gods, one should apply the Bhairava [mantra] situated at its base;
and one should cause the Mahāsenodbhava [mantra] to be placed before it.
One should place the protection upon the head; that seed-syllable originates from Rudra.
O Goddess, these three seed-syllables arise from the three deities. (Alternatively, these three seed-syllables of the armor arise from the three deities.)
For these remain in a state of deep sleep, yet when awakened, they bestow the fruit;
therefore, I shall explain the *haṃsa*, which stands as the most secret of secrets.
The threefold supreme secret knowledge is the illuminator of Tripura;
therein lies Chagalaṇḍabhairava, where Dahanī is established.
By means of the method of extraction, both syllables are repeated again and again;
joined with Ananta, Vajriṇī stands before him.
Wherein Bhairava is fivefold, that syllable stands at the forefront.
One should cause him to receive that which has arisen from the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and resides at his head;
before him is the seed-syllable *saṃ* (the *saṃvaka*), the Goddess Khaḍgīśa, who moves upon her seat.
Bhairava, born from blood and endowed with the secret Śakti,
is the Great Vidyā of eight syllables that illuminates the seed-syllable of Brahman.
Having raised the color of wrath, one should cause Pinākin, who is seated upon his throne and has arisen from the left eye, to bestow union upon him (Rudra).
The first seed-syllable of Mālinī is conjoined with Jhaṇṭīśa;
the third syllable is mounted by Pūtanā and originates from Wrath (Krodha).
Lord Dhātṛ, mounted upon the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), stands before him;
and in front of him is Meṣavarṇa, adorned with the secret power (guhyaśakti).
O lady of excellent complexion, one should extract the great syllables before it;
adorn it with the Gāyatrī known as Varṇasaṃvartaka.
O excellent lady, one should join that [syllable] which is at the root of the right arm with a *bindu* when it stands upon its peak,
and thus extract it.
In front of that, Karālī is seated upon her throne starting from Dhruva;
in front of her is situated the seat of the letter *Makāra*, born of blood.
This eleven-syllable vidyā is indeed a great agitator;
born from Kāmarāja and others, it awakens the splendor of Viṣṇu.
O Goddess of the gods, having extracted the *dhruva* from the third [syllable] and having extracted Mahākāla,
it is joined with Sadyojāta.
And the second is declared to be the extremely rare seed-syllable of the Self (ātma-bīja),
which is the Goddess named Saṃghātikā, adorned with a bindu upon its head.
Having given the command to Amarī, one should then paint Krodhavarṇa;
and then, O Goddess, a serpent seated upon the throne of the syllable *U*.
This five-syllabled vidyā awakens the seed of liberation;
one should worship it within the limbs of the vidyā, the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga), the faces, and during the ritual offerings.
O Supreme Goddess, the Vāgbhava [syllable] of Kāmarāja bestows liberation;
whichever is one's own "lamp" (dīpinī) mantra, that is the foremost for one who recites it.
By this very procedure, she becomes the life-force of all;
born from the three splendors, Tripurā is the illuminator of light.
They should be known according to the division of the cities as bestowers of all accomplishments;
O Goddess, when merely the ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed, one brings the three worlds under control.
I shall fully explain that, as well as the locations for the ritual placement (nyāsa):
the first location is at the head, where the splendor of the vow (vratatejas) is established.
Furthermore, one should place the splendor of Nārāyaṇa in the secret place;
having carefully performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in the heart with the splendor of Rudra.
O lady of excellent complexion, one should place the Vāgbhava syllable in the right eye, Janārdana in the left, and Śiva on the forehead; thus it is said.
O Goddess, the Vāgbhava syllable should be diligently placed on the right ear, and the Kāmarāja syllable is situated on the left ear; of this there is no doubt.
O Great Goddess, one should place the splendor of Rudra in the center of the face;
on the right arm-staff, however, is the god Pitāmaha once again.
The splendor of Keśava is situated and established in the left arm;
one should place Rudra in the middle of the back according to the prescribed rule.
The Vāgbhava syllable is located on the right calf, while Kāma is established on the left;
Rudra resides in the center of the navel, and likewise [the other syllables] are in all the joints.
This is the Nyāsa consisting of the Vidyā and the six limbs; therefore, listen:
one should apply that which is named Māyā-Vāgīśvarī to the location of the heart.
The Kāmarāja [bīja] given for the head bestows liberation when placed in the locations of the crest-lock (śikhā);
the Vāgbhava [bīja] is to be joined with the armor (kavaca), and the two Kāma [bījas] are established in the eyes.

Having assigned the weapon-mantra with the seed-syllable of Rudra in the cardinal and intermediate directions, O Goddess, perform the six-limbed assignment; now hear from me the assignment of the faces.
O Sovereign of the Gods, one should perform the deposition on the left: the Vāgbhava [syllable] situated in the eastern face, conjoined with the Vidyā-tejas, and the Kāmarāja [syllable].
The wise one should also perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Dīpinī-vidyā situated within the mouth; he should place the Rudra-seed-syllable in the mouth and likewise in the right [mouth].
Through the application of the *pūrvavidyā* and so forth, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the faces is very difficult to attain;
it consists of the *vāgbhava* syllable and the five arrows together with the bow.
I shall describe that [arrangement] as it is established in its placement:
the Rudra-mālā and so forth, situated like fish within the temple of the Vedas (or gods).
O lady of excellent complexion, these indeed abide in three places;
you should diligently draw him seated upon the command of the Immortals (Amarīśa), positioned in the center.
Since this bow consists of three syllables and is established as the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable],
I shall now describe those five arrows which exist within its seed-component.
Having extracted the trident-staff situated in the eastern ninth [square],
one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the arrow of all Gahabhairava in the center of the secret [mandala].
The eleventh is situated in the place of the sages (Ṛṣisthāna), in the middle of Cāṅga;
having extracted the syllable Ambikā, they are the creators of the manifestation of all phonemes.
They call the second arrow that which is situated in the circle of the navel;
then, that supreme syllable is further ignited within the center of the heart.
They call the third the arrow, wherein the three worlds are established;
it is produced from the navel and the garland, and rests upon the peak of Niṣadha.
They know the one arisen from Sarasvatī to be the Lord of All Speech;
and the fourth is the Great Arrow (Mahāvāṇa), the placement (nyāsa) in the center of the face.
O Great Goddess, the fifth is the lamp of light (āloka), which is fierce and established there; it is the supreme placement upon the head (mūrdhanyāsa) that revives all.
These five arrows, born from the limbs of the seed-syllable of Brahmā,
bring about accomplishment through speech when they are placed in the middle of the *piṇḍa*.
I shall now describe the five arrows produced from the limbs of Kāmarāja:
having taken the letter situated between *vi* and *lu*, it is placed in the ninth left abode.
One should know that the first letter belongs to Māṃsa and Bhairava;
the second is Rudramālā, and above it is Vināyakī.
The second supreme syllable is joined with the letter *na* (ananta), adorned with a bindu,
and mounted upon Raktabhairava.
In front of that, however, fashion a seat consisting of a trident-staff of its same color;
they call this the third seed-syllable, adorned with the face of Bhairava.
Having extracted the letter ending in *ca*, where Ambikā is established;
they know the fourth syllable to be the letter at the throat (or mouth) of Mālinī.
One should extract the seed-syllable at the beginning of the group and the fifth one;
furthermore, these three seed-syllables are established hereafter.
First, one should place the arrow of Kāmarāja upon the head;
this eight-syllable arrow is established as being red in color.
Having extracted the syllable Karālī, which stands as the eleventh from the beginning,
one places the first syllable of the second [group] before it, with Dahanī following immediately after.
O Goddess of the gods, the letter situated in the ninth [group] and others is mounted there;
it is adorned with the letters of the Viśvamālā and the like, and joined with the Bindu.
Bhairava is situated in his mouth; the third [syllable] is in front of him.
Ambikā Devī is the fourth; make the sinews the seat of Rudra.
A ram joined with the end of the Viśvamālā stands before it;
O Vāgīśa, there is no doubt that the sixth [letter] is before that.
Furthermore, these four seed-syllables stand before one;
this ten-syllable arrow should be placed in the center of the mouth.
Furthermore, Kakulīśa is situated in the third [position] as established from the beginning;
the letter *ma* is above it, while the letter *cu* stands at its front.
Practice the color of Bhairava at the back; perform the final seat.
Lokādi is given as the head, and Arghīśa is the second.
Again, taking the *saṃvartaka* [syllable] conjoined with the end of the *rudramālā*, this is called the third seed-syllable; one should draw Bhīma before it.
The fifth [seed-syllable] is situated in the wind-velocity, located upon the peak of the left [hand];
furthermore, one should write three of these seed-syllables before it.
And the third great arrow is Vasuvarṇa, situated in the heart;
it is the primordial Trimūrtibhairava, arising from wrath and established in the syllable LA.
The third seed-syllable is Mālinī, distinguished by the color of the tongue (red) and joined with the Bindu; it is the Illuminator, adorned with the power of knowledge (Jñāna-śakti).
Taking the letter situated in the middle of *tāra*, established upon *meṣa* (the Ram),
and joined with the fourth bindu— this is known by the name Āṣāḍhī.
Furthermore, O Goddess, make Mahākāla joined with *dhruva* and the others;
the fifth seed-syllable, which is the best, has a cruel color and is placed at the head.
The third eye of the Goddess is endowed with Ananta;
the seventh seed-syllable is red and originates from the right side of her belly.
One should join Vāgīśa as the eighth; then again, four [syllables] in front:
the letter of the Goddess’s color, Bāṇa, and the fourth [vowel] in the middle of the navel.
Having first extracted the syllable *krūra*, one should place *sambaka* before it;
they know the second syllable to be that which stands at the end of the world within its city.
Furthermore, that seed-syllable of Saṃvarta is adorned with Ananta;
it is mounted upon the seat of the trident-staff and is the fourth, originating from the sinews.
The fifth is Vāyuvega; these three are again at the forefront.
Know them to be numbered by the [five] classes; the fifth is situated as an arrow (Bāṇa).
When the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed in the center of the womb (*yoni*), it becomes a bringer of great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*).
These five syllables arise from the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*).
One should diligently perform the placement according to the rules during the time of worship.
The Goddess said:
"The seed-syllables of desire, the arrows, and those which are the limbs and faces."
I have heard all about the god and the deliverance of Tripura.
"Now I wish to hear the procedure for worship according to the rules.
Śrī Bhairava said: "The Vidyā is Tripura, consisting of three locations and joined with the three seats (dāsana)."
The three seats, as well as the seed-syllable and the three forms, have been proclaimed;
the three modes of conduct have been fully described, and the utterance is of three kinds.
They say that dissolution (laya) is threefold, distinct in each respective place;
however, nine varieties are proclaimed for each individual seed-syllable (bīja).
In each division, the goddesses residing in their respective places should be worshipped with effort, joined with their names and encapsulated by the primordial seed-syllable.
In a solitary, secluded place, devoid of the sight of cattle,
beautiful and endowed with fragrance, one should worship Tripurabhairavī.
Clad in the directions (naked), with disheveled hair, and eyes adorned with collyrium—
this should be performed at the time of worship, as it bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
O Goddess, the three-colored lotus is situated at the Pūrṇapīṭha;
it resembles molten gold both externally and internally.
One should know that seat to be the city of Brahmā as it is celebrated;
therein, situated in the center, is the seed-syllable Vāgbhava, worshipped by the gods.
One should encircle it with its own measure three times and a half;
one should meditate upon it as shining brilliantly, resembling perfectly pure gold.
At its extremity are nine yoginīs and likewise the five arrows;
this divine [mandala], which brings about the perfection of speech, should be worshipped with great effort.
Furthermore, O Goddess, in Jālandhara there is an auspicious six-petaled lotus;
one should contemplate it as being red in color within the body, just as it is externally.
O Goddess of the Gods, the wise one should meditate upon the Kāmarāja [Kāmadeva], joined with three and a half measures,
having a form resembling the hibiscus flower, and revolving.
O Goddess, that which is endowed with nine messengers and possessed of five arrows is proclaimed as the supreme [weapon] of Viṣṇu, which causes great agitation.
Furthermore, O Goddess, Uḍḍiyāna is praised as the city of Rudra, beautifully adorned with eight petals and possessing a luster like that of jasmine or the moon.
Above *kāma* is the great seed-syllable situated upon a lotus; it is declared to be the third, which is *nirvāṇa*, bestowing the state of *nirvāṇa*.
It should be worshipped with diligent effort together with the nine goddesses;
it is divine, brings about great peace, bestows liberation, and destroys obstacles.
One should offer the three kinds of *phalgu* with yellow, red, and white flowers, fragrant with camphor and other scents; one should employ these in the three locations.
Having performed the incense, lamp, food offering, and libation according to the prescribed rite,
make everything complete and seal it with the appropriate mudrās.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the binding of mudrās as they truly are—
divine, bestowing all accomplishments, free from obstacles, and the destroyer of impediments.
The left hand should be placed in the middle of the right, its face turned toward it and not appearing as if scorched;
one should join the backs of the hands together, with the index finger positioned between the little fingers.
One should place the right [thumb] on the left [ring finger] and the left [thumb] on the right [ring finger],
interlacing them with the thumbs and ring fingers.
Having taken hold of it with effort using both the left and right hands,
one should form a hook (aṅkuśa) with the fingers of the right hand, directed downwards and upwards.
This is that Drāviṇī mudrā; one should display it preceded by the arrow-gesture (vāṇa).
The index finger (tarjanī) of the left hand is positioned above the thumb (jyeṣṭhā).
The little finger of the ring finger should be placed upon the thumb in the middle,
and one should perform a touch with the index finger and the little finger.
She is renowned as Kṣobhaṇī, known by the wise as the one who causes great agitation;
she should be diligently displayed, joined with the second arrow.
This is the queen of great accomplishments, the agitator of the three worlds.
Having joined the two hands in a hollowed cup with the fingers interlaced,
the index finger of the right hand is placed upon the ring finger of the left hand.
The left index finger should be carefully interlaced.
Having grasped the ring finger of the left hand with that [right hand],
one should then again raise the two middle fingers upward.
One should place the thumb of the left hand in the middle of the hand;
O Goddess, this is the supreme Yoni-mudrā, which bestows all accomplishments.
By means of the third arrow-yoga, one should display the [mudrā] at the place of the womb;
having contracted three fingers, one should restrain them with the thumb.
One should place the index finger of the left hand at the left ear;
threatening all directions, one should whirl it about while keeping the eyes fixed upon it.
Accompanied by the fourth vowel (Ū), she is the pacifier of great obstacles;
one should form the fist gesture with both the left and right hands.
One should form a union with them and extend the two index fingers;
one should also join the pair of thumbs at their bases.
The supportless Mahāmudrā, conjoined with the fifth arrow, should be diligently demonstrated; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Goddess, among those [deities] of the King of Passion who are established as the five arrows,
the second seed-syllable belongs to each one individually.
One should first display that mudrā and obtain the fruit of the four aims (caturvarga),
as well as [the benefits of] flowers, incense, food offerings, recitation, and likewise worship.
O Goddess of the gods, spirits, rākṣasas, and others seize the vital energy of those who are devoid of the mudrā; they prevail over them, without a doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, it should be sealed; thus it will bear fruit.
When sealed, the splendor remains, and when sealed, the vow becomes steadfast.

Through the seal (mudrā), worship becomes stable; when sealed, that which is supreme is made firm. By means of the mudrā, one attains accomplishment; whatever one desires, that one shall certainly obtain.
O Goddess, [a rite] devoid of the mudrā brings obstacles to Tripura;
therefore, with every effort, perform the sealing at the conclusion of the worship.
By the mere utterance of which lustful people melt away,
that auspicious [mudrā] is known as Drāvaṇī, the bestower of great joy.
In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, she is the mudrā that agitates all women who are proud with passion; she is the agitator who causes agitation.
By the power of the *yonimudrā*, one can bring under control the Siddhas, Gandharva maidens, gods, Asuras, and serpents; of this there is no doubt.
By the mere threatening gesture of the index finger, wicked women, evil kings, and especially enemies— all are terrified and fall into a state of delusion at that very moment.
One obtains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and especially sovereignty;
there is no doubt in this matter, provided the bride is free from disease.
These qualities of the Sealed One have indeed been described by me to you:
the melting Yoni-mudrā, the agitating [mudrā], and likewise the threatening [mudrā].
Having bound the four mudrās and the fifth, which is without support,
and having performed everything to completion, one should begin the recitation at the conclusion of the worship.
One should place [the first letter] in the middle and join both at the ends;
having led the three into the supreme reality, she is the Mistress of Desire, the three-fold divider.
Having repeatedly brought about the dissolution of the peak in the form of the lamp-flame,
one should again [dissolve] three, then both, and finally one, in their respective places in reverse order.
This procedure for recitation has been declared, revealing the secret:
one who is a celibate student, who has conquered anger, who eats only at night, and who is firm in his vows.
Whoever performs one hundred thousand recitations according to this very procedure,

One should offer honey, lac-resin, and milk into the fire-pit with flowers produced from the Brahma-tree, such as Karavīra, Jātī, and others.
O Goddess of the gods, I shall tell you what his power may be:
the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda.
The Itihāsas and Purāṇas, as well as logic and grammar,
and all the Āgamas without exception, have originated from the five faces.
Song, instrumental music, as well as dance and charming poetry—
whatever beings have existed, whatever will exist in the future, and whatever branches of knowledge there may be.
By the power of this vidyā, everything becomes directly perceptible to anyone—
be they a fool, a woman, a youth, or a maiden.
One becomes a literal master of speech from the tips of the hands up to the head;

Whether she be a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriṇī, a Vaiśyā, or a Śūdrī of excellent complexion,
they become agitated for the sake of the preeminent practitioner and bestow abundant wealth.
If one recites [the mantra] twenty-one times while interspersing it with the name of someone, that person will be brought within a distance of twenty *gavyūtis*; of this there is no doubt.
There is no doubt that he dies if he does not desire it,
provided that one hundred thousand recitations have been performed and the fire-oblation (homa) has been conducted according to the rules.
He becomes the Lord of Speech in person, with the form of the one whose banner is the makara;
by the power of this vidyā, he enjoys vast pleasures.
When the mantra has been recited two hundred thousand times and the fire sacrifice (homa) has been performed, the practitioner becomes a lord of kings; of this there is no doubt.
When the lord of practitioners recites four hundred thousand [mantras],
the power of the command (ājñāsiddhi) shall proceed, and he shall even cause the netherworld (pātāla) to burst open.
Taking his stand at the entrance of the hole, he should strike that entrance one hundred and eight times with white mustard seeds and black mustard.
There is no doubt that the maidens dwelling in the netherworld—
those wives of the Nāgas, Rākṣasas, and Daityas who reside there— are agitated.
They come without a doubt to where that lord of practitioners is;
they pay homage and carry out his command.
O Goddess, when the lord of practitioners has entered by way of the path to heaven and the netherworld and it does not please him, he should perform eight hundred thousand recitations.
They cause great agitation among the gods, dānavas, and siddhas who dwell in heaven and the netherworld, and they bestow the fruit desired by one's wishes.
When ten lakhs of recitations have been performed and the fire-oblation has been accomplished,
one shall become the lord of fourteen crores of Vidyādharas.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the Extraction of Tripura, in the middle of Meru, according to the Pārameśvarīmata.
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, I have heard everything regarding the procedure for worship and recitation, as well as the nature of the efficacy of the mudrās, concerning Tripura."
That which is the Saṃjīvanī lore, the destroyer of old age and death,
by whose very grace the gods are proclaimed to be immortal.
How is she situated as the very essence within the center of Meru?
What is her extraction like? Tell me that, O Great Lord.
O Lord of Gods, by whose recitation immortality is attained,
and by the power of whose ignorance the dead are raised up.
From here [it is unclear]:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme Vāgīśī Kālikā,

Then, having taken the pair beginning with Tripurā, omitting the letter *ka*.

Having taken the seed-syllable of Pinākin situated in the middle of *nān*, one should bestow the supreme Vāgīśvarī with the *bindu*; this becomes the first mantra of Rudra. One should extract Lakulī and Mahākālī; Indra is not [extracted] by means of the blood-red [syllable].
In the friction of the wind, that vital breath stands protected in two ways;
O Goddess, following the ritual action, one should extract me, who am fierce, cruel, the threefold death, and not red with blood.
Then, one should extract [the essence] according to the proper method, neither repeating nor omitting anything, [beginning with] Mahākāla... [and so forth].
[The text is unclear up to this point. Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the knowledge that is most difficult to obtain.
The deities, Indra and the others, all arrived before me.
In the past, for a hundred divine years, I was praised with various hymns.
Then, being well-pleased, I gave [her] Amarasuryā.
Among them, O Great Goddess, she was brought down by Śukra.
The great vidyā of twenty syllables, endowed with the ten messengers, is renowned as Saṃjīvinī; this is proclaimed as the second name.
"May she, who was extracted by me from the center of Mount Meru, quickly grant immortality;
for the benefit of the Dānavas, she was indeed preserved by Śukra (and accomplished in due course in the past)."
In the great battle with the gods, those great asuras who die—
Śukra restores their lives through the power of this vidyā.
In whose body the Vidyā together with the Dūtī resides,
he who performs the recitation one hundred and eight times day after day—
I shall describe the qualities that arise through the application of the ritual procedure for worship:
[the subduing of] ghosts, spirits, and demons, as well as untimely death and great fear.
Fever, colic, and other diseases, as well as weapons such as thunderbolts and the like, do not prevail over one who recites [this mantra] in battle; he shall not be overcome by great obstacles.
There is no fear of lions or tigers, nor likewise among wild beasts;
I shall fully explain that means of deliverance, such as it is.
O woman of excellent complexion, it should be given to a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who have been examined and who provide instruction on the path of their lineage.
O lady of excellent complexion, one should draw the great Mount Meru with four peaks in a solitary, secluded place, free from the sight of cattle.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛtya, Varuṇa, Vāyu,
Kaubera, and Īśa— [these are] in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should prepare a jar filled with the five jewels and accompanied by a vardhanī vessel,
having them colored white with sandalwood paste.
Having repeatedly wrapped it in divine flowers and cloths,
one should place a jar made of jewels and gems, or in their absence, an auspicious golden one.
Alternatively, O Goddess, one should cause a lotus made of gold to be offered before him,
having worshipped it again and again with flowers, incense, and food offerings.
Therein, one should perform the extraction of the supreme *saṃjīvanī* vidyā,
which is situated in the center of Meru and is established as the *dhruva* named [Gha].
Having extracted the first letter, which is the supreme life-force of all letters,
one should place the letter Arghīśa at the end of the Dhruva, situated below it.
Gathering [the syllables] within the space of one cubit, make the beginning of the world adorned;
the second is thus declared, and the third is the color of Bhṛgu.
Furthermore, on the fourth [digit] is Bhṛgu, adorned with the color of Venus;
Mālinī is at the right foot, where Dhātrīśa is situated.
Having extracted from below that [syllable] which is Bhairava with four faces,
endowed with the power of the tongue, it is the fifth, most excellent seed-syllable.
One should know that Mālinī is produced from the throat (or mouth) of Mahāsena (as if from the letter *ma*), above which is the color of the seasons; and Mālinī is indeed the crest.
The seventh supreme seed-syllable is conjoined with the letter *vi* at its beginning;
when it is again conjoined with *krū*, it becomes the eighth.
The seed-syllable beginning with *dhruva* and ending with *āsana* wards off death;
having again extracted that same syllable, there where *jayantī* is situated.
He too, with the letter beginning with *vi* (*va*), should be joined with the three forms (*trimūrti*);
and the letter at the throat (or mouth) of *Mālinī*, situated below the end of *Kūrma*.
One should also make it joined with a drop (bindu); the sinew is the supreme abode of Rudra.
This is declared as the tenth, the nectar characterized by life.
Furthermore, the color lohitta (blood-red) is situated in the east at the end of Rudra;
it is mounted upon the staff of the trident and adorned with the final letter of Viśva.
Furthermore, O Goddess, the twelfth [form] of Umākānta should be Kevala (the Corpse).
Mālinī, who is Śivādūtī, is established as the Garland of Planets (Grahamālā).
One should mount the serpent [mantra] of Pañcārtha-Pracaṇḍabhairava;
its head is the bindu, the syllable of universal color.
Where Bhairava is at Āṣāḍhī, situated at its very limit,
that is declared as the fourteenth, adorned by Sūkṣmarudra.
Having extracted Bhṛgu and Rudra, with the Bindu adorning the end of the former,
and at its conclusion the syllable of Krodha, which resides previously in the eleventh position.
They know the sixteenth seed-syllable as Rudra mounted upon Amarīśa;
O Goddess, there is again the trident and the staff, situated once more beginning with the syllable *Oṃ*.
Furthermore, that Bhṛgu-ka is adorned by the end of the world of Rudra;
it is the color situated in the midst of Śukra, where Bhṛgu is established.
Mounted upon the color of sinews and adorned by Viśvaṃta,
Ambikā is in front of him, where Lakulī-Bhairava resides.
When not joined with Ananta, it is said to become the twenty-syllable [mantra].
O Goddess, I shall now tell you what its constituent limbs are.
Having taken up the name, the syllables, and so forth, and being established at the root of the vidyā,
one should perform the heart-placement (hṛdinyāsa) ending with "namaḥ," O lady of excellent complexion.
At its end, the syllables of the elements are established upon the head;
one should know that this is the Śikhā-mantra, ending with Svāhā and consisting of the phonemes of the Vedas.
Joined with the ending *vauṣaṭ*, it destroys untimely death;
the three (or six) seed-syllables are situated at the end of the *huṃ* syllable within the armor (*kavaca*).
One should know that there are two syllables in the middle of the eye; at its end is that which is established ending in *vaṣaṭ*. Three [syllables] are situated at the tip of the weapon (*astra*).
And at the end of that, they say "phaṭ"; this is the six-limbed [mantra] for deceiving death.
I shall now proclaim its messenger; listen with a one-pointed mind.
These ten, which bestow accomplishment, should be worshipped with effort;
one should extract the five components beginning with *prāṇa* and those beginning with the syllable *hrīṃ*.
And in front of that, perform worship ending with "namaḥ" to Saṃjīvanī;
one should worship the fourteen syllables in the eastern quarter.
Furthermore, Nāgā and the others should likewise exhale the wind before her;
and before that is Saṃjīvanī, the fourteen-syllable Dūtī.
O Great Goddess, filled with devotion, one should worship the five elements beginning with Earth in the southeast corners; first, perform the rite of Saṃjīvanī.
Having extracted the mantra beginning with *hrīṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, situated on the right,
this fourteen-syllable *dūtī* should be worshipped with diligence.
Sound and the other [objects], as well as the sense organs, are deluded by the seed-syllable of Māyā;
and the Saṃjīvanī [mantra] should be placed before that, ending with "namaḥ," in the southwest (nairṛta).
One should utter "namas" and then "saṃjīvanī," followed by the seed-syllable of Māyā and so forth;
ending with "namaḥ," one should worship with these nine seed-syllables in the western direction.
Having uttered the mantra beginning with "māyā" (hrīṃ), one should again recite the previously mentioned Saṃjīvanī;
indeed, this [mantra] consists of nine seed-syllables and, being situated in the wind, one should worship it.
Furthermore, from the Saṃjīvanī [mantra], the ego (ahaṃkāra) and so forth arise;
his worship begins with Māyā and others, following the color of Rudra in the northeast (Kaubera).
O Sovereign of the Gods, they say that at the beginning of the northeast [direction] is "satva(nava)," and then again the *saṃjīvanī*;
having first uttered that, O Goddess, [follows] the seed-syllable of Māyā.
Place its nine seed-syllables within the center of the dust;
at the beginning is Saṃjīvanī, starting with the syllable Hrīṃ and ending with Namaḥ.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ) together with Namah, and joined with Saṃjīvanī,
one should perform worship located in the center and upon the petals of the lotus.
One should offer a seat, white flowers, incense, a lamp, sandalwood paste,
and various kinds of food offerings before her.
One should perform the binding of the mudrā and thereafter the recitation;
I shall now describe its mudrā, which is the supreme means for ensuring steadfastness.
The Vidyā born from the Five-Faced One, by whom Time was brought under control;
join the backs of the hands together and interlace the fingers.
The maiden should block the left [nostril] with the big toe of the right foot;
then, indeed, she should do the same for the right [nostril] with the left foot.
Having carefully grasped the left thumb and the index finger with the right hand, and likewise the right [thumb and index finger] with the left.
In the middle, however, the two ring fingers (anāmikā) should be carefully raised up;
she who is established as five-faced is named Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī.
By this very procedure, she should be worshipped with diligence;
this supreme secret Vidyā, known as Jīvā, is the destroyer of death.
Death does not arise for him when he accomplishes this,
being a celibate student of firm vows, fully endowed with the practice of the steady observance.
One should recite the mantra ten hundred thousand times and perform a hundred thousand oblations of guggulu;
O Goddess, she shall abide within one's body and bestow immortality.
"By the power of this vidyā, all those gods shall become long-lived.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the extraction of the Saṃjīvanī-vidyā, according to the Pārameśvara-mata.
The Goddess said:

By means of the division of the Vajraprastāra, the Kulanityā is likewise extracted;
furthermore, in the very center of that [mantra] is the twelve-syllable Vidyā.
The seat consists of the five arrows accompanied by all the messengers;
such is the yoga of the knowledge of the instruments and the meditative absorption (samādhi).
Stambhana (paralysis), kīlana (pinning), as well as māraṇa (killing) and uccāṭana (expulsion),
the subjugation of women, and whatever kind of good fortune there may be— [all these are accomplished].
O Lord of the Gods, how and by what means is it ever accomplished? For what purpose do practitioners achieve success through that?
"Destroy the great doubt that has arisen and the great delusion.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you have asked."
The phonemes, the bindus, the mātrās, and likewise the oral traditions (saṃpradāya).
One should know that the pure [deity] abiding on the path of the family is situated in the center of Meru;
this applies to all other tantras as well as those arising from the five faces.
Devoid of the color of individual souls, those perfected sciences are manifold;
that soul is indeed entirely free from the mixture of seed-syllables.
It bestows complete accomplishment and is situated in the center of Meru;
I shall describe it to you so that it may become complete in every respect.
The twelve-syllable vidyā, according to the division of the Vajraprastāra, is devoid of the three seed-syllables; it constitutes the beginning, the middle, and the end.
O Goddess of the gods, I shall now declare its extraction, which was previously hidden by me; it is situated within Bhārabhūti, O Rudrā, and existed there in former times.
Whatever syllable occurs at the end of the left [hand], that shall be the first seed-syllable;
its utterance should be joined with a nasal drop (bindu), and at its end shall be Ambikā.
Mounted upon a red-colored [form], with Lokādi situated at the head,
and joined with the Dhruvamālā and so forth— this is the second, most excellent seed-syllable.
If the letter *ṛ* is above it and the white Rudra stands before it,
the wise one should take that color and fashion a seat of the color of flesh.
The head preceded by *ṛ* is given, and it stands before the secret [syllable]; those who know the tradition understand that for its head, beginning with *vāma*, there is simply *ṛ* and so forth.
And the fifth is declared to be the supreme seed-syllable, the seat of the letters;
O lady of excellent complexion, having first extracted the letter from the eleventh [chapter].
The syllable ending with Rudra (Ra) is for the head; Dīpanī is situated on the seat.
Preceded by Ṛ (Ḷ), it is given as the head; that is the sixth auspicious syllable.
One should apply this seed-syllable beginning with ignorance (avidyā) to the tip of the goad;
it is declared to be the seventh seed-syllable, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
That which is above the letter Āṣāḍhī, situated between the eyebrows,
of that same color and joined with the subtle— this they know as the eighth syllable.
In the Mālinī meter, where the long (tārā) syllable is situated in the middle of the foot,
the letter preceded by *ṛ* (ṛ), mounted upon the measure of Vāgīśa (four morae), is situated at the head [of the foot].
The ninth is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), and again, the buttock (nitaṃba) alone;
however, they know that in the third [position], the garland of sages (ṛṣimālā) is situated in that same color.
Having extracted the phoneme *pha* and that which is situated above the *chi*,
one should know that alone to be the eleventh seed-syllable (*bīja*).
Furthermore, that supreme twelve-syllable seed-mantra is mounted upon that red [syllable];
and above it is the goddess Ambikā, situated on the left and in the middle.
And the thirteenth is said to be preceded by *ṛ* on the head;
its *avidyā* and so forth are situated within, with that seed-syllable standing before them.
And at the end of this, O Goddess, one should again employ the first;
this is that supreme Vidyā, the bestower of all accomplishments.
The fifteen-syllable Vidyā was born in the midst of Meru;
now I shall further explain another [method] according to the rule for the seat.
The first seed-syllable ends with the vowel *ṛ* and is Mālinī, whose weapon is a flower;
before that is La, the Lord of Kula, situated below the end of the *dhruva*.
Make the second, supreme seed-syllable illuminated, mounted upon its seat, adorned with the Viśva and other ornaments, and pressed down by the head of Krūra.
Having grasped the letter *ī* at the end below, *pūtanā* is its seat;
place *ṛ* preceded by *pu* upon the head, and make that also endowed with the nasal dot (*bindu*).
O God, extract the deity from the middle of the *śukra* and place it at the end of the world;
they call this the fourth seed-syllable, which stands at the beginning of that Vidyā.
The divine seat of the root-vidyā consists of the five seed-syllables;
those which are called the five arrows are the syllables that constitute the shafts.
Having extracted each one individually, they become complete;
having extracted from the eleventh onwards up to the end of the delusion (bhrānti), one should cause that to be given.
Having taken the letters from Rudra to the end, together with Jhaṇṭīśena,
[one places] the letter Ha above that which is in the ninth [square] of the six-column grid.
One should know that as the fourth, the supreme abode of Rudra, which consists of sinews;
it is situated within the ninefold [city], in the center of the name, and in the middle of the bilva fruit.
O Goddess, the seats of the Vedic castes begin with the letter *ka*; those which are situated there are divided into three forms by means of the third [vowel], excluding it.
All four syllables should be provided with the nasal bindu;
the fifth [syllable] should be placed at the beginning, joined with the bindu at its end.
By means of the Bindu-mastaka yoga, these five bestow accomplishment;
these five seed-syllables are the illuminators within the five arrows.
O Goddess, without this [knowledge], your [rites] become fruitless;
the seat consists of the five arrows, while the root-vidyā is the messengers.

O Goddess, whatever rites such as killing (māraṇa), expulsion (uccāṭana), and so forth are performed here in the middle, they are those previously mentioned by me in the *Rurubheda* in the middle section.
Those [mantras] which were previously extracted by me through the method of the Vajraprastāra become fruitful by this very procedure.
Those who are devoid of the lineage tradition are never born without seeds; they are declared to be full of obstacles. One should never worship that which is seedless.
The Goddess said:
"That knowledge which was described by you as the agitator of the three worlds,
and by the grace of whose ignorance this Makaradhvaja has become a perfected being— "
And then, O Lord, a second [weapon] appeared that was likewise destructive of him;
what kind of bow would it be, and what kind of arrows?
And of what nature is that which was spoken by him himself? What is the root-mantra like?
What is its power, and how indeed is it accomplished?
"O Mahādeva, O Bhairava, grant your grace for all this!
Śrī Bhairava said:
"In this center, there has arisen the Vidyā who destroys the bodies of those desiring passion."
The supreme [goddess] consists of twenty-eight syllables and is the destroyer of desire.

the bow, the five arrows, and the root-vidyā have been offered.

These, established in the form of mantras according to their distinction of color, consist of recitation, fire-offerings, ritual practice, mudrās, and flowers.
The seat, the efficacy of the rite—all that was made manifest;
then, O Goddess, Keśava went to Hemakūṭa and took [it] from there.
There, intent upon the propitiation of the Vidyā for half a thousand years,
he first performed the recitation of the Vāṇa mantra to the extent of one hundred thousand syllables.
The oblation was performed with ten parts of flowers from those *parijātaka* trees;
the sacrificial offering, mixed with ghee and honey, was poured into the fire.

Furthermore, O Goddess, if one performs the same rite for the second [syllable] as well, to the extent of one hundred thousand recitations of its phonemes, that too will be recited; of this there is no doubt.
Milk mixed with *aśoka* flowers is offered as a *homa* for him;
and the recitation (*jāpya*) of the third [mantra] is performed to the extent of four hundred thousand times.
An oblation mixed with ghee offered with red *karavīra* flowers,
