Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Śāla," in the *Śrīkubjikāmata*.
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, you who bestow grace upon the worlds!"
O Lord, by your grace, the meaning of the scriptures has been heard by me in detail.
Now I desire to hear the supreme sequence of Bhairavī, beginning from the blink of an eye and extending to the measure of time known as nimeṣa and muhūrta,
in the form of kalās, kāṣṭhās, and so forth.
When the word *pakṣa* was formed there through the conjunction of the Kali and Dvāpara ages,
O Goddess, other [names] also arose, such as Śukti, Īhā, and Sura.
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine;
ten, eleven, twelve, thirty, fourteen, and fifteen.
Seven thousand, ten thousand, thirty thousand,
fifty thousand, one hundred thousand, four, five, and five [thousand].
O Lord of Gods, by means of millions of divisions, she clearly brings forth that entire infinite triple-ocean, permeated with both theoretical knowledge (jñāna) and realized wisdom (vijñāna).
The ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), and likewise worship (pūjā) performed with the Vakrā bestow the accomplishment of all aims;
from Brahmā down to the very last, the universe is pervaded by the splendor of the Goddess.
"Thus, O Lord of the Gods, O Master, tell me all this in detail.
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Goddess, O beautiful lady of the gods, although all this knowledge which you have inquired about is to be kept secret, I shall nevertheless speak it out of affection for you.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Know that the goddess who is called Bhairavī is Garuḍadhvaja;
the goddess who is called Hari is remembered as the god Bhairava.
O Pārvatī, know that Nakulīśī is Śakti; then there is Repha, Ha, and Tu, followed by Vara; then Nāda and Bindu—know me to be composed of these elements.
Its end is vomited forth by the power of vision (dṛg), it is pierced by the bowstring of fire (śikhijyā),
it is known as beginning with Nāda, it is noble (kulīna) at its beginning, and it is adorned by all the vowels (sarveḍa).
O lady of excellent complexion, this entire sequence of the tradition must be understood;
and having worshipped the deity according to the previous rule, one should likewise worship the lineage succession.
The two feet are in the Viśvamālā, and the name Dhruva is established there;
O Goddess, the seed-syllable of the Goddess is then in the midst of the many for those who are departing.
Having extracted two from the three places, they are pierced by Āghaura and Utta;
Dīpanī and Śūladaṇḍa are pierced by Navādya and Krūra.
Furthermore, the wise one should fashion Mahākāla as the second [deity], seated upon a heap of bones, with Pūtanā holding a trident and staff at his feet.
Furthermore, O Goddess, in the northern region of Niṣadha, on Mount Mandara, the fourth [letter] is mixed with a cruel [element]; of this there is no doubt.
But the third, O Queen of the Gods, is adorned with the fields beginning with Navā;
then, O Goddess, Saṃhārikā is situated between the two and one.
The eleventh [letter], however, pierced by the *dīpanī* and having a cruel head, is not of the same color; furthermore, O Goddess, when endowed with its qualities, it becomes solitary (*kevala*).
And in the center, one should worship Mahākāla with his head split by the Gāyatrī;
Guṇeṃta and the goddess Nādinī, and Ananta on Gandhamādana.
Having extracted that [syllable] along with the *valla* and others, and [placing] only the center of the self (*ātman*),
the great goddess Nārāyaṇī is adorned by Ananta.
Furthermore, O Goddess, Vāyuvegā shall restore the end of Caṇḍikā;
furthermore, that kingdom which is spoken of throughout the three worlds as belonging to Gaurī shall be restored.
Though mute, one may become a lord of speech; though devoid of vows, one may become a lord of wealth;
through coolness one becomes equal to the moon, and through splendor, equal to the radiance of the sun.
In the presence of the Guru, one succeeds by these very [mantras] alone; there is no doubt in this.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with diligence, for it is supreme and brings about all accomplishments.
O Maheśānī, at the end of the speech [mantra], place the seed-syllable of the Goddess on the eastern petal;
having made the firebrand (ulka) possess the luster of the moon, one should place the heart-mantra of Bhairavī in the heart.
O Goddess, [the mantra] is Kāma; likewise, O Goddess, it is Maholka;
again, Dharā, Tripada, Prokṣa, Bhairavī, Hṛdaya, and Śiva.
The goddess Bhairavī likewise beholds the meteor (ulkā) divided by the third [vowel];
one should apply the first seed-syllable "Devī" in the same manner.
O Great Goddess, one should place the seed-syllable of desire and the thousand-spoked wheel facing forward;
furthermore, one should apply the rising [mantras] as before.
O Dear One, one should fashion the Great Wheel which is pierced on all sides by Tripurā;
the Heart, pierced by Vāstu, should be arranged ending with Caṇḍikā.
Then, while applying the supreme seed-syllable of Caṇḍikā to the mouth,
one should subsequently utter speech, desire, and the third syllable again and again.
Viṣṇu is assigned to Sadāśiva, Rudra to Brahmā, and then Aravi;
O Goddess, O beloved, listen now to the yoga of the assignment of the eight groups of eight.
In the middle of the seat, you go; pierce it with the *kulī* staff.
One should cause the eight and so forth, as well as the long and so forth, to be pierced at the head.
Likewise, the goddess Brahmāṇī is with Akrūra and Asitāpnu;
Māheśī is at the division of the thighs, and Kaumārī is joined with Candra.
Vaiṣṇavī is pierced by Krodha; Vārāhī is Unmattabhairavī;
Indrāṇī is known as Sakapālā, together with Candrikā and Bhīṣaṇa.
One should indeed fashion the Mahālakṣmī-yāmala through the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra);
likewise, the seed-syllables are both short and long through the union of the Mothers and Bhairava.
O Goddess, [one should worship] Keśava first, Nārāyaṇa immediately after,
then Mādhava, Govinda, and Madhusūdana as well.
One should know that Trivikrama, Kubjāṅgavarasambhairavī,
and Vāsudevasaṃbhinnā exist in exactly this same manner at the end of the Viṃśati.
One should perform this practice with the middle of the back, the right arm, the sides, and the supports for the sides, without touching the neck or the head.
And likewise, one should worship the eight-faced and eight-armed Bhairava,
preceded by the goddess Mātṛkā according to the sequence of their previous births.
Having offered the eightfold earth and the eight parts of the region as oblations, one should then offer the eight seed-syllables;
by merely performing this placement (*nyāsa*) here, the destruction of all sins occurs.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Prīti, Rati, Kānti, and Kaṃ—
by performing the ritual placement (nyāsa) of these alone here, the destruction of all sins shall occur.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Prīti, Rati, Kānti, Satī, Jayā, Maṅgalā, and Sarvapūrvā; [these names] end with Keśava as before.
Then, O Goddess of Gods, one should prepare a mandala measuring one cubit,
using white pigments, saffron, vermilion, and musk.
Having smeared a seat or a cloth made of gold, silver, or copper, he,
being composed, should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the entire Wheel of Delusion (mohana-cakra) there.
One should establish Śiva and Śakti, the Lord of Devas, as being of the nature of mutual churning,
so that the central thread may form the central wheel.
Having pierced through the *prāgyoni* equally, one should draw the *śakti* with its characteristic marks;
one should place the previously mentioned [mantra] before Śiva and Śakti, and the seven oceans outside.
Then, by way of encircling, one should surround the tip with fire;
having rotated it, one should then [draw] an eight-spoked wheel and the lunar disc according to the verbal instruction.
One should draw a circle with a broken rim and a protruding front;
in its center, one should place the seed-syllable of Maheśānī, and the entire [mantra] outside.
The great seed-mantra is surrounded by the *saṃvarta* [syllable] conjoined with fire;
it is interspersed within the expanse of the *kṣemanta* according to the prescribed rule.
When the *vṛnda* has been asked, there is no doubt that the eight syllables are as before;
one should place the letters beginning with *ṭha*, and at the end, the *vidyā* of Sureśvarī.
In the center of the Praveṭena-saṃbhinnā, one should place the Saṃvartaka [mantra];
in its midst, one should meditate upon Sureśāna together with Bhairavī.
Likewise, speech and hearing have transcended them; they are devoid of the states of being and non-being, free from creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and are the cause of all causes.
These two, beneficial for the sake of the Ardhanārīśvara form, should always be worshipped together;
they are without dispute on the left and right, with the book held in the right and left hands respectively.
[He holds] a crystal rosary fashioned from various jewels;
at the lower left [hand] is the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), and in the [left] hand is a full skull-cup.
With a head adorned with a garland of skulls and decorated with all the ritual ornaments,
always perform the worship of the Goddess according to the method taught by Naya.
O Goddess, all the deities beginning with Brahmā are stationed at the soles of her feet;
likewise, O Goddess, the sages and whatever other classes of beings exist are there as well.
By performing one hundred thousand recitations of Rudra and offering oblations with Svayambhū flowers, the Lord becomes self-manifested;
he becomes restrained in conduct and free from the vision of the fettered (paśu).
The sin committed throughout all lifetimes shall be destroyed by this extraction;
what is the use of saying more? He accomplishes everything therein.
One should know this regarding the afflicted; it should be given to the learned and not otherwise.
I shall now fully explain the mutually [related] vidyā and mantra, which are very difficult to obtain.
Seated between Ambikā and Bhṛgu, established upon the seat of the trident-staff;
the elemental [syllable] is placed on the head—at the beginning, at the end, and in the middle.
Or one should meditate upon the God thus: holding a noose, a goad, and a lotus, as well as a rosary, a book, and two others—a sugarcane bow and an arrow.
And [one should worship] the Kaumodakī mace and the lotus, adorned with white ornaments,
in the center of the discus, according to the instruction of Sureśānī.
Outside the *suraṃbha*, there is the *prajāgara* and at the end of the *hrāsa* the sixteenth;
the *daṃtapatra* consists of the number of *tattvas*, and the *pārthiva* is joined with the wheel.
Outside of that is the maṇḍala, adorned with the doors according to the ritual rules;
for this, O Sovereign of the Gods, is the wheel consisting of eight enclosures.
The Praṇava is placed in the middle, encapsulated by the Śrībīja;
the mantras of the six spokes and the pairs of lords of the eight spokes [are likewise arranged].
One should place Manmatha on the twelve-spoked [wheel], and the twelve Asuras along with the Bindu;
having placed Caṇḍikā on the sixteen-spoked [wheel], one should write the mantra on the twenty-four-spoked [wheel].
In the thirty-second [square], one should draw the letters of the alphabet, the Vajra, and the Māhendra [weapon];
and in the Vāruṇa [square], one should likewise encircle the Vāruṇa [weapon] with the Śakti and the Aṅkuśa.
As before, one should worship the goddess Vāgurī,
Madanāvatī, the goddess Nārāyaṇī, Ramā, Yāminī, and likewise Nādinī.
Then one should worship Yamajihvā, the irreproachable Great Goddess;
O Maheśānī, her seed-syllable is adorned with the eight long vowels.
They hold a rosary, a book, a noose, a goad, and display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; numbering as many as the vajras [twenty-four], they are mature and bestow all desired aims.
O Goddess, standing before that fire, having taken up a rosary of beads adorned with the initial syllable *krā*, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand and one hundred and eight times.
Alternatively, for one desiring liberation, the Bahvṛca should perform [the rite] with fifty [beads] made of pearls and other gems; for nourishment, twenty-seven.

Thirty *dhanas* are for prosperity (*saṃpatti*), fifteen for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), fifteen are to be known for pacifying rites (*śāntika*), and [fifteen] for the attainment of wealth (*arthalābha*) in the *nāmika* [rite].
Through these, characterized by one hundred thousand recitations, all accomplishments shall arise in the little finger.
[The shapes are] a square, resembling a womb (triangle), a triangle, and a beautiful circle.
Other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should also be constructed, O Supreme Goddess;
three mudrās are prescribed for the fire-oblation (homa): the deer, the swan, and the sow.
A fire offering (homa) that is devoid of the mudrās shall be fruitless.
[The mudrā is formed by] contracting the fingers like a sow, with the little finger joined to the swan (haṃsī).

The three mudrās described [using] the little finger and the index finger of the deer-maiden (mṛgī) are: the eṇī, the śūkarī, the goddess (devī), the knotted (grathinī), and the fist (muṣṭi). The arjinī [is also mentioned].
In rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), it should be the *śūkarī* [mudrā], while in other rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth,
one should proceed starting from the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) in a clockwise direction.
O Goddess, [if performed] up to the ring finger, that [merit] becomes multiplied ten million times.
[The fruits of recitation using] the *kamalākṣa*, *rudrākṣa*, *palāśa*, and *japā* beads are like an ocean.
Or one should offer honey mixed with bees into the fire during the Phalgunī asterism;
thus, being well-restrained, one should commence this worship of the Lord of Gods for three years.
He shall become equal to Śrīyādhanada in speech and a master of eloquence like Vāgīśvara;
and in fame he shall be equal to Viṣṇu, his mind fixed on attaining heaven.
What is the use of saying more? This Maheśvara is to be saluted by me.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Determination of Bhairavī," in the Kubjikāmata.
The illustrious Goddess said:
Through her, who is the form of the grace of the Knower and whose nature is eternal bliss, one attains dharma, kāma, and artha, as well as absolute liberation (kaivalya).
He created everything clearly, including all things distinguished by minuteness, grossness, and so forth;
he who was the former immortal god, along with Agastya and other great ascetics.
That which the wise constantly cultivate through various diverse means,
and which is called Brahman because it destroys [suffering] by virtue of its abundance of letters, sciences, and meanings.
And because it is equal to both knowledge and Brahman, it is remembered as Brahmavidyā;
therefore, [one should worship] the Goddess, the supreme Vidyā, who is the perfection of all auspiciousness.
O Supreme Auspicious One, no one else in the three worlds knows Your end,
as declared in the *Tāmarādi-mahātantra* and through the traditional teachings (*āmnāya*) concerning Vāmana and others.
And it has been said by you that not everything is known even through the process of proof;
therefore, please explain in brief the threefold Veda, together with its limbs and sub-limbs.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! This is indeed extremely profound.
O Goddess, it exists in each of the *Yāmalas* to the extent of ninety million verses.
Thus, O Kubjikā, the five have been declared in detail.
Listen here also, O Goddess of Gods, to how they were previously extracted by me.
In the Jayadratha and Yamala scriptures, there are three *kīlas* for the *Pañcakīlī*;
in the Rājarājeśvara and Skandayāmala, there are five and six *kīlas* respectively.
By those who know the piercing of time (kālavedha), beings are bound and yet become stainless;
in various tantras, the Great Vidyās have been revealed as being devoid of life (jīvahīna).
O fair lady, those who cause obstacles do not succeed when they are pinned down after having previously given their pledge for the worship of the Śrīkramāvali.
The family preceptor, well-endowed, learned in the scriptures, and possessing all auspicious marks,
[performs] the rites of perfume, flowers, excellent incense, lamps, and food offerings.
The practice is perfected by all [means], free from the view of a sacrificial animal,
even with a thousand horse-loads or hundreds of loads of gold.
I am not satiated, O Great Goddess; the five stakes have been proclaimed. They are as follows: death, ignorance, poverty, and the loss of one's lineage.

O Goddess, you who abide in the midst of the moon, endowed with compassion and the power of illumination— may you, in your form as Aghorā, listen to me as I seek to follow that which is to be realized.
Then, that which stands at the end of the five [vowels] should again be joined with the subtle [consonant] on Mount Mandara;
likewise, it should be joined with the end of the qualities (guṇa), followed by the syllable *phaṭ* and the *dīpanī*.

Having joined the Mātṛkā-mantra— which begins with *rū*, consists of a combination of phonemes, ends with *caru*, has a *bindu* at its head, and concludes with the feet of Viṣṇu— one attains all-encompassing perfection.
O Goddess Caṇḍikārākumāri, you who are eternally and perpetually delighted;
by means of the awakening through the fourth case-ending, there is indeed only the seed-syllable of Śakti.
Karālikā and Pūtanā shall become the station of the Kula-cakra;
these are the female leaders (nāyikās), namely the Blessed Lady Caṇḍā and Karālinī.
O Maheśvarī, on the peak of fragrance is Ananta and Mālinī; O Ambikā, that which is the excellent and long royal [state] is likewise distinguished by mortals.
That same [seed-syllable] joined with the sixth vowel is indeed Caṇḍikā;
likewise, that same [syllable] as Caṇḍā, when placed at the beginning of the lion [mantra], is the goad that bestows the power of desire.
And Pāvanī, Śūladaṇḍā, Bhe, Madhyamā,
Haṃsinī, Nirvāraṇā, and Daruṇā [are worshipped] with Mandara.
Kāntā, Śāntā, and Saṃvalantī;
Pūrapraśamanī, Śakti, Krodhā, and Pūtanā—these are the eight swift goddesses arising from the afflictions.
In the hell between Dahanīkā and Tṛmā are the Pūtanās;
there resides the power of the entire ocean, Brahmā, and the Lord of Śacī.
The first goddess of Śakra is joined with the house and the couch;
indeed, she holds only the impure trident and likewise the staff.
O Goddess, you who are without deer, who are weak, who are a devourer, and who are joined with Time;
you who are joined with your own enemy, the serpent, and who repeatedly pierce and cut through the unborn.
One should mutter the mantra "asinā taṃ japa" and likewise "chedayeti";
[therein reside] Bhairava, the goddess Bhairavī, and Cāmuṇḍā joined with Caṇḍa.
O Goddess, you who are the purifier and joined with the trident-dwelling, you accomplish Mahākāla and Mahākālī, as well as all desires— this pair of siddhis.
In the compassionate Blessed One, it is Kālahā; furthermore, in Bhairava, it is Rūpadhāriṇī; O Goddess of the gods, in Tridaśa, it is Vāruṇī.
The *śūla*, *daṇḍa*, and *aguṇa* [weapons] are for you according to the sequence of mantras;
the mantra, however, is "O Goddess Mother," ending with "Rudra" in the temple.
Residing in Bhujangabhairava, situated in the midst of the serpent Rādhā and others, that which is called "Japa" is within the Bindu; the wise know it to be pure, ending with the Guṇas.
O affectionate Goddess of the lords of gods, Mahākālī,
before her one should extract the syllable situated between the Rudra (R), Agni (Ra), Indu (I), and Bilva (Va).
The seed-syllables extracted at the beginning of the Vidyā are *pra*, *sīda*, *mada*, *na*, and *arī*.
O Goddess of gods, O beloved daughter of the Guru, make [the disciple's] evil intellect [submissive] to the Cakra.
Having joined the maiden, who is adorned with the goad, place Ambikā in the center; [the mantra is] "Ṣaṣṭha-śūlaṃ sa-padma phaṭ."
Then, from the *arghya* [offering] at the *tapanī*, there arose the imperishable refuge of all beings;
O Goddess of Gods, she who transcends the world has emerged as the granter of all desires.
This goddess Pratyaṅgirā is by name the Enchantress of the Three Worlds;
by means of this vidyā, O Janārdana, she [is the sovereign] of the three worlds.
This goddess, who consists of the universe, effects the creation and maintenance of the world;
she is the sovereign science, the great goddess, the supreme secret, and the most ancient.
The best of kings, she who purifies even the purifiers for a month,
[is present] in forest fires, great conflagrations, and amidst serpents, fire, and other dangers.
O Goddess, by means of this sādhana beginning with Yama and so forth, one attains victory in battle, becomes a sovereign lord of the earth, and acquires the eightfold qualities such as aṇimā.
Añjanā, Grasakalpā, and other mantras with their respective mudrās;
Rūpabījā, Kṛśānī, and others headed by Tapanī as well.
Such is the power of the Goddess; indeed, those accomplishments (siddhis) are attained.
O Goddess, one should bestow the twenty-two-syllable mantra at the end of the kalpa.
Having first performed the ritual at the edge of the body, one should write two seed-syllables upon the body;
then, when the autumn season has arrived, one should remain without food and with senses subdued.
Every day, as previously described, one thousand [offerings] should be made day after day;
and when the nine nights have arrived, they should be performed with extensive displays according to one's means.
By propitiating the Supreme Goddess, he shall become dear even to the gods;
for that reason, I too have been slain by him, and thus I dwell in eternal happiness.
O Goddess, in former times, Daśagrīva was overcome by pride despite my grace;
his eldest brother, however, who was highly fortunate and my friend, was defeated.
Having thus abandoned both his wealth and his kingdom, which were inferior to those of the virtuous,
that lord of wealth approached him with a serene mind and sought refuge.
By my command, he became so fortunate that Daśagrīva,
having conquered his senses, conquered the ten worlds.
Jayadratha, Kāmadeva, Brahmā, Vinatā, the Lord,
that Vaikuṇṭha, Duścarya, and others as well— [all these are] Vādirāja.
O beloved, let these always carry out the command of the Great Goddess,
having first performed the ritual of the Goddess Mātṛkā in the sequence beginning with *na* and ending with *pha*.
Śrīkaṇṭha, the goddess Nādinī, and she who is known as Ādi—these possess the primordial sound (nāda).
Both Parānātha and Arvā are established in the station of the Pādukā.
Then the Supreme Self [unites] with Ambikā;
thereafter, O Queen of the Gods, that which is distinct from Ka and the others is indeed the second deity.
One should employ Jāpinī, Śūladaṇḍa, Mahākāla, and Haṃsinī;
then, one should apply her again as Dīrghasaṃbhinnā throughout all [the rites].
O Pārvatī, he who [meditates upon] the Omniscient One, inseparable from the Heart,
and the Goddess within the lotus of Nirvāṇa as being fully satisfied, shall become Śiva.
The Vāruṇī is subtle and intermingled; it is white, black, and moving toward its end.
The Pāvanī is mixed with floating matter, and again, the Pāvanī is in Naraka.
The corpse Kālabhairava is joined with the illuminator Navādi;
the great goddess Nārāyaṇī is conjoined with Sūkṣma on Mount Mandara.
One should visualize the fourth [syllable] as the goddess and the seed-syllable for awakening;
having extracted the seed-syllable of the goddess, one should place the wrathful one within the center of the *bilva* fruit.
Then, O Maheśānī, from the hundred afflicted petals,
the Great Goddess Haritā becomes independent, with her petals as a protective covering.
Huṃ, the purifying goddess Gurvā; Dhātrīśa with the long bindu;
Bhīṣaṇī conjoined with Raṃ; the lotus (Aṃ) pierced by Sūkṣma (Ha).
Furthermore, Śrīkaṇṭha, whose power had been eclipsed, [acted] with the *taraṇābhi* [mantra],
having extracted the entire *pada*, including the phrase "avipraśamanī."
Having sprinkled the divine body with the weapon-mantra *phaṭ*, [one should worship] the serpent, the spear, and the sword;
the lineage of the gurus' sandals should be known through oral instruction.
O Goddess of the Suras, one should perform the placement of the feet with the various distinctions of phonemes and other placements as well,
which have issued from the mouth of the Guru.
She has many faces and eyes, and many lotus-like hands;
she possesses many feet and is adorned with many eyes.
Then, with a steady inner self, one should meditate upon that Goddess of gods, who is radiant with many ornaments and whose hair on the crown of her head is dark blue.
Resplendent like the rising sun, crowded with many rays,
resembling the bandhūka flower, and comparable to vermilion.
She has five faces and ten arms, with full and elevated breasts;
she is adorned with all ornaments and endowed with all auspicious marks.
She has three eyes and five faces, is gentle, with loose hair and the luster of snow;
she is the Great Goddess Siddhalakṣmī, the bestower of spiritual perfection and liberation.
To the eternally established Yogeshi, the Great Goddess of Kula and Akula,
who holds a rosary, a skull-cup, and is endowed with a sword.

The goddess, standing upon a corpse, holds a shaven head and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) in her hands, while her other hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she also bears a noose and a sprout.
One should arrange these two blades of kuśa grass with the syllables following the order of recitation;
then, one should again place the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu on the tip of the petal in due order.
Endowed with five petals, surrounded by seven lines,
marked with eighteen upper lines, it is the supreme *bhūtirāgraha*.
One should worship the three-crested [form] at the tip of the crest of the mandala of Indra;
starting from the center upon the arrow-petals, extending as far as the outer compartments.

One should place the *kaṇṭaka* and other [syllables] of the Vidyā, starting from the young woman (the letter *ya*) and proceeding in sequence through sixteen [positions]. Within those sixteen squares, together with the one situated in the middle of the *mājīna*, there are the tips of the arrows (*śarapatra*), which are like the tips of the leaves of the *rāṣṭrasapa* tree.
O Great Goddess, it has sixteen spokes and is adorned by thirty-two groups.
In the Brahma [mandala], it is preceded by sixty-four [squares], endowed with three subsequent lines,

Ānanda and Nivṛtti; the goddess Kalā again and again;

O Maheśānī, this seed-syllable is everywhere invincible;

To Varada, Virūpākṣī; to Vareṇya, Subhadrā;

To Aghora, who is most formidable, and to Kumāra, by the supreme command;

The goddess Ādityayoginī, likewise Śrīmahāyoginī,

Navabhojanī, Phaṭkārī, and Vīrabhadrāntimukhyakā;

Śakrandanāgni, Parama, Pitṛ, Niśācara, Puretara, Śākhāgra, Jñānapadma, and Cakrin.

Krodhinī and Stambhinī, as well as Śaṅkhadhāriṇī and Munidhī; and Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Durgā, and Sarasvatī.

Atri, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, Bhṛgu, Gautama, and Kaśyapa.

O Sovereign of the Gods, having meditated upon this Śivā, who holds a trident joined with a severed head and is adorned with a garland of heads, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
With rice grains, white lotuses, parched grain, and those born of filaments—

Having raised up Karālikā, the supreme self-natured Great Goddess, who is seated upon a serpent-throne and adorned by Rudra;

One should place [the mantras] on the crown of the head, between the eyebrows, in the eyes, in the two ears, in the nostrils, in the mouth, in the throat, at the base of the arms, in the elbows, and in the heart.

One should recite [the mantra] while extending the feet, avoiding the utkaṭāsana posture,
or likewise when facing west, on a road, or in the presence of low-born persons.
One should not recite [the mantra] on barren ground, nor on a bedstead, nor in the middle of a palace;
nor where there are donkeys, cats, embers, or camels, nor in dust.
If one should touch the water from bathing cloths that has come into contact with hair, banners, or nails— water which brings misfortune to men and is impure— [it must be purified].
Even when these occur, one should look at the sun or fire;
having sipped water (ācamana), one should recite the Vājas, or else perform the remaining rite by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Contentment, looking at the sun, being pierced by a stake, having disheveled hair, being surrounded by attendants, impurity, being forbidden, the nine types of verbal confusion,
anger, intoxication, hunger, drowsiness, spitting, and yawning.
The seed-syllable of Haṃsavāgeśvarī is to be used as an enclosure (saṃpuṭa) everywhere here;
having placed it in the middle of the altar, the *śaṅku* (sacrificial peg) is the support therein.
From the initial application of the cord at the meeting point of the peg and the cord,
one should successively lay down the cord situated from east to west, and likewise from south to north.
Having established the center of the circle, one should mark the corner-fish;
by means of the method of laying down six lines, that thread is based upon the four corners.
There, one should strike out the lines twenty-eight times;
the lines running eastward and northward should be measured by the span of a thumb.
One should certainly place seven hundred and twenty-nine cells situated within the circle of Indra, with two rows on the outside.
The door-ornament and its subsidiary ornament consist of four rows and four sets;
there should also be a set of four on both sides of the great pathway.
In the center of that, extending to the edge of the upavīthi, two rows are prescribed;
in the middle of those, by means of fifteen rows, the lotus is formed.
This is declared to be the nine-petaled lotus, adorned with nine pathways;
each door is radiant with eight doors, consisting of six squares each.
With four [squares] and four [squares], it is adorned with primary beauties (śobhā) and secondary beauties (upaśobhā);
with six squares at each corner, it takes the form of two rows.
Having described the path by this very means, one should draw the outer circle;
then, having repeatedly divided it into four large sections, one should delineate it.
The first is the field of the pericarp; the second is the beauty of the filaments;
the third should be the junctions of the petals; and the fourth consists of the petals themselves.
There, by means of the application of eight lines, one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus;
in all four corners, one should draw eight vajras.
This ninefold seat (navapīṭha) of all the Mothers, as well as of Devabhadrā and Gaṇeśa,
is proclaimed to produce immediate conviction.
The lines of those lotuses situated in the wind [direction] should be sky-lines;
having thus drawn them with a leaf, one should fill the auspicious [design] with colored powder.
One should fill the pericarp with yellow color, all the lines with white,
the exterior with red and yellow, and the filaments with white.
One should color the petals with red and dark green;
however, the area outside the lotus, which is the field (kṣetra), one should fill with black.
One should fill the doors with white color for beauty, and the secondary ornaments (upaśobhā) with red;
one should fill the corners with dark blue.
One should adorn the pathway with offerings that are both firm and moving;
one should fill the eastern quarter with yellow-colored powder.
One should fill it with black-colored powder and finally with white;
thus is described the mandala that has come down through the sequence of all the Āgamas.
In the maṇḍala, the Great Goddess should worship all the deities;
when she is worshipped, all [the deities] are worshipped by the practitioner.
One should perform the consecration that has come down through the lineage of succession;
one should perform that consecration until the state of realization is attained.
But the great queen, by the power of the Guru’s command,
shall proceed from one flower to another, like a bee greedy for honey.
Likewise, a disciple greedy for knowledge may go to another teacher;
O beloved, having obtained a teacher devoid of power, how can there be liberation for the disciple?
When the root of a tree has been severed, from where can flowers, fruits, and the like arise?
[Likewise, what arises] from the single or multiple distinct vessels and other objects born from the letter *ma*?
O Goddess, without the letter *ma*, they do not attain satisfaction in due order;
one should first employ the two joined together in the *kuṇḍa*.
Then, having sprinkled water everywhere and satisfied the lineage (kulakrama),
one should devotedly satisfy Bhairava and Bhairavī, the destroyer of worldly existence.
O Goddess, assuming that very form oneself with effort,
and realizing "I am Bhairava," one should then form the mudrā with the right hand.
Having performed the recitation on the left, perform the mantra whose nature is Śiva;
there, having paid homage according to the prescribed rite, [worship] the Cakramelāpaka.
O Goddess, bathe the circle of Yoginīs; act so that victory may be achieved.
O Goddess, within twelve years, one shall always attain perfection.
Thus has this entire procedure, honored by the gods, been declared;
it is unattainable by those devoid of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), even for the most excellent of teachers.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of Bhairavī," in the *Nava-koṭi-saṃhitā* according to the *Śrī-kubjikāmata*, consisting of eighty-four thousand verses.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O lady of excellent complexion, those previously mentioned [syllables] are divided into single and multiple forms;
through repeated practice, one should rely upon the initial syllables up to ten million.
The *saṃhitā*, the *adhyāya*, and the *kalpa*— this is said to be the threefold *tantra*.
O Goddess, the *saṃhitā* is considered the best, while the *adhyāya* is likewise remembered as middling.

If one who possesses the name "Kalpa" should forget the *saṃhitā* for a *kalpa*, then meditation (*dhyāna*) is prescribed; however, the *saṃhitā* is established through ritual installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).
O Goddess, in this chapter, regarding worship, ritual procedure, mantra recitation, and so forth,
I shall specifically describe their merits and defects.
One should avoid the *piṇḍa* consisting of groups and letters, which is natural and born of the gods, as well as those nine [syllables] interspersed with the *praṇava* that bring about misfortune.
The Vārāha, Nṛsiṃha, and Akṣaya temples, as well as the Dhruva temple, are endowed with structural supports (bhāra) in sequence— at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end.
Females, males, and neuters are to be known; those ending in *vauṣaṭ* are considered females, those ending in *ṣaṭ phaṭ* are males, and those consisting of three principles (*tritattva*) are neuters.
The Mātṛkā is the supreme mother of all sciences and mantras;
therein one should perform the extraction (uddhāra), by which a person is liberated from all obstacles.
One should extract the life-force (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa) from the center of Kuhū;
O Goddess, that which is the color of the ear-ornament in the temple of Kailāsa—
Then, the third letter situated below that is Caṇḍanāyaka;
it is in the left foot of Mālinī and in the temple arising from the crest (śikhā).
One should worship the goddess Bhujangabhairavī in the left temple,
and the seed-syllable given by Śiva, which is Akṛūra and possesses the brilliance of the fire of destruction.
O Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, by the recitation and fire-offering of this [mantra],
there is no doubt that even the Siddhas, the gods, and those whose wealth is austerity will be overcome.
O Goddess, what more can I tell you regarding the power of Aghora?
By the power of its seed-syllable, the majestic Padmanābha [attained his state].
With the *sutī* and *sutī* [mantras], one should perform and apply the *prāṇāyāma*.
Thereafter, O beautiful one, I shall explain the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of this Aghora [mantra].
First, however, Viśvamālā is in the infinite Gandhamādana;
Śivā is in Akrūrasambhinna; and [Viśvayogeśvarī] is in Niṣadhālaya in the north.
Having considered the goddess Māyā as the end of Dhruva and the head of Krūra,
they know the second and the third to be Ananta, which is the first.
O Goddess of the gods, these are the seeds in the three places at the head of Ghorā;
they are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and they are Will, Knowledge, and Action.
Having thus applied that according to the oral instruction,
one should recite the *mālinī* mantra which resides within the center of one's own heart, moving subtly within the *maṇḍala*.
O Goddess, one should place Jhaṇṭīśa upon the head in the temple of Kailāsa;
furthermore, O Maheśānī, that [mantra] ending with "hūṃ" becomes the head.
Karālī is preceded by the three Ṛks; Vajriṇī is situated in the middle.
Having extracted Krodharudra, it is adorned with Jhaṃṭīśa.
Having extracted the seed-syllable from the three locations— the first and the middle one, O Goddess, situated within the cruel [syllable] Ananta— resting upon Niṣadha as the triple-formed [seed].
And one should cause Prajñā, situated in the left ear and established in the region of the cheek,
to bestow the five groups of letters before them.
Then, the syllables of the previously mentioned Vidyā are known as the thirty-three [deities];
Māninī, with two eyes, is in the temple of the Mothers at Dāruka.
O Goddess, there are two dots on the head and Caṇḍīśa in the left abode;
in the southeast, there are four syllables in the sequence previously mentioned.
O Goddess, one should place the syllable situated on the right knee at the beginning of the worlds upon the head;
below that, O Madanī, one should place the *prāṇa* and the *jīva*.
That which is the manifestation is inseparable from that; now hear the second [part] from him:
O Goddess, one should place the two initial seed-syllables at the head, ending with Vāmā.
O Goddess, having again written the description of the qualities and the three seed-syllables as before, Śrīkaṇṭha is established here in the temple of Kailāsa.
And make the eleventh [verse] adorned with the Gāyatrī;
O Goddess, in the group of nine, make it adorned with the Lamp and then with Īśa.
O Great Goddess, once again, one should extract those two syllables before that;
furthermore, one should extract another pair of syllables according to the oral instruction.

O Goddess, that which is divided by infinite-infinite [repetitions], situated between the letters *ṭha* and *ṭha*, arises as the Single Eye (*ekanetra*) at its forefront, differentiated by the infinite [vowels] through the method of illumination (*dīpanī*).
Having again written the letter *A* with the tip of the tongue standing upwards, one should place it upon the head;
likewise, one should do the same for the letter *Krodha* (Ra) together with *Kāntaka* (Sa).
Furthermore, O Lord of Aśvadeva, [one should contemplate] the subtle Vāruṇa [mantra] as differentiated;
then, amidst the sages, one should proceed from the left [side], beginning with Āmuḍā, up to the head.
Thus, this Great Vidyā is the goddess who bestows success upon the head;
O Goddess, she places Brahmā at her feet and Viṣṇu in the secret region.
One should likewise place Rudra in the stomach and Īśvara in the throat;
one should place Śiva between the eyebrows, and above that, the successive [deities].
O Goddess, Dviraṇḍabhairava alone is situated in the midst of the sages;
within the body of Śivā, one should place Cakrin on the left and in the center.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the intermediate space between the thighs and the middle part above Mount Meru, and upon its summit, one should duly install the goddess Kalā.
One should employ [the mantra] thus everywhere: "O Saṃdhyā, Caṇḍā, Ambā, Nityā, Klinnā, Dureśvarī, Raktā, Ghorā, and Viśālākṣī."
The two vidyās, Bhadra and Ādyantā, are [placed] at the end and the beginning, and in the middle;
likewise, by the transposition of the seed-syllables, they are at the beginning of the liquor, and at the beginning, middle, and end.
One should first delight in the five lutes, starting from the infinite within the self, then at the end, and finally that which is non-self at the very end, proceeding in reverse order.
O Goddess, one should place the *māninīgrathana* at the end of the *guṇa*,
followed by the *lokānta* at the head, and again four [syllables] at the front.
One should place Padmodbhava, Hasa, Ananta, Lokādi, and Mastaka;
having placed Graha in front, one becomes fourfold in the fourth [case].

Māyādevī is threefold; elsewhere it is ninefold, consisting of the nine-fold self (navātmaka). O Sovereign of the Gods, having likewise extracted [the mantra] from that [source], ending with Krūrmeśa.
First, the letters of the Kṛta [age], Nakulīśa joined with Dīpana,
the middle of Bhāga, Krodhīśa, and Kāla situated in the middle of Kṛta.
One should go to the infinite Peak of Fragrance (Gandhaśikhara) and the center born of the lotus;
one should perform the placement upon the heart through the union of the five seed-syllables.
Having extracted Karālikā from Dhruva and the others, perform the placement (nyāsa);
having placed Pūtanā in front, [place] Mudrīśa born of Kātaka and Oha.

One should know that Atrīśa is situated on Mount Mandara, born subtly from the crown of Pāvanī; and by the Lotus-born One, he was established at the beginning of the temple for the destruction of sins.
One should perform the Śivanyāsa in front of that virtuous person;
having split the serpent in two with the Vajra [mudrā], one should place it upon his head.
O Goddess, one should draw the terrifying Bhujaṅga alone in front;
one should install Śikhādūtī upon the crest, of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, one should place the armor (kavaca) of the messenger with the endings of the elemental pairs;
and that seed-syllable which begins with the letter 'lo' resides in the abode of the elements.
Having taken up that alone, one should place it before oneself;
having raised the Raktabhairava [mudrā] with the middle finger of the left hand.
O Goddess, that imperishable syllable which is the beginning of the Vedas stands before Amarīśa; it resides within the heart of Pāvanī, stationed in the center of the yantra.
O Goddess, one should cause it to be placed upon the tip of the nose and then upon the head;
one should assign Rudra, Āditya, and Padmayoni to the northwest.
Above [the head], one should place the four syllables, the letter *ka*, the *prāṇa* (the letter *ha*), and the *bindu*;
having uttered the *tārikā* as the cause, one should install it with the gaze of the eye.
One should cause the heart-center of Karālī, pierced by the descent [of the power], to bestow [the fruit];
having raised Krodhabhairava, one should place Umākānta before him.
O Goddess, in the temple that is the beginning of the worlds, one should first [worship] Bindubhairava;
then, O Mistress, one should extract that weapon along with the infinite Lord Cakrin.
In every case, these are applied as the life-force of the vidyā, without a doubt;
[one should perform] the placement on the face as before, and likewise the vidyā of the Goddess of the Asuras.
The ritual placement of the *kalās* (syllables) should be performed from the tip of the crest-lock down to the feet:
*cā*, *uṃ*, *daitye*, *bhagavatiṃgya*, *kuleśvarīṃ*, *krīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hūṃ*, *hūṃ*, *āṃ*, *kṣīṃ*, *haṃ*,
*kṣeṃ*, *hauṃ*, *uṃ*, *iṃ*, *ṇa*, *na*, *mekṣaḥ*, *śvaṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *prauṃ*, *prīṃ*, *tyaghorāmukhi*, *muktikā*.
O Aghorī, O Aghorī, yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ haṃ saṃ kli, O Lokinī, O Mahākili, O Piercer!
In the sixty-four-fold sequence, the Vidyā is to be placed on the head according to the rule;
she is to be known as being at the end of the Kalās, especially during worship.
That Goddess, who is eternal, establishes her presence here in the ocean of the Kula;
the Śaktis take the form of arrows, and the Kuśa grass is bent upon the bows.
The Veṇī, Vajrā, and Viśālākṣā [are formed] by the counter-clockwise rotation;
the Akṣoḍa is at the tip of the crest, while the Vāgbhava is to the west.
One should place Ṛkṣakarṇī in the middle of the crest-lock or at the roots of the crest-locks;
then one should place Kṣaṇadā on the region of the head, and again Ikṣayatā around the binding.
Piṅgākṣī is in the middle of the palate, Kṣayāvatī in the bow (the throat),
Kṣamā at the tip of the right [nostril], and Iḍā is said to be at the tip of the left.
One should place Nīlā in the right eye and Lūpā in the left eye;
one should place Lolā on the right cheek and Lekā on the left.
One should place Laṅkeśvarī on the upper lip, Nālasā on the lower lip,
Vimalā on the right side of the neck, and Ṛteśī on the left side.
Having placed Viśālā at the chin, Tārā at the right ear,
Vaḍavā at the left ear, and Śrītārā at the ears;
One should place Mahākrūra at the region of the throat, Krodhāṅga on the belly and the armpits,
and Bhayānakā in the left armpit, according to the conjunction of the seed-syllables (bījas).
Having placed Sarvajñā and Karālī on the left and right breasts,
one should place Tārakā in the heart and the Ṛgveda in the navel region.
At the end of the channel, that goddess Sārā is at the base of the *liṅga*;
at its tip, she collects the essence from both the right and left [channels].
One should place Śavarī on the heels, Tālajaṅghā on the ankles, Raktākṣī on the anus and the perineum, Bindu who is well-known in the middle of the anus, and Jihvā on the tongue.
One should place Meghanādā on the right ear, Caṇḍā on the middle of the right arm,
and Īśānī on the fingers of the hand.
One should place Kālakaṇṭha on the tips of the nails of the right hand;
one who bestows fresh grace should place [the deity] on the left neck and in the eyes.
O Goddess, one should again place Caṇḍā on the arms, Caṇḍāvatī on the hands and fingers,
and Prapañcā on the nails of the left hand.
One should place Pralāyāntā on both sides of the two cotton-cotton-mouthed [vessels];
Piśācī on the left side and Piśitāśī on the right side.
Lolupā and Ajñeyā are to be known as being on the two breasts;
Vamanā is at the right knee, Tapanī at the right shank, and Vāmanī at the base of the right thigh.
One should place Vikṛtānanā on the fingers of the right hand;
then, O Goddess, one should place Vāyuvegā at the right door.
O Goddess, one should place Vṛhatkukṣi on the sole of the right foot, Vikṛta in the middle of the foot, and Viśvarūpiṇī on the left thigh.
In front of her is Yamajihvā, stationed on the left knee;
Durjarā is on the left calf, and Kāma is at the ankle.
O Goddess of gods, there is no doubt that Yamāntikā resides in the toes of the feet;
Viḍālī is at the gate of Yama, and Vegagā is on the left foot.
O Goddess, one should perform the worship of the letters upon the sole of the left foot.
O Goddess, when the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) has been performed in this manner, one shall become beloved by the *yoginīs*.
O Goddess, she brings about all accomplishments and removes all obstacles from the very beginning;
thus, O Great Lord, this Goddess bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
When worshipped, these grant the practitioner whatever he desires;
O Goddess, one should perform the recitation for all [mantras] according to the daily ritual injunctions.
At the end of the recitation, one should meditate upon the Guru; at the end of the meditation, one should recite again.
When weary from recitation and meditation, one should cause even those present on that day to hear [the teaching].

Without recitation (japa), there is no success; how could [the mantra] be a bestower of fruit? Without meditating, one does not attain liberation, O Goddess; thus, the practice is considered to be threefold.
The Yoginīs stand all around each and every wheel;
they are said to be identical to that [central deity] through meditation, especially in the context of worship.
Through recitation one destroys impurity; through worship she becomes the bestower of enjoyments;
and for embodied beings, O Goddess, she becomes manifest solely through the yoga of meditation.
Whether standing, walking, lying down, or even during sexual intercourse or eating,
the recitation (jāpya) must be performed with diligence, except when using a crucible (mūṣā).
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the venerable Kubjikāmata. || 0 ||
The Goddess said:
"The ancient god Nārāyaṇa is the imperishable lord of the gods;
this secret was indeed commanded by him—thus has it been told by you to me."
In former times, there were highly powerful and arrogant sons of Aditi and asuras in the midst of the city;
tell me everything regarding how their destruction was brought about.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, in former times there were Dānavas who were indeed the destroyers of the worlds;
[so too were] the gods along with the Ṛṣis, the Nāgas, and Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds.
The twelve Ādityas and the fifty Rudras, along with all their qualities,
having reached Viṣṭaraśravas, abide there where he dwells in the great ocean.
Brahmā and the other gods praised him with words of liberation released by Śakra;
then the Blessed Lord, his mind well-pleased by that, spoke.
"O Keśava, I am pleased with this hymn; let a boon be chosen," [said the Lord].
Hearing those words, the gods reported everything exactly as it had occurred.
Therefore, having reached that mountain together with him,
they also offered praise here for that auspicious thing which was desired by us.
Having heard these words, Viṣṇu said, "O Goddess, let the destruction of the Daityas be carried out.
To him she replied, "O sinless one, tell me the means by which this may be done."
"How can those Daityas who are devoted to the worship of the Liṅga be slain?
Having heard this, the enemy of the Daityas said, "Let them be killed by her."
The thirty-two-syllable weapon-mantra of the god called Nārāyaṇa is here the supreme weapon; another great one is Aghora.
O Goddess of gods, I shall relate to you that ancient account just as it occurred to you,
concerning the true nature of the syllables and their wonderful, auspicious ritual application.
For the sake of protecting the worlds, it was spoken by the God of gods;
O Great Goddess, she who is the essence of all beings dwells in the midst of the Viśvadevas.
Having written the one called Kriyā at the end of the left [hand] in front,
and the second and third [syllables] arising from Mahādevī on the left knee;
Then, having gone to Mandara, which stands high above the Rudras, one should offer it upon its summit; there is no doubt that one will go to Ananta.
One should not place a snake-skin before it, nor a rough hide;
one should place the Nārāyaṇī mantra in the left eye, and the syllable *ḍāṃ* in the house of the planets.
One should place the serpent upon its head; there is no doubt that it rests upon a tortoise. The peak is situated on the left arm, and that [peak] arises from the left.
On Mount Mandara, place Sūkṣmarudra, and below him, place Vajriṇī;
having raised up Vinatā and the Earth (Gā), one should draw Kāla below her.
Having extracted Prāṇarudra and Ambikā in the center,
one should write the letter *sa* with its vowel (*ā*) in its half, that [letter] whose abode is Puṣkara.
In the same way, O Goddess of gods, up to the end of the planets (grahānta), where it was previously extracted by me,
one should extract the Vajra-seed (vajrabīja) adorned at the end with the left [vowel] and the final [consonant].
One should draw the goddess Sadyojāta situated in the middle at the front of that [mandala];
Atri, Rudra, and Kāma in the middle; and Jhaṇṭīśa above.
Furthermore, one should cause those others to be given first and before him;
having written the final portion, it should be placed in the peaceful temple.
One should cause [the practitioner] to apply [the mudrā] at the tip of the nose with the secret power (guhyaśakti) and at the region of the head;
the great Rudra named Kāla is established in the middle of the Bha.
Having again written the completed *prāṇa* [syllable], one should place the *śakti* upon the head of the secret [syllable];
O Goddess, the union with its color is in the middle of this, at its tip.
In the middle of the wide space [of the body], one should place the letters beginning with *meṣa* (the signs of the zodiac) and so forth;
then, upon its head, the syllables *sthāṇu*, *rudra*, and so on should be bestowed.
O Goddess, the ninth [syllable] ending with the letter 'gu', adorned at the end of 'rudra' by the letter 'na',
and the group of nine ending with 'moha'— this is Vajriṇī in the temple of Numa.
One should know that [the letter] is situated on Mount Mandara; one should draw the radiance at its tip, and below that, the radiance-born [letter], adorned with the end of Dhruva.
O Goddess, one should place Caṇḍikā in front, adorned with fierce ornaments;
O Goddess, she is red as the blood at the end of a ram, established upon the seat of a lamp.
Having first drawn the boundary of the field adorned with the Gāyatrī,
one should place Atrīśaṅka alone in the middle, situated directly in front.
Taking the end of the sage's name (munigehānta) and placing it before the end of the portion (bhāgānta),
and then adding the end of the Praṇava (praṇavānta) at the end— that is declared to be "tridaśatva."
Having placed [the mantra] ending with Rudra in the heart, and the two heads above that;
O Goddess, one should place the tuft (śikhā) with the Vasus and the armor (tanucchada) with Śakti.
One should perform the placement with the Rudra-mantras; thus, the weapon (astra) is proclaimed.
In this manner, it is performed for the Earth, the Water, the Fire, the Wind, and the Space, as well as for the Self.
O Maheśvarī, one should employ this very [mantra], which lasts until the end of the eons and is adorned with the five notes, by means of ten repetitions.
Beyond that, there are three syllables; in front of that, nine syllables;
and beyond that, six (rasa) are proclaimed, likewise with five (bhūta) syllables.
One should worship Vāmadeva on the upward face, Īśāna in the southeast,
Aghora in the south, O Goddess, and Sadyojāta in the mandala of the west.
One should place the Puruṣa in the western face and the Parāpara in the upper-left;
this must not be given to wicked beings who lack the lineage of transmission.
One should not bestow [this] upon the ignorant, those devoid of the scriptures, or those of cruel nature. Should it be given through negligence, one's own treasury of knowledge will be lost.
The preceptor goes to hell for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras,
O Goddess, [having failed to recognize] Keśava residing upon his head in the temple of Kailāsa.
One should place Śiva above that and Āsya on the forehead;
one knows Nārāyaṇa to be in the right eye and Mādhava on Mount Mandara.
Goviṃda is in the left eye, and Niṣadhālaya is in the north;
likewise, from the right ear to the left, there are Dhruva and the others, ending with Śrānta.
O Goddess, one should worship Viṣṇu, Sūdana, Vāmana— who resides within the middle of the Vedas—
and Śrīdhara and Hṛṣīkeśava, facing eastward.
In the same manner, one should place [the mantra] upon the two nostrils and cheeks with the seed-syllable of the Goddess;
and at the end of that, with the first [syllable], upon the origin of the body hairs, one should place Padmanābha.
There is no doubt that the pair of hands is placed upon the two lips;
Vāsudeva is in the east and Saṃkarṣaṇa is in the west.
Thereafter, one should place Pradyumna at the end of the head and Aniruddhaka;
having extracted [the syllables] beginning with the eleventh, one should place the Wielder of the Discus (Cakrin) at the base of the arm.
From the tip of that [middle finger] down to its base,
one should again place Gādinī, Śārṅginī, Khaḍginī, and Śaṅkhinī, submerged in the [middle finger].
O Goddess of the gods, [the mantra] consists of *saṃ*, *taṃ*, *taṃ*, *nā*, *di*, *me*, *ghaṃ*, followed by *ta* and *ḍā*;
then *kā*, *lāṃ*, *taṃ*, preceded by *prāṇa* (ha), for the movement of the central Bhairava.
O Goddess, having extracted the letters from the beginning (A) to the end (Kha), one should place Hali, Yugi, Śūlin, Pāśin, and Aṅkuśin on the right and left sides respectively.
First, the color of the Mothers arises from the end;
then the middle of the planets, and at the beginning, the head of the qualities.
O Goddess, that [syllable] preceded by *tat* is again in the temple of *ruṇā* in the west;
O Goddess, the letter *ka*, situated in the midst of the *dhenu* [vowels], is worshipped as the most excellent of qualities.
Mukunda, Nandaja, Devī, Krūra, Naraka, Arddhari,
Hṛṣṭa, Sadyas, Sātvata, and Śauri— these are remembered as the ten [incarnations].
One should place on the right side the syllable "ya," which is the source of auspiciousness;
having extracted the phoneme "bhu" from "bhūtādi," one should likewise recite the name Janārdana.
One should place the letter *kr* (the mountain-bearer) above in the sixth house, the abode of beings;
and the letter preceded by *muni* (the sage), namely *gu*, one should place upon the navel and the belly.
The Goddess is the universal form in Vaikuṇṭha and the seed everywhere; she is the Person among the gods and the one born of no source within the heart.
One should place Valina at the base of the waves in hell, Raktasambhava at the tip of the hump, and the younger brother of Bala (Aniruddha) in the center of the heart.
Vṛṣadyraṃ is in the left armpit, and Āveṣṭa is produced from fat;
Vṛta is on the left and right sides of the chest and arms, situated in the region of Soma.
If one does not tolerate that beloved semen mixed with marrow located within the breath in the right foot and the arm, [it leads to rebirth] in hell.
One should place the pure vital breath (prāṇa), which has entered the channel of desire (chaṃda) and resides in the left foot,
as the Self in the form of Nārasiṃha within the heart, in the midst of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Thus, O beloved, this auspicious method of Nyāsa has been declared regarding the elements;
having first performed it starting from the throat and ending with the *tasyaḥ*, as it was taught by one's own teachers.
These Rudras, along with the consort of Viṣṇu, are fully enumerated;
they are the destroyers within the three worlds and are exceedingly proud in their role as protectors.
O Sovereign of the Gods, the mothers of Viṣṇu and Rudra, beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, along with Sūkṣmā, Asomā, and Tṛṇā, have been extracted by me previously just as they were before.
Neither difference nor non-difference exists here; all the deities are capable [of this].
He is the God even of the gods, and he is my eternal [Self].
One should worship Siddhanātha and the others, beginning with Brāhmī, as before;
[and worship] the discus, sword, trident, scimitar, axe, noose, and mace.
One should contemplate these weapons— the conch, the trident, the thunderbolt, the arrow, and the Śārṅga bow— as possessing a brilliance equal to twelve suns.
The primary forms are the images of Brahmāṇī and the others, along with the Bhairavas;
furthermore, the forms originating from Viṣṇu are the elephants of all the directions.
And having propitiated Maheśāna, one shall obtain everything as before;
beginning from Amareśa up to where he [is] in that temple of Śiva.
O Maheśānī, the Viṣṇu-seed from which the moving and non-moving world was produced;
it is the second among the lords of seed-syllables, possessing a radiance equal to fire and the sun.
O Goddess, Prāṇarudra is situated between the end and the middle;
O Goddess, Bhujaṅgabhairava is located below that in the lower region.
Upon their heads, one should place the Bindu-Bhairava ending with the letter 'ga' (i.e., *kṣaṃ*).
This Vāgurī shall shine forth as the mother of the universe.

The fourth [vowel] is in the eleventh [house], the Goddess, and likewise the beginning of that is Mādana; its beginning is established as the month, and those two are above, in the middle of the wheel.
One should cause the *prāṇa* to be bestowed upon it with nine [syllables];
and by means of the *trimūrti*, it was previously given to Śiva in the abode of Niṣadha.
O Goddess, on Mount Mandara there is something unprecedented, adorned by Bindubhairava;
by me this entire universe is pervaded in two, five, nine, ten, and eight ways.
O Goddess, my seed, which rises upward and ends in the cruel [letter], is situated from the middle of the world upward within the temple at the tip of the nose.
Below that, one should write the syllable Bhuja;
O Goddess, having dissolved it into the heart, it should be placed between the letters Ṣa and Na.
In front of him, one who dwells in a new hut should be given;
first, Dviraṇḍabhairava, who resides in the abode of the sages, [should be honored].
One should write below the auspicious *ṛ* which has been stepped upon by the serpent;
there, Bhairava, the Goat-like One, is situated above Krūra.
One should place that syllable upon his head with the left knee;
one should apply the Vāyavya syllable to the tip of his left arm.
They know the first seed-syllable of Mālinī to be the end of the qualities (guṇa) alone;
having extracted that soundless letter, they run to the abode of the Seer.
Interpenetrated by Bindubhairava, the Vidyā is both supreme and non-supreme;
O Goddess, this supreme goddess should be recited, for she bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
This [mantra] is most highly secret; when recited, it destroys death;
when meditated upon, that Goddess grants liberation; when worshipped, she fulfills all desires.
For by means of this all-encompassing lore,
one accomplishes every purpose through the performance of protection according to the ritual rules, as well as through recitation and extraction.
I have conquered all the worlds and even the Dānavas of old; yet I am alone, O Great Goddess, for you are the sovereign of the King of Vidyās.

O Smara, for that man whose slender body is weighed down by the burden of broad and firm limbs, and who is overwhelmed by the multitude of your arrows, his pride slackens as the sweat born of intense passion flows forth;
whatever eightfold virtues exist within these three worlds have come together into his hand.
Or all the sciences on the seat of Sakala, as well as the Daityas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Just as deer and other creatures pierced by the arrows of the God of Love come under his control, even like the Lord of the Immortals;
hear now, O Goddess, how she is worshipped by the practitioner.
In the *ava* group, the goddess is Vimānā; in the *ka* group, she is remembered as Maṅgalā;
in the *ca* group, she is Sarveśvarī; and in the *ṭa* group, she is Vināti.
The goddess Māninī resides in the *tavarga*, while the omniscient one resides in the *pavarga*.
With the *pavarga*, the sovereign Goddess Sattāhaṃsī should be joined.
Having placed the seeds beginning with *mā* at the end of the groups (*varga*) in a disordered manner of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*),
[one places] Viṣṇu’s seed, the desire of Śrī, Hara, and [the syllable] joined with *vana*.
One should apply the fire of the desire for women as all-pervasive;
the water-element situated in the middle of the form, ending with the syllable *dhruva* (oṃ) and adorned by the Guru (the letter *m*).
Having extracted Raktabhairava, one should place Kālapūtanā above him; this should be placed upon their heads according to the northern direction, without a doubt.
The first [syllable] ending in *vāma* is on the head; [then] Akrūrabhāṣita, Krodhīśa, Bhūtanātha, and Bindubhairava in the three forms.

O Goddess, you go into the midst of creation; [the syllable] *sadya* ending with a bindu-adorned *m*—this is the Great Goddess Vidyā, the auspicious one who performs the ritual placement upon the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
O Great Goddess, this is the family lore (kulavidyā) itself, O Mistress of the Kula;
one should place its eggs upon the nine supports, on the two temples, and on the chin.
I salute Śivā, who has a dark-complexioned body, three eyes, and a slightly reddish moon as her garment;
she holds a rosary, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and a noose and goad, and is the embodiment of knowledge.
I pay homage to that entire Vidyā, who is like a mass of lightning,
who bestows the fruits of righteousness, happiness, wealth, and liberation, and who sits upon a lotus throne.

Having aroused the Goddess in the temple, one should fashion the body from the crown of the head, through the heart, the mouth, and down to the genitals— the source from which the moving and the unmoving have arisen.
One should again and again divide the goddess Tripura, the sovereign of the gods, who consists of thirty-two syllables, into sixty-four parts.
One should diligently worship the Mothers situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions, whose forms are those of the limbless Bhairavas, following the very same path previously described.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the venerable Kubjikāmata.
The illustrious Goddess said:
O Blessed One, the lineages of the families have been extracted from the continuum of Meru,
as well as the extraction of the sacred seats (pīṭhas), along with their sounds and designations.
O Lord, what kind of flower is it, and how is its extraction determined? O Protector, O Master, please explain this doubt of mine exactly as you know it.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
In the continuum, the second flower is Ekāvijñānabhairavī;
O Lord of Devas, the group of letters from 'Na' to 'Pha' is remembered as being within her.
The twelfth, Rudra, has emerged; the sky-flower, however, is by means of duality.
The Sūtra is the continuity; as for Prajñā, I shall speak according to its hidden meaning.
The Saṃvarta-maṇḍala garden, fashioned by the void planets— thus,
those two Siddhas remained silent in meditative absorption within the cave of reality.
In that case, there should be the command of the *pratyaya*, as well as the *kadaṃbaka* tree;
Maṃthānabhairava is divided by twenty-seven cuts.
O Goddess, the two names of the seats (*pīṭha*), which consist of the practice of Śiva and Śakti and belong to the lineage of non-dual conduct, have been told to you as they are in the *Gahvara*.
One should perform the nyāsa, the yoga, the extraction (uddhāra), and likewise that which pertains to Śaṅkara;
having written the sequence of letters upon the pīṭha and other supports, one should [recite] the ninefold verse consisting of five parts.
Kāmarūpa, Hākaḍoka, Nepāla, Pauṇḍravardhana,
Purasthira, Kānyakubja, Pūrṇāgiri, and Arbuda.
Āmnātakeśvara, Kāstra, Triśrotas, Kāmakoṭara, Kailāsa, Bhṛgurnagara, Kedāra, and Candrasūryaka.
One should repeatedly install Śrīkaṇṭha, Kākiṇījāla, Kaluta, Herikoṭa, Gokarṇa, and Merukeśvara.
Aṭṭahāsa, Viraja, Rājaveṇī, Mahāpatha,
Kollagiryā, Kollagiriya, Saurāja, and Jayantikā.
He established the city named Ujjayinī, Caritrakīri, Hastināpura, Indukeśa, the one called Prayāga, Puṣṭa, and likewise Māyāpurī.
Jarasāṃkalaya, Śailabhekāṇḍa,
Mādreṃdra, Vāruka, and Hiraṇyapura.
Beyond this is the Mahālakṣmī-tanodyāna-chāyā-chatra;
these are declared to be the sacred seats (pīṭhas), proclaimed as fifty in number.
Arising according to the principle of emanation through a counter-clockwise rotation,
she is Vāmā and the others among the powers, located at the center-front of the maṇḍala of the peak-syllables (kūṭa).
The arising of vowels and consonants is indeed released in the form of the sacred seat (pīṭha);
it is made dense by Māyā in the midst of the maṇḍala of mudrās.
O Meru, O Śrī Śaṅkara, you have explained the classification of vowels and consonants,
the sequence of the primordial expansion (ādyaprastāva), the lineage, and the means for attaining spiritual perfection.
The light is blissful and stainless; the power is Kuṇḍalinī and the digit (kalā); Umā is free from forgetfulness or heated by penance; she is the primary one, the sole one, and the single-footed.
The snare, the womb, and the three-footed one are in the ocean of Brahman;
in the phoneme-duality is the great jewel, and the fallen [is] the heated chowrie.
Tāṇḍava, Mahāhāra, Sthalam, Unmattasiṃhaka,
Japāna, Saṃvartti, Kaṅkāla, and Trilocana.
Vāsudeva, Virūpa, Kamalodaravāhana,
Dhanurdhara, Jihvaja, Dvija, and likewise Vāra.
Amṛta, Bhadrakāla, Māruta, Agni, Pārthiva, Varuṇa, Śaktipāla, and likewise the one named Pavana.
The goddess Bhairavī is proclaimed as Kubjikā;
one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in direct order and extract [the mantra] in reverse order.
These are indeed the names of sounds established upon the bell and other instruments;
Mahāmeru has four peaks according to the method previously described.
I have described Kālikā as previously stated; now I shall speak of what is above her.
Below is Kālāgnirudra, and above that are thirteen [deities].
And those beginning with Āruṇa, who reside in the lower part of the body, are declared to be the Daṇḍas;
furthermore, the eleven Rudras residing in the upper part of the body are the authorities in Maṃthāna.
Above those nine Siddhas, there are again seven Yoginīs;
above the fifth maṇḍala, however, are the six beginning with Aḥ in sequence.
Above those three powers, however, is the Lord Ciñcinī;
indeed, that which begins with Kālāgni and ends with Nātha has been described by you as the three worlds (kurutraya).

Regarding the meaning of the "cavern" (gahvara) within the body, that which is devoid of the lineage of the Siddhas has no prior teacher, nor any subsequent one; thus it is said that the Kādi division is indeed distinct.

O Great Goddess, listen to the supreme arrangement of the letters (varṇanyāsa), the excellent expansion (prastāra): the letter *a* is the primordial lord (*ādinātha*), established as the central peak (*meru*) of the diagram.
The letter *a*, the letter *ja*, and the deities of the three *oli*s;
the letter *bha*, the letter *ma*, the letter *ta*, and the letter *i*.

Just as these were recollected by the God of Gods, Maheśvara: the letter *ca*, the letter *va*, the letter *ka*, the letter *ra*, the letter *sa*, the letter *ka*, and likewise the letter *ha* and the letter *ya*.
O Goddess, these seven mothers are the performers of grace for the worlds:
Japhakāra, Pakāra, Śabalāgni, and Lāṅgali.
And the letter *ṭa*, O Maheśānī; those are the planets, there is no doubt. And the letter *nya*, *pa*, *ka*, *ra*; and the letters *na*, *dha*, *ka*, *da*; and the letter *tha*.
The letter *ta*, the letter *da*, and likewise the letter *ṭa*—
these are declared to be the Rudras who hold authority through their lineage.
O Maheśvarī, [one should recite] the sounds ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ; likewise the sound e, o, and au; the syllable oṃ, the bindu, and the visarga; and the letters from ka to kha and ga.
These well-known Rudras are proclaimed as those perfected through command (ājñāsiddha);
O Maheśvarī, I shall now relate the name of the Lord known as Ciñciṇī.
But the "all-empty" (sarvaśūnya) is situated in the middle upon the bow;
thus have I explained this twofold prior convention.
And in the triad, O Great Goddess, is the flower that expresses the Triple City;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes part of the lineage succession.
First, accomplish the upward-moving *piṇḍa*, adorned at its beginning and end; [she] whose nature is the seat of leaves exists in the primordial place as long as the world endures.
One should indeed join this [syllable] at the very beginning of the Vidyā, both above and below;
this triple seed-syllable stands upon the seat of the Vidyā-mantra above.
Having taken each single phoneme from the first [group] and the third of the first [group], one should place them upon the head with the *sādhya*;
this is the Vidyā situated on the Cakrāsana.

But in the case of the *taurārau* [mantras], it is reversed; however, when the *ūrdhva* [mantra] is applied upward, one should place the *kāmajāva* mantras according to their respective locations within the third *vidyā*.
Seated in the Siddhāsana, she revealed the seven sciences;
having understood the course of dharma and adharma, one should employ the power of Śiva.
The Vidyā, ignited by fire, becomes throbbing with radiance;
and having placed [the seed-syllables] above the triad of seeds, one should accomplish that which resides at the end of the phonemes.
One should place the two initial obstacles situated within [the heart], which are supreme in the rite of invocation;
one should deposit the great seed-syllable ending with *karpūra* (the letter *ha*) and ending with *śānta* (the letter *sa*) below.
This great mantra of Netra, which bestows the fruits of all desires, is crowned by the head-mudrā upon the practitioner and adorned with the upward-pointing [gesture].
One should join the head (the letter *u*) with *Śunāśīra* (*sa*), and below that, the breath (*ha*).
The first [letter] is conjoined with the fourth and adorned above with the bindu.

The third syllable indeed belongs to the Goddess; it is joined with the letter following *nā* (i.e., *m*) and conjoined with *Indra* (*r*), and is differentiated by the fourth letter from the beginning (*dh*).
The third, most excellent seed-syllable is joined with the letter *na* as its head;
this is the Vidyā of Kuleśvarī, the protector of the conduct of the observance (*samaya*).
Through the procedure of recitation and worship, the Imperishable One bestows all accomplishments.
Now, therefore, O fair-faced one, I shall fully explain the root-mantra.
Whatever is correctly understood by this, all of this is established;
now, place that which is situated in the center within the secret circle in the center.
Thereafter, one should place within its center the letter 'a' situated above,
ending with the letter 'ya' which is the means for attaining the beloved, followed by Māyā, the Bindu, and Nirodhana.
This is declared to be the "noose" (vāgurā) mudrā, which correctly produces conviction;
one should place it upon each of the three seats of the six-syllable [mantra].
O Maheśānī, the seed-mantra of Kāma, which consists of the first two [syllables] ending with the letter *pa* and joined with the vowel *a*, has been revealed as a secret.
I shall now fully explain the third, the most wonderful seed-syllable of Śakti, by the mere utterance of which the agitation of the universe is produced.
The letter *tha* joined with *nādha*, then *gādya* joined with *nādha*, and that which is below *sa*— above this,
the venerable one joined together, the seed-syllable of Śakti is thus extracted.
By this mere knowledge, one should effect the destruction of the seven poisons;
this is declared to be the supreme ignorance (avidyā), which performs all wonders.
(This is the supreme Vidyā known as Avidyā, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
By means of this Vidyā, one should correctly accomplish that for which there is no [other] river.
The letter *ka* is to be known as Modana; the convention (*saṃketa*) is Bindu-Mālinī.
The seed-syllable of Śakti is the letter *sa*, while the remaining letters remain as they are;
the letter *ha* is the Lord Kāla, and *su-rā-pe* is indeed the wind (*vāyu*).
The syllable *A* is the *praṇava*, the Lord himself, whose nature consists of both the Moon and the Sun;
and the two syllables *ha* and *sa* represent contraction and expansion.
The first is called the letter *ka*, the second is the letter *ha*, and the third is the seed-syllable of Śakti; however, [the sequence] is reversed as *oṃ i oṃ*.
Above that is Mahāyoni, named Kuṇḍalā, the spreading one;
and the fourth is Mahāmāyā, most terrible, according to Sureṇu.
The Guhya-śakti, by her own nature, is the great blaze known as the letter J;
the Rudra-śakti is the letter K, known as Kuṇḍalā, and she is the moon of Hari.
In the midst of that, one should offer as an oblation the flower of the mind, which is the tree of Brahman—
that flower which has arisen in the station of Brahman through the cosmic illusion (viśvamāyā).
One should offer that flower into the sacrificial fire-pit (kuṇḍa), and not with flowers of other species;
for marrow, fat, and semen are likewise [to be offered] as the three sweets (madhuratraya).
O Goddess, blood, fat, and semen emerge from the letter E of Śiva; one should then recite [the mantra] a hundred times upon the eight-petaled [lotus] and perform libations.
That which is declared as the vessel for the sacrificial ground is obtained from the mouth of the Guru;
having then drawn a square, one should perform four enclosures.
Thus, the supreme maṇḍala should be provided with four corners;
it always consists of eighty-eight squares on each side.
In the Bhairava-gama, even for that which consists of eight times eight (sixty-four) words, there is a guru;
he who has ascended to the essence of the eight through the sequence of the manifestation of the words.
O Śivā, the venerable Bhairava divides [himself] into eight forms;
through the wheel of sixteen supports, he is the sixteenth, the protector of the vowels.
He who wears the sixteen ornaments...
[is] at the end of the fourteen steps, by means of the fourteenfold expansion.
Devoid of the fourteen [qualities], the wise Kaulīśvara, from the beginning of creation, is the Bhairava of the people of the ten directions.
Situated in the midst of the Pāśa and Aśvamedha [mantras], it is praised as fourfold; O Knower of the Sequence, it is extended in four ways according to the rule.
He who is the Lord Caṇḍeśa, eternally obstructive, whose form consists of those [elements] situated at the hundred thousand points of the Bindu;

who, at the conclusion of the triple oblation, is the mover within the sacrificial pit of the three-naved wheel; who alone subdues [all] along with the fires; and who is the leader standing in the single step.
Established in the single syllable and the single wheel, that Guru resides in the Bhairava-āgama;
he consists of sixty-six threads joined by seven groups of seven.
Having first established a square measuring twenty-four finger-breadths, auspicious,
one should then lay out the thread extending westward from the recitation site and further extending westward from the fire.
Having fixed the first thread, one should stir the remaining three;
this is known as the triple-staff womb, which consists of three nights and has three deities.
In each individual *daṇḍaka*, they say one should apply six sūtras;
by this means, all the *yoni*s are concluded with equal joints.
One should arrange those fifty-four squares in the form of the female organ (bhaga),
beginning from the northeast with the letter 'A' and ending with the letter 'Va' in the west.
One should install all the Mātṛkās in the western direction of Viṣṇu;
one should draw these wheels upon cloths or on a base made of wood or stone.
In a triangular [mandala] and on a tripod, with the syllables and the characteristics,
success arises within six months for one devoted to worship and recitation.
Therefore, listen to the extraction of the mantra according to the goddess:
the letter situated in the middle of *uja*, joined with the head above.
Then, the letter situated in the middle of the first [syllable], placed upon the middle of the second,
is said to be this second [syllable], consisting of the vowel *ā* with the bindu in the middle.
Having established the syllable *ra* in the center and the letter *na* in the middle of the lap,
