this first-syllabled vidyā is known as that which effects the purification of the hands.
O Dear One, having performed the reversal of both the *sakala* and the *kalākhya*, which are purely blissful,
by means of the enemy seed-syllable from before;
In the ritual of *aṅganyāsa*, the second Vidyā is Kṛśodarī;
therein, the manifest Yoginīs reside in the Cakra known as Trailokyamohana.
O Great Goddess, the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* are established [therein],
as well as the secret yoginīs who fulfill all hopes.
The deities beginning with Kāmākarṣaṇī and Rūpā are proclaimed [to reside] in the Guptā,
Guptatarā, and Śaurī cakras, which cause the total agitation of all things.
Anaṅgakusumā and the others, established by Śakradevī,
have come down through the lineage of oral tradition (saṃpradāya) in this wheel that bestows good fortune.
Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, who was previously established in the east, is the most beautiful of women;
she and the Yoginīs of Kulakaula are the bestowers of all accomplishments.
In the wheel that accomplishes all aims, there are those who bestow all siddhis;
indeed, by means of the sequence of the eight siddhis, they grant the fruit of all siddhis.
O Great Goddess, praised by heroes, all the deities of the inner essence (nigarbha), beginning with Sarvajñā, are established within the supreme wheel that provides all protection.
O beloved, in the wheel that removes all diseases, the secret deities—
the great goddesses beginning with Vaśinī— are established in the ultimate sense.
In the wheel consisting of all accomplishments, the supreme secret goddesses reside;
Kāmeśvarī is situated in the east, as are the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) who bestow immortality.
O Sovereign of the Gods, Mahātripurasundarī, the primordial one consisting of mantra, is established within the perfectly full wheel that consists of all bliss.
O Dear One, the supreme worship is that which transcends the Kula, is endowed with the sequence ending at the limit of one's own nature, abides in the state of non-duality, and is the highest.
The Supreme (Parā), the Lower-Than-the-Supreme (Aparā), Gaurī, and the Triad (Tritaya) which is both Supreme and Lower (Parāpara)—
her worship is eternally manifest and established through these three divisions.
Among them, the first division is Tripurā; the second is Tripureśvarī;
the third is Purasundarī; and the fourth is Puravāsinī.
In the fifth [chapter] are the Tripurasiddhas; in the sixth, Tripuravāsinī;
in the seventh, Tripurāsiddhi; and in the eighth, Tripurāmbikā.

But in the ninth [cakra], O Maheśānī, is Mahātripurasundarī; furthermore, she resides within the midst of the infinite seats (pīṭhas) beginning with Ananta, specifically in the middle of the anus, in the north-eastern corner of the anus.
One should satisfy the six and so forth, as well as the four supreme [deities],
and also those from the central *yoni* and the eight-petaled *yoni*, as well as the venerable sandals of Ruru.
And in the midst of the universe, he beheld Śiva, who was wandering together with Dharmamāyā and Indu, shining intensely like fire at the beginning of the world and bestowing everything upon all.
In the Mālinī [alphabet], first is the syllable Śiva adorned with the nasal bindu (ṃ);
at the end of the fourth [vowel] is the Heart, conjoined with the form of Mahāśambhu.
O Goddess, by this one should perform the crushing of Bhairavī’s seat;
thereafter, I shall protect your supreme wheel in its entirety.
It is considered to exist in three ways according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
it is called the triple-fold (trikarda), the triple-flow (vipravāha), and the triple-consciousness (trivedana).
In the Great Method, the fifty seed-syllables are dug out and divided threefold;
by this, one truly understands everything correctly according to its intrinsic nature.
This, which is the essence of the ultimate truth, is mine;
I have related in brief the supreme ritual of the wheel.
O beloved, the movement of the wheel must be performed upon that seat of grain;
then, [one should recite] this mantra which is eternally arisen...
Having first drawn the ear outside and having bowed down again and again, one should,
facing north, draw the supreme wheel.
In the sixteen-spoked [mandala], one should create the great lamp, which is the form of emanation through its own splendors;
it is joined with the *karṇikāra* and *aśvattha* trees, exceedingly sharp, and most beautiful.
Having specifically assigned Rudra and Nimi to his Brahma-mantra,
one should indeed draw the supreme, divine, and most great wheel.
Having diligently placed the goddess Nimi, who is supreme among the eternal principles (tattvas),
one should indeed draw the third wheel, which has the form of saṃsāra.
This triple wheel is formidable, effecting creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
the Goddess Mātṛkā residing therein manifests in three ways and likewise in two ways.
One should by all means cause [the lineage] to be established in succession within the Nādi;
however, when two castes, fierce and arrogant, are abandoned during the birth [of the lineage].
O Goddess of the gods, the nets and other [obstacles] are not to be concealed;
first, at the beginning of the wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra), there are sixteen [spokes] equally arranged from that point.
The wise one should then arrange the colors, the pegs (kīlaka), and so forth, extending from the east to the northeast; or alternatively, he should first render them empty.
Thereafter, O beloved of the elephant-faced one, sixteen other colors of the wheel remain in the directions starting from the east, according to the sequence of the mantras.
Then, O fair-faced one, the knower of the nature of the wheel of withdrawal (saṃhāracakra) should employ the other sixteen syllables for the gods and asuras.
O virtuous one, from the east up to the northeast, or as far as the northwest, one should quickly place those [syllables] within the belly of Acala; thus one makes the auspicious Cakreśvarī.
She should cause this wheel to be arranged as a transition between wheels;
that which is the first syllable of the wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra) has the nature of Śakti.
Know that the first phoneme-nāyaka, conjoined with the nine emotions (rasas) in their state of stability,
is in truth Bhairava, the bestower of all auspiciousness.
The knower of existence [perceives] the station of the wheel as the second, the experiencer;
joined with the twelvefold creation, it makes Indra the leader.
Know the second to be the conjunction of letters that brings about all manifestations;
then, O Goddess, the third is proclaimed as the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī.
O Goddess of the gods, one should extract the tenth [letter] as the station of the wheel;
one should know the fourth [letter] to be proclaimed as the bestower of all sovereignty.
One should take the first letter of creation and the eighth of dissolution;
one should know that as the fifth, and thus the Vidyā becomes five-syllabled.
This is the Vidyā of the forms in the sequence of Kālikā in every respect;
this supreme and auspicious extraction of the Rudra-mantra has been told to you.
But the fourth should be known as supreme, the flower of the lineage of transmission;
it resides in the North, O Great Goddess, as it has been taught in the Kālikākrama.
Here, the path has been shown to you in brief according to the final sequence.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the illustrious *Kubjikāmata*. || 0 ||
The Goddess said:

O Lord, please explain in detail the secret convention of the wheels (cakrasaṃketaka), the secret convention of the deities and mudrās, and the other secret convention of the sacred seats (pīṭhasaṃketaka).
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, that which was spoken as the entire convention, the entire tradition descended through the lineage, born of the secret, has been declared: Parāśakti is indeed Mātṛkā.
Because she is the essence of the Mothers and precedes them, she is remembered as Mātṛkā;
she is declared to be the power (śakti) of Rudra, since she is the Mother of the Rudras.
O Father, these eight lords of the Gaṇas here are declared by you to be your own group;
likewise, there are those eight divine Mothers, as well as the Yoginīs.
And all of them are seen to be ever-present, bestowing visible fruits:
splendor, strength, serenity, beauty, knowledge, and purity.
Supreme joy and effort—these are the seven most excellent qualities;
by these alone, this entire triple world would be produced as supreme.
If the two sounds *jya* and *sa* are not given as the essence of the light (*jyotis*),
then thus is the great characteristic of the Rudras taught in due order.
All these hands beginning with Parā are clearly bestowers of grace;
by them the entire world, consisting of word, meaning, and cognition, is pervaded.
The womb, heat, that which is obtained, the hexagon, Kuṇḍalinī, the Kula,
Maya-vowel, glory, and the Swan— these are remembered as the eightfold Vāgbhava.
First is Vāgbhava, then Suvarṇa, renowned throughout the world;
the second is Haṃsadeva, and the third is Vahniromaṇa.
The fourth is renowned as Māyā; the fifth should be Praṇava.
The sixth should consist of four kalās, and the seventh is dear to Īśvara.
In this regard, that which is produced by the conjunction with fire through inherence is the supreme illuminator, the essence of the Kula, which is always proclaimed as the *vakūra*.
The cauldron is the aperture of Brahmā; the cauldron is the temple of Śakti. Having joined it with Kālarudra, the dissolution occurs within the Great Self.
That Śiva is manifest on the surface of the earth; he is the knower and the liberator.
[He is] brilliantly radiant, circular in form, and marked by two points (bindus).
Mounted upon the letter *Ī*, seated on the crest of the great flame,
you are indeed slightly present within the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*), having the nature of supreme bliss.
It is proclaimed as the essence of bliss, eternal bliss as it has been described;
for that is indeed the first *vāgura*, since the letter *pa* is its garment.

When these [energies], having attained a state of differentiation, proceed as the manifest sun, fire, moon, and lightning, then the letter *ma*— renowned throughout the world— is situated within the triangle.
For the nature of the moon, sun, and fire arises from the high-pitched utterance of the syllable *a*;
since this [syllable] is established as a single utterance consisting of the letters *i*, *e*, and *ai*.
Thus, by the sequence of *ojā-pūka*, and by the sequence of *kā-pūjā-oka*,
this sequence has been fully described, which pertains to both emanation and reabsorption.
This path reveals that which abides in the states of the manifest and the unmanifest.
By means of knowledge, those who uphold the rod [of authority] [attain] dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
The accomplished one (siddhā) is both the impeller and the impelled, grasping the object with intense passion.
And in the practice of the dharma, one should be well-composed in the six steps of the *piṇḍastha* state.
The form-abiding [state] consists of the desire-sphere, the form-sphere, and the earth-maṇḍala;
these four reside in the mouth of the Guru, following the sequence up to the limit of the bean.
Then, the pair of yugas beginning with the Goddess (Devī) is at the top, and the middle is [the lineage] of * * *.
Within those, there is the lineage of gurus for those whose birth occurred in the Kāra [age].
They are to be worshipped in the Pīṭha of Pūrṇagiri, situated between Kāmarūpa and Anta;
the first Nātha is in the command of liberation (mokṣājñā), and the second is in the command of desire (kāmājñā).
The third is for the attainment of purpose, and the fourth is for the knowledge of the Dharma;
the single Linga is thus divided threefold, and these twelve are the three lights.

The first is the wheel of vowels (*svaracakra*), the second consists of the letters from *ka* to *ta*, and the third consists of the letters from *pa* to *ma*; these three are traditionally taught as being located in the *liṅga*.
Through the union of the three signs, these twelve verses abide in the form of gnosis, transmitted from ear to ear.

From the letter *a* to the final *visarga*, encircled by the sounds of the *jyotika* vowels, the great *liṅga* resides within the three peaks; it is composed of the vowels and consonants, self-arisen.

One should remain stationed at the location of the *kanda*; staying there, one should recite the *vāgara*. Thereafter, that which begins with 'A' and ends with 'Kṣa', surrounded by the three peaks (*trikūṭa*), should be applied.
It shines within the heart through manifestations that have entered the supreme interior;
this is the supreme, eternally blissful reality known as the Vāṇaliṅga, which has been revealed to you.
The King of Desire (Kāmarāja) remains there with one *lakṣa*;
above that, within the world-realm, is the letter *e*, which is the form of the Fourth State (*turya*).
That [vowel] beginning with 'a' resides in the letter 'sa' at the end of the cerebrals (mūrdhānta); the other is remembered as being situated there.
The sphere (golaka) located therein should remain motionless for one hundred thousand [breaths].
O lady of excellent vows, having performed one hundred thousand repetitions for each of the Svayambhū, Bāṇaliṅga, and the other [liṅgas], one should practice the three seed-syllables.
The Pīṭha is said to be Mātṛkā; I am its Lord, and He is so called.
That which is named Nāda is the supreme form, while that named Visarga is the intermediate (parāpara).
Through the sequence, the family [of deities] enters;
through that very sequence, the temporal [impurity] is removed by the wheel, leaving nothing behind like chaff devoid of fault.
She bestows the good fortune of others; therefore, she is proclaimed as Nityā.
A single triangle, the tenth house, the abode of fire, and the womb [are her forms].
The *śṛṅgāṭaka* is proclaimed by the names of the letter *e*;
that which arises here through their conjunction is supreme, born from the union of men.
O beautiful one, that which is always called Vāgara is the lamp and the essence of the lineage;
it consists of words and phonemes, both true and untrue.
For the vessel, which consists of the manifest meditations and so forth, is established here;
O fair-faced one, the deity is situated beneath it within that fire.
To that extent, the sacrificial thread remains established upon this [body];
it is said to be abandoned by Śākya [the Buddha] upon the dissolution of the body.
p. 100b) Here too, the presiding deity Rudra, the consumer of oblations, is to be known;
by his will, O Maheśānī, the speech of Bhārata proceeds.
Vāmitri, as well as Vahni and Dhātṛ, who bestow speech and intellect;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain the determination of the conventions of the wheels (cakrasaṃketa).
For that purpose, O Goddess, one should prepare an excellent mandala measuring three cubits;
within it, one should divide it into three parts and fashion a pericarp marked with the sign of a wheel.
Having first laid down the Brahma-thread from the center of the three pericarp circles, one should [draw] two lotuses with half that measurement, and the area of the gate should be equal to that.
One should draw a line extending from south to north; upon that, one should place seven threads.
Then, having removed the fourth thread, the central portion is divided accordingly.
And having divided the third part into equal portions devoid of fractions,
one should further expand the middle section by that same path.
For the third and the second [circles],
one should extend each of those two strings downward as they were held.
In that very *Saptaka-sūtra*, which is connected to the *Brahmasāman*,
one should join the word "namas" at the end of the *praṇava* for those [deities] situated below up to the fifth station.
One should join that very [mantra] with the sevenfold *brahmasāman* as it occurs in the Sūtra;
and for those situated below, one should apply it ending with the *praṇava*.
In that very seventh [chapter], there is the twenty-third;
in the third, two sūtras; and two others—thus these sūtras become six.
In this manner, it becomes established as having fourteen spokes and ten spokes;
thereafter, a pair of threads joined at its extremities is stretched out.
This single ten-spoked [mandala] with four faces is described as being formed from the second and sixth lines on both sides of the Brahma-line.
O Goddess, two threads each are extended horizontally and vertically;
from the fifth thread, one should extend two threads upward.
One should place a thread from the upper point, through the center of the lower face, up to the second vital point (marman);
then one should apply a third thread connecting those two so that they meet each other.
Thus, the fourth, the eighth, or the fifth letter *e*—
in this way, the wheel is perfectly accomplished, producing both beauty and radiance equally.
That group of five powers is brought forth in the fourfold sequence of emanation;
through the union of the five powers and the four fires, there is the convergence of the cakras.
In that [mandala], O Maheśvarī, there is one [triangle] in the center, fourteen at the two ends,
fourteen at the ten pairs [of corners], and one eight-spoked [wheel].
In the yoga of creation and withdrawal, one should sequentially form the locations of the powers;
for fire, one should create two lotuses with eight and sixteen petals respectively.
Then, having made it square, one should provide four doors;
thus, endowed with four corners, it shall be the most excellent maṇḍala.
The Sun is [marked] with red powder, the Moon with white, and the fourth is the gateway;
the power of the Supreme Lord, which is the source of the universe, is indivisible.
She is endowed with the ninefold form, consisting of a body of beauty, and is auspicious;
she is united with Śiva, who is adorned and likewise the void.
She who maintains form yet is without support, eternally with her body above;
she is not overcome here in this world, for she moves upward from the place of birth.
O Goddess, you are the mother of all beings, the one who effects their non-dual state; for the world, O Goddess, there is dissolution even while living beings exist in their own essential nature.
O Goddess, she whose form consists of imperishable syllables brings about the destruction of all [impurities] by her own lap;
having bound the fourfold womb, one should thereafter perform the worship.
Within this, the wise one [should place] the eight [deities] born from the faces along with the armor-mantras.
The fire should emerge from the tip of the tongue, rising as high as one *guṇa*.
O Goddess, this is the source of the wheel; now hear the armor-mantra (kavaca), O Pārvatī, [which is located] between the little finger and the ring finger of the left hand.
Having inserted all the fingers of the right hand and encircled the thumb and ring finger,
one should bind the little finger of the left hand between those two.
This is the Elephant Mudrā, which bestows the fruit of all desires;
the two feet are positioned facing each other in the svastika posture.
Between those two, one should not contemplate a vulva-shaped seat;
this is to be known as the "feet-on-seat" (apādāsana) yoni by the best of practitioners.
Having thus assumed the fourfold womb, one who desires the welfare of the world should meditate;
one should contemplate the body as consisting of eight triangles and six corners.
Seated upon the seed-syllable of the support, one should meditate on Tripurasundarī;
O Goddess, when the wheel has been crossed over, the practitioner should raise his hand.
One should worship with gems, pearls, and corals placed in the center,
as well as with flowers that have not yet blossomed, while reciting the root mantra.
One should always render [the area] non-empty; one should ward off many obstacles.
One should place the letter *ka* in the middle of the crest of the three-parted [tuft] on the forehead.
One should place a ten-spoked [lotus] between the eyebrows, a second one in the region of the throat,
a four-gated one situated in the heart, and an eight-petaled one at the navel.
In the foundation, at the feet, is the sixteen-petalled door-wheel;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which abides in the Great Samaya.
Through the yoga of one who has ascended to the root, within the body of the family of poison,
he completely destroys [it] by casting it into the end, having made it difficult to overcome.
Having realized that you are not truly obstructed in reality,
the wise yogi perceives the Goddess who has entered from ear to ear and again from eye to eye.
And wherever one performs the practice of the channels at all times,
there the oil flows by the power of the thread of knowledge.
Salutations to you who move through the sky; salutations again and again to those who move upon the earth;
and salutations to those who move in the intermediate space among all the hosts of yogis.
Jaṃ bhe me hi ta thā kṣe kṣīṃ strīṃ kṣe kṣaḥ phaṭ, likewise ending with svāhā and beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ); this is declared to be the bali-mantra.
One should offer the directional oblation (digbali) at the beginning of the sacrifice, in the middle of the sacrifice, and at the end of the sacrifice.
Likewise, there is the Cakrasaṃketaka Māna and the Mudrāsaṃketaka.
O Supreme Goddess, the convention of the goddess Tripurā is threefold;
O Goddess, [the syllables] beginning with the eleventh are Karālī joined with Krodha.
That thread is situated in the middle of the sword, and above it is the one seated on the throne;
it has four colors and is joined with the trident of Nakulīśa.
Pūtanā is situated in the middle of the sky; Mṛtyu is at the end of the breath, moving upward;
Mahādevī is in the middle of the left [side], stationed in hell, residing in blood.
Below that, one should undoubtedly place the trident-handle;
then, having worshipped the god Bhairava situated in the Naraka hell, one should offer [the oblation].
And Pūtanā is situated in the center of the Bimba, standing upon the seat of Krodhadaṇḍa;
and Māyādevī is on her side, with her head pierced by Akrūra.

O Goddess who causes the agitation of the three worlds, you are yourself the celestial wish-fulfilling tree; O Goddess, you exert yourself with great effort to destroy the twenty [sins] and the transgressions.
Above Raktabhairava is Bhairava conjoined with blood;
again, he is clearly of a reddish hue by means of the true manifestation of blood.
Above Bindumālinī is that which arose as Pūrvasenaka.
O Queen of the Gods, this is the Vidyā that is the mother of the origin of the three worlds.
One's own *māyā* is uncreated; it is adorned with the syllables of its own *māyā-sva-mādhava*, and the primordial seed-syllable is placed upon the head, self-arisen and pierced upwards.
The establishment through *māyā*, the center, the wheel of desire (*kāmacakra*), the womb (*bhaga*), and the ego-sense (*asmitā*)—
these eight forms of the *kanda* [are established] by the gods, preceded by the lineage of the Siddhas.
In the practice of ritual application (nyāsa), worship, and so forth, one should employ the deity of the lunar mansion;
and in the lunar mansion named Kṛttikā, the deity is said to be Agni.
Prajāpati is said to be in Rohiṇī, Soma in Mṛgaśiras;
Rudra is declared to be in Ārdrā, and Punarvasu shall be Aditi.
O Goddess, Puṣya has Guru as its presiding deity; Āśleṣā belongs to all the gods;
Maghā is for the ancestors; and Phalgunī is indeed the asterism of Aryaman.
Bhaga is declared to be in Phalgunī, and Savitṛ is considered to be in Hastā;
Indrā is Citrā, Svātī is Viśākha, and Indrāgni is proclaimed [to be] in Viśākhā.
In Anurādhā, Mitra is the deity; in Jyeṣṭhā, Indra is declared [the deity];
the Pitṛs are in the Mūla nakṣatra; and in Āṣāḍhā, this one (Viśvedevas) is the deity.
The Viśvedevas are the presiding deities in Āṣāḍhā; in Śravaṇa, Viṣṇu is the deity; the Vasus are in Dhaniṣṭhā; and they know Śakra to be the deity in Śatabhiṣaj.
O Great Goddess, in Proṣṭhapadā it is designated as Ekapada;
and again, in [the second] Proṣṭhapadā, Ahirbudhnya is proclaimed.
Pūṣā is to be known as Revatī, and they know Aśvinī as Aśvinī. Bharaṇī is indeed the destroyer; the goddess [bestows] colors by means of the god.
The goddesses conquer the lotus-foot of Hara, which bestows the nectar of liberation upon those who are gracious.
I bow to the family of the eight-times-eight Rohiṇīs, which awakens one to the attainment of infinite philosophical conclusions.
I bow my head to the Lord Bhairava, the beloved of Bhairavī, who stands in the center of the circle of Yoginīs and is surrounded by the mandala of Mothers;
he is the sole cause for the destruction of the disease of this beginningless and terrible saṃsāra.
Homage to the venerable Lord-Physician, the ordainer of the medicine of the Kula.
May all misfortunes, diseases arising from the transgression of traditional conduct,
and all my debts be destroyed through union with the divine wheel.

The Blessed One, the Lord of the Family, bestows peace upon those who worship, those who teach, those who have conquered their senses, and those whose wealth is austerity; he brings peace to the region, the kingdom, the city, and the king.
May there be joy in the sixfold [system] for the sake of burning away all things; indeed, in the fourfold ocean of the great bow known as Hiṃsāsana;
may there be joy in the supreme Siddhakula-Kaulika state, which is distinct from others and characterized by the differentiation of the special Śāmbhava stage.
May the Siddhas and Gurus, the lineages of the transmission, the Jyeṣṭhās, the Yugas, the Samāyins, the Vaṭukas, and the Kumāris;
may the Saṃyoginīs born of the noble Vīra-kula, and the lords of the earth, rejoice!
The groups of virtuous twice-born ones.

But Nanda was skilled in policy, devoted to the faultless, free from envy, possessing incomparable forms and the essence of beauty; he delighted in the eternal, the stainless, the partless, and the peaceful, having cast off all sorrow and fear.
May those devoted to yoga rejoice, as do those joined to the Kulayoga, the preeminent noble ones, the practitioners, and the spiritual sons;
may cows, brahmins, young women, ascetics, and maidens find joy in their duties; and may devotion to the Guru be free from endless obstacles.
May the lineage-yogīs rejoice; may the sons of the lineage rejoice;
may the noble ones rejoice through their splendor, as well as all others who have been initiated into the lineage.

But the *naṃda* [lineage] consists of practitioners who achieve the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā*; however, the *pata* [lineage] belongs to those yoginīs who are hostile to the rules (*samaya*). This [latter] is clearly characterized by the attainment of the state of existence (*bhava*), and it is obtainable only from that Guru whose lotus-feet serve as the support for one’s practice.

Those goddesses who exist in hundreds within the channels (*nāḍī*) according to the sequence of the wheels (*cakra*), those who reside in the pores of the skin within the body, those who abide in the elements (*dhātu*), and those who, having carried away the dwellings [of the mind], remain in the water of the great waves of the surges of exhalation— those are the goddesses.
By whom, indeed, have these moments been acquired, which are otherwise overcome by obstacles?
Homage is incessantly paid to all those yoginīs, by the power of whose command the three worlds abide in well-being.
The illustrious city of Candrapura, a world of monasteries, was effortlessly subdued by him; he brought his disciple Sāpādalakṣa under his sway and led Kṣecara to his feet.
In the midst of that, the Lord Śrī Ādinātha—the master who pacifies the defects and suffering of existence—was drawn forth by the Earth-Lord through his own command; [there she saw] that deity.
The illustrious Mitrīśanātha is the one who acts in the Kṛta Yuga; Oḍhranātha [acts] in the Tretā;
Ṣaṣṭhīśa is the lord of the Dvāpara; and Viranātha of Ciñciṇī acts in the Kali Yuga.
I bow my head, touching the surface of the earth, to the pair of lotus feet of that Goddess Mitradevī, whose face is like a lotus of noble lineage, who bestows success, and who is auspicious.

May Bhairava, who has brought about the destruction of the worlds and whose nature is composed of all beings, purify us— he who is contemplated by those who are deluded by constant effort and who are filled with the radiance of the Bindu-cakra, resembling the clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
This divine [power], which is the primary mover of the obstruction of the non-attainment of arms and faces,
belongs to those gods born from the conceptualization of the meaning of weaponless scriptures in the cremation ground known as Ekavīraka.
Victory to the Supreme Reality, who is the destroyer of the acquisition of worldly existence; may he, who shines with the unfolding of the supreme state and is established in the ultimate truth,
cause the splendor of the earth to blossom with his unrestrained gaze upon the auspicious play of all the worlds.
The auspicious glory born from the sacred seat.

Salutations to the Kula-yoginīs of self-awareness, who dwell upon the sacred seat of Kailāsa, who delight in divine and celestial garments, and who are kissed by the crest-jewels of the lords of yogis.

May I find happiness by consuming the speech from the mouths of those who are intoxicated with pride, who are full of abundant worldly existence, whose names are not to be experienced [in this life], who are like flesh-eating demons, and who roam through the quarters of the world as wandering witches.
And those who are situated at a distance, as well as all the people assembled there,
may they all rejoice through the union with the splendor of the divine wheel.
May the nectar-like drink of those sky-dwellers— whoever they may be, the worldly ones who have departed for the next world— be effective for them.
May desires be the fruit for heroes; may yoginīs be for the sake of yogic accomplishment;
may kings be righteous; and may the clouds rain in due season.

Those who mock the divine sequence and the practitioners of the *bhū-samaya*, those who are greedy, miserly, or hateful toward the minds of the *kula-yoginīs*, those who hate the *kula*, those who revile the substances of the heroes (*vīra-dravya*), those who laugh at the wives of the *kula*, and those whose intellects are dependent on [worldly] worship—[may they be destroyed]. p. 104a) [May they be destroyed. Those who mock the divine sequence and the practitioners of the *bhū-samaya*, those who are greedy, miserly, or hateful toward the minds of the *kula-yoginīs*, those who hate the *kula*, those who revile the substances of the heroes (*vīra-dravya*), those who laugh at the wives of the *kula*, and those whose intellects are dependent on [worldly] worship—[may they be destroyed].
May these fall into the maṇḍala of the six yoginīs.

The protection is not the *hākinī* who has moved swiftly; the *kākinī* and *lākinī* reside in the flesh. The *kākinī* and *ḍākinī* reside in the fat for the sake of benefit. The *kākinī* is well-established in the full [state], surrounded by the *hākinī*; from that, the secret is protected by the mountain-dwelling *yākinī*.
Śrī Bhairava has sustained my life.
May the happiness found from the celestial realms up to the state of the Guru, and from Brahmā down to Kālāgni and ending with Śiva— the entire world— be satisfied by this heaven.
One who recites this sūtra constantly shall enjoy auspiciousness and good fortune;
it brings peace from all evils and is the eradicator of all sins.
His diseases perish, and he shall live a hundred years in happiness;
thus has it been declared by the Goddess, emerging from the Path of Meru.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the Kubjikāmata.
O Blessed One, I have heard of the convention of flowers arising from the lineage of succession,
as well as what was spoken by Kālikā and Tripurā, O Lord of the Gods;
that which is the supreme knowledge, O Supreme Goddess, which is beneficial to the gods.
O Goddess, how is it that the Vidyā which increases the buffalo exists in the center of Meru?
O Vidyā of Hari, O Vidyā, O Teacher of Vidyā, O Sovereign of the Gods!
O Lord, O Leader of the Gaṇas, tell me all this in detail:
by the mere glance of whose eyes the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas [are subdued].
O Great Goddess, they flee like deer from a lion;
now listen in due order, O Queen of Gods, to the ocean of words of the Vidyā-mantra.
O Goddess, in the temple of Kailāsa, Sṛṣṭibhairava is situated at the left end,
while Madhyamapañcākṣa is seated upon a throne of bilva wood in the center.
And his head is adorned with a golden crest;
he stands within the *dhruva* (pole star) in the *ruvavarta*, and those two [shoulders] are joined by the staff of the trident.
Having drawn the *vajriṇī* upwards, one does not cut it through the middle of the *sarga*;
then, having obtained [the syllables] situated starting from *dhruva*, one draws the *vajriṇī* again in its entirety.
Having drawn the trident-staff (*śūladaṇḍa*) with a spear (*śakti*) piercing its top,
[the syllables] adorned by the sons [of Brahmā] at the end [are placed] in the middle of the *bindu*.
In the same way, having drawn the [mandala of] Time, one should place this [deity] in the center of the circle at the top;
taking Meṣa (Aries) as the end of the qualities (guṇas), it is adorned with the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
One should draw her as standing on an upright staff, self-controlled yet fierce;
and in the midst of all the ritual preparations, one should depict Śakti in front of her.
The Vajrinādaṇḍa-tejātavedaśa is joined with the Prāṇa-śūla;
it is proclaimed as the subtle, firm, cruel, and blazing Vajra-form.

O Great Goddess, one should worship on the path those who are trembling with joy, those who have become lions again, those whose anger is like fire, those who are hunchbacked, and those whose heads are severed by speech.
This Vidyā was born from the great Mahiṣa of exceeding fragrance;
she is the Blessed Goddess, the Vidyā who dwells in the great divine realm, for the sake of his destruction.
The heart [mantra] consists of the syllables of the worlds; the head and the end of the thighs consist of the syllables of Rudra;
the tuft (śikhā) is established with the syllables of the planets and the syllable of Bhūti; and the armor (kavaca) is situated with the syllables of the elements.
One should place the weapon-mantra consisting of one syllable using the letters *na*, *e*, *tra*, *sa*, *ra*, and *ṛ*;
likewise, [one should place] the mace (*rakāśi*), the pestle (*muṣala*), the trident (*śūla*), the skull-cup (*kapāla*), and the chisel (*ṭaṅka*).
She who bears a bow and a shield, possessing the luster of a rain-cloud,
terrifying with her claws and fangs, and has a lion at her side.
One should first worship here all these [goddesses], beginning from the very start: Sumukhī, Durmukhī, and likewise Nyāyā and Siṃhamukhī, as they are seated upon their lion-thrones.
Endowed with her own manifestations and pervading the three worlds,
she is attained through a hundred thousand recitations on earth, or by the taking of a single [offering] for every hundred thousand.
Through recitation, libations, worship, and other rites, success is attained here without a doubt.
Now, O Goddess of gods, listen attentively to my further words.
In the *Pañcāntaka*, one should cause the Vāyavya [mantra] situated within the Bhagavat to be given;
having written the end of this with the letter *Agni* (Ra), one should write the *Sṛṣṭi* syllable (*Ha*) oneself.
One should cause the resounding [deity] to be placed upon his head on the peak of fragrance;
in the center of the lunar mansion (Bha), one should place Mahākāla, and in front of him, the staff and other [emblems].
One should employ the *pāvakī* [mantra], which is distinguished by the luster of dust (*pāṃśubhā*), in the northwest (*vāyavyā*);
the other [mantra] should be emitted at the front, and one shaped like a cow's face (*gavākara*) in the middle of the head.
One should place Bhairava in the vital breath (prāṇa) and the Illuminator (Dīpana) in front of him;
one should likewise cause the color of Krodha to be placed in the fire of Umākānta.
One should draw the upper half of Kālikā and the lord of Ḍhī (Ḍhīśa) in the half-measure;
one should then draw Bhairava joined with Dīpana, situated within the domain of Trimūrti.
O Goddess, the seed-syllable of the Goddess is declared to be inseparable from the head of the beginning of the worlds;
it has red hair, O Goddess, ends with the word "pāna," and is established upon a staff.
O Goddess, [the mantra] consists of *kāṃtavartma*, *kevala*, *tu*, *ḍevumadhya*, *chāgala*, *yāṃta*, *gānta*, *muda*, *goṃta*, and is adorned with subtlety.
In the middle of the body and at its tip, on the left, there is only the center;
it is situated like a drinking vessel, beautiful, and established in eleven.
The left [channel] and so forth, conjoined with the head, bears half and is joined with dust;
and that which is joined with Vajriṇī is again subtly divided.

O Goddess, Bhujaṅgabhairava is joined with the power of peace (Śānti-śakti) in the netherworld; it ends with the letter *dh* and is situated in the left [channel], resting upon the throat. This eleventh field is fierce, consisting of thirty-five syllables.
O Goddess, Brahmā and the other deities are established in their own five locations by means of the nine syllables, the eight Vasus, the ten directions, and the number of planets.
One should worship the deity who is the state of sovereignty over the Nāgas and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
furthermore, one should worship the book, the rosary, the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), and the pedestal.
O Goddess, [he holds] a conch and so forth, a lotus, a mace, and garments of silk;
resembling a cloud, he is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) whose nature is white.
One should worship Nivṛtti and the other [kalās] in the directions starting from the east;
then the Brahmāṇīs and others in front, followed by Indra, Agni, and the Lord of the Ancestors (Yama).
Kṣapācara, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Dhanada,
Hara, Brahmā, and Ananta should be worshipped along with their vehicles and ornaments.
O Goddess, having diligently placed the five *ṭha*-letters here,
one should cause them to enter into their own sequence, that syllable situated in the center of the wheel.
O Lord of the Gods, one should place that deity in the center of the pericarp (karṇikā), and outside of that,
one should place the eight groups of letters (vargāṣṭaka) and the Mātṛkā on the exterior.
All this, O Great Goddess, is marked by the letter *su* (sura);
the fire (*agni*) is the companion of the Knower of the City (*purajña*), and it likewise has three feet and a head.
O Goddess, wherever this written [mantra] remains within the interior of a house,
all things belonging to that person shall be accomplished, as many as there are upon this earth.
O Goddess, the accomplishments (siddhis) are always attained just as the Supreme Lord has declared;
I shall now describe its true nature, which is honored by gods and demons alike.
O Goddess, by means of this [knowledge], Indra attained the state of the Moon;
likewise, Rudra attained the state of Brahmā, and the Lord of Sacrifice attained the state of Īśvara.
O Goddess of the Gods, this Vidyā, more secret than the secret, has never been spoken of anywhere prior to this; now listen to that Vidyā and the Cakra as they are currently being revealed.

O Goddess of gods, where there is Āṣāḍhī, one should write the sequence of letters below that which has the head of a fierce crocodile above the *kṣa*, and which possesses a great roar and gives birth.
O Goddess of the gods, one should write the syllable *yā* at the end of the *dhānta* (the letter *dh*) above the *mūrdhan* (the letter *ṇ*),
and on its peak, one should write the *vala* (the letter *v*) within the interval between *yā* and *oṃ*.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the *nārāyaṇīkānta* in the hand; above the Lord (*īśa*), one should draw the *vāgura* ending with *dhruva* at the top of the head.
Beyond that is the center, and at its tip, with the syllables and marks of the ram and the trident, one proceeds; there it is merged with Ananta, and Dharmarudra is in front.
O Great Goddess, the lovely Saṃvartaka, born of Vāyu, is situated at Someśvara; beneath him stands Śavaka.
One should understand that "Svasti" belongs to us; one should offer him a red seat.
Having placed the color of the Śakti upon Śiva, it is endowed with the void (śūnya) and the primordial sound (nāda).
One should place the Dūtī on the front portion, endowed with the eight groups [of consonants];
she is the supreme auspiciousness of the Vidyā, the remover of all calamities.
O Goddess of gods, O lady of excellent hips, her power cannot be described even in hundreds of kalpas,
nor can anyone hear the fruit of it.
At the beginning of the Vidyā, one should describe the collection of letters, the Muhalakṣmī, and the Vaiṣṇava;
the Hṛdinyāsa should be performed, as well as the armor (varaka) in the region of the head.
O Vāgīśa, one should place [the mantra] conjoined with Sadāśiva, preceded by Aṃśumān and Anila, along with the Goddess and Rudra, in the middle of the crest-lock (śikhā).
Then, on the path before him, the Lord again established that pair [of eyes] for the sake of the Kurus, situated within the eyes by means of the Brahma-Gāyatrī.
Having meditated upon the assembly of the Gaṇas, one should place the word "Saṃvat" in the middle of the scripture;
O Goddess, one should place the syllable Phetkārī everywhere throughout the entire [text].
Then, in each house, one [mark] should be placed on the head, then on the two eyebrows, on the cheeks, the throat, the arms, the heart, the navel, and the private parts.
One should place [the mantras] on the two knees, the two ankles, and the tips of the feet;
the remaining syllables, conjoined with the Navātman and so forth, constitute the pervasive [placement].
Within the syllable *E* mentioned previously, one should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa reclining upon the coils of the serpent Śeṣa,
his body embraced by Kamalā.
In the ocean of milk, frequented by hosts of elephants and served by sages, Brahmā, and others;
filled with various trees and creepers, and crowded with diverse people.
Or [he saw] the Lord of the gods of gods standing there, bearing a conch, a discus, and a skull-cup;
holding a rosary, a lotus, a mace, a full jar, and nectar.
He was attended by [attendants] adorned with crowns, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments;
he was marked with all the auspicious marks and held the lotus in his hand resting upon his own lap.
Having propitiated Maheśvara, the God of gods, who was intent on beholding the Daityas,
with ritual offerings, [he likewise worshipped] Gāyatrī, the daughter of Brahmā.
O Goddess, one should thus worship Sāvitrī together with Viṣṇu, Vāgīśa together with his speech, and Dhanada accompanied by Śrī, within the womb itself.
One should worship the eight Mothers on the tips of the petals, Vāsudeva in the center,
Saṃkarṣaṇa on the right side, and Pradyumna in the west.
One should worship Aniruddha in the north, and [the deities] starting from the southeast (Āgneya),
along with Śānti, Śrī, and Sarasvatī, who are all highly adorned with the three [ornaments].
O Goddess, by reciting it a hundred thousand times, one is liberated from all sins;
the essence of lac becomes the Lord himself, Brahmā-Sadāśiva.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter in the *Nava-koṭi-saṃhitā* according to the *Śrī-kubjikāmata*, consisting of eighty-four thousand verses.
The Goddess said:
The one renowned by the name Tripurā is red-limbed and joined with the ritual placement (nyāsa);
she is named Nityā, the wish-fulfilling cow, and Saṃvartā, according to the sequence of the mandala.
O Śaṅkara, please graciously explain what kind of liṅga is to be known, as well as other matters,
along with the ritual worship, the fire-oblation, and the libation.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, that which was manifested by me long ago in the ocean of Tripura,
that has now been well-composed here in summary, exactly as it occurred.
For the essence of all scriptures has indeed emerged within the compendium of Meru;
therefore, one should perceive Meru with a joyful inner self.
Having smeared the ground— or a cloth— with cow-dung, saffron, and aloe-wood paste, one should [draw] the Śrīdruma tree and Mount Meru.
The seed-syllable situated in the center of the navel arises from the tip of that [lotus];
before it, the third Rudra-seed-syllable should be placed.
Having extracted the fourth face from the abode of the navel,
one should place the red Rudra situated therein as the seed-syllable of Vidyā residing in Śivā.
Having first stepped upon the head with the feet, and likewise the middle and the front of the *stha* [mantra],
one should raise the right trident, which consists solely of the element of air.
Having written both of these again, with the *karālī* seed-syllable in front,
one should establish the state of Bhārabhūti; one should write [the syllables] equal to *majjārudra*.
Having placed [the syllable] *deṇa* in the middle, with the *vidyādhāra* and *kuṇṭha* at the beginning,
he [should utter] again the continuous sequence starting with *śveta*, followed by *bhairava*.
Below that, Rudra is red and stands upon Mount Mandara;
in front of him is the seed-syllable Dāruka, and immediately after that is the root-syllable.
O Goddess, the Mālinī heart-mantra is situated at the beginning and the end;
one should place a hundred [repetitions] upon the heads of those two, which is the supreme yoga of Mālinī.
O Goddess, having extracted the Ṛṣimālā from the beginning in this manner, one should place it in front;
O Goddess, that which bestows measurement as previously stated is indeed red in color before it.
One should place the first of the nine [syllables] upon the seat of the trident-staff;
one should know Rudra to be situated on Mount Mandara, facing the thirty [deities].
One should place the seed-syllable alone on the head, starting from the left, during the upper half of Aries;
that same syllable alone should first be written in front of Kūrmarudra.
O Maheśvarī, having extracted the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, which is endowed with the power of knowledge and arises from the semen, one should place it eternally before Bhīmā.
One should place Bhairava, born of wrath, in the middle of the thighs;
with the word *lokāntena* and the falling of the beloved, the fifth becomes the *praṇava*.
One should first write the seed-syllable of Mālinī;
before it, one should draw the letter Ka, which is the end of the world and is conjoined with the head (the vowel *u*), and this shall again become the cause.
This is the ancient knowledge that agitates the root-egg;
it bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation, and produces immediate conviction.
This is that eternal Bhairavī; this is the perfected Makaradhvaja.
In the temple of Kandarpa, one should install the sequence beginning with Bhīmā and the others.
One should place Saṃvartaka at the end of the journey to the city of Kaṃdarpa;
"viṣaṃ sa visadvitva" is the obstruction of the Nivartaka path.
O beautiful goddess, this is the maṇḍala named Saṃvarta;
indeed, it is remembered as being effective at the end of the dissolution, bringing about the destruction of the world.
When the world-process has become fruitless, one finds that bliss within oneself,
having contemplated the non-conceptual state which is devoid of both cause and example.
O Goddess, that is the supreme bliss wherein this world of the moving and the unmoving arises;
from that [bliss] it pervades, and upon that it is established as the entire universe.
The powers of action within those three locations are the Bhairavas;
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī arise from the center or from space.
Śakti, the mother of the universe, is the primordial Mātṛkā who differentiates from the root;
she is the vomiter [of all things] through her conduct, and the wise know her as the terrifying sun at the end of the aeon.
O Goddess, this yoga of the sequence of dissolution has been revealed though it is to be kept secret;
it is stainless bliss, the light of consciousness, the power that bestows the fruit of the Self.
Furthermore, the union with the state of the universal self and the other directions are likewise described;
in that same manner, the form was proclaimed by the seers, and so too the Goddess with great effort.
Through the union with the letters of the Mātṛkā, she who dwells in the center of the Guru’s body is Bhairavī; situated within the body, she is the liberator from the mass of suffering.
[He saw] Bhairavī, endowed with the thirty-two marks, together with Viṣṇu;
or likewise Gāyatrī, as well as Lakṣmī, the sole mother of all the worlds.
She who is the goddess Lakṣmī-Bhairavī, whose form is like the essence of aesthetic flavor (rasa),
possesses five long [vowels], four short, five subtle, and six marvelous [qualities].
It is said that [the body] has seven red parts, three deep parts, and two broad parts:
the two arms, the two eyes, the two flanks, the two knees, and the space between the breasts.
O Goddess, the five long [limbs] have been declared, and then the Śrī-vaktra, Jaṅghikā, Pṛṣṭha, and Geha—
these four are said to be short.
The joints of the fingers, the hair, the skin, the teeth, and the nails; the armpits, the belly, and the chest; the nostrils, the shoulders, and the forehead—all these are subtle.
Thus, these six should be known as elevated; and beyond that, whatever the animal possesses—such as redness in the palms and soles of the feet, the eyes, and the palms of the hands.
The palate, tongue, lower lip, and upper lip are proclaimed to be the seven red [parts].
Voice, character, and the navel are proclaimed as the three deep [qualities].
O Maheśvarī, the Urolalāṭikā [lineage] has two branches;
he who is endowed with the thirty-two marks worships the God of gods.
The Vidyā is the string of beads; with the other two [hands], she holds a discus and a conch.
Her hands are joined with one another, and she rests upon the lap of Śiva.
They gazed intently at the infallible Kṛṣṇa as he sang, his flute joined to his mouth,
while they themselves were adorned with bright pearl necklaces.
She who possesses the knowledge of the discus, the conch, and the rosary, as well as the serpent and the void;
she who, endowed with the marks of a Bhūta and a Puṃdruka, bestows fearlessness through her speech.
Seated upon the Bhairava posture, adorned with a garland of severed heads and marked by the bindu,
her eyes are filled with the abundance of supreme bliss.
That which is called the conjunction of the qualities (guṇasarga) is said to be the subtle form of Māyā;
it exists within the supportless Saṃvarttaka fire, situated at its waist.
There, in that exceedingly cool abode white with the rays of great lotus-jewels, he beheld the Lord himself, endowed with all auspicious marks.
Śivā is seated upon the auspicious throne, as red as the bandhūka flower;
surrounding her in the eight directions are the eight Śaktis, whose forms are the foremost manifestations of Power.
Having uttered the syllables *lakṣmī*, *kamala*, *vasinī*, and *aṅkuśa* again,
[one should visualize her] mounted upon Raktabhairava and accompanied by the grahas Pūtanā and Prajñā.
O Goddess of the Gods, place the fivefold Pañcātmikā in front of Varaṇā;
and one should meditate on the sound "Dhare Dharaṇi" located in the direction of Agni.
Having extracted the seed-syllable ŚUKRA, one places the non-poisonous [syllable] in the middle of the group;
the first is at the beginning of the ten, and the third is in the ninth.
Then, one should write the seed-syllable pervading the directions, with the "beginning of the worlds" (loṃ) at the head; in this manner, one should write the letters in sequence starting from Ananta.
At the end of the Bhāgavata, Niśca is [the daughter] of Svaṣṭṛ due to the similarity in meditation;
Kālindī, Satyabhāmā, and Nandinī were born again from Mitravindā.
O Goddess, you should fashion other forms of Tripura in due order— namely Lakṣmī, Anagnijitī, and Ākhyā— just as you have done with the supreme form.
By means of the recitation and fire-offering (homa) of this [mantra] performed to the measure of one hundred thousand,
even a dead stone or a piece of wood would, upon being seen, become sentient.
Whether among the gods or mortals, or even in the netherworld, the abode of the serpents,
that hero, the son of Devakī, moves according to his own will.
Next, I shall proclaim another vidyā that deludes the three worlds,
which was revealed of old in the Trailokyamohana Tantra.
Surely the cruel Mārāṅka, with his head [bent] toward the Modaka and Śukra, has not returned again;
and the Mādana has set upon the head of Śukra.
One should cause the Śakti to extend downward from the end of the Guṇas, situated at the head;
endowed with the five [elements], it is the Garbhādhāna, and by that, she is the Nādinī.
Dīpanī, as well as Vidyā, Māyā, and that which is in the middle; then before that, Māninī in the left eye, and the beautiful Rudra with the vowel *a*.
Having placed Viṣṇu on the left breast, one should draw [the other deities] around it as before;
then, O Goddess, one should again extract another [mantra], which was secret but has now been revealed.
This auspicious five-syllabled Vidyā has originated from Viṣṇu;
likewise, one may worship the goddess Bhairavī and the nine-syllabled Kaṇṭhaka.
O Caṇḍikā, perform the dwelling and the removal [of obstacles] in the midst of what was previously mentioned;
O Blessed One, likewise for Viṣṇu, and also for Śambhu and Pārvatī.
O Maheśvarī, through the yoga of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, she herself is that very Vidyā;
she is Māyā, she is Vāgīśvarī, she is I myself—listen to me as I speak of Vāgīśvarī.
Before the *haṃsa*, the Goddess; at the end of the *samā* [mantra], the *haṃsa-śakti*; furthermore, *sarasvatīm agre*, *nati*, *svāhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*.
Having fully extracted Vāgura, Viṣṇu, the Goddess, Vāyu, Rudra, Kāma, and So'haṃ, together with Adyasāhā,
[I shall proceed].
In the *Prapañcamuṇḍamālā*, it is stated in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"This Viṣṇu is declared to be Śiva; Brahmā is Vāk, and Taraṇi is Bhairavī."
Furthermore, the goddess Dhvaṃsikā should place the one situated in the middle of the mouth [of Mālinī] and the one situated on the Mandāra tree, which arises from the thigh of Mālinī.
In the eleventh [digit], the white [line] below that is born from the bilva;
it is declared to be Śrīkara and the pride of the fire.
Born from the midst of the ocean of milk, seated upon an excellent lotus and Garuḍa, Acyuta has eight arms and is presided over by Bhairava.
Resembling molten gold, with veins as red as the bandhūka flower,
and bearing the lotus, sword, mace, and discus, as well as the conch, noose, and goad.
One should incessantly place the five limbs— Vidyā, Kapāla, Manas, Manolaya, and Bhībhīsatrāsamada— upon the mind.
With the eight syllables beginning with *pṛthuṃ* and *sava*, conjoined with the ten [syllables] beginning with *sarvajña*, those ten [mantras] are placed in the ten locations.
The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth, and the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) was indeed his arms;
that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya, and from his feet the Śūdra, in this order.
O Goddess, from the soles of the feet upward is Pātāla; above the feet is Vitala; further, from the ankles to the soles of the feet is Nitala; and extending up to the knees is Jānata.

One should likewise contemplate Talātala in the two thighs, Rasātala in the auspicious region of the hips, and Pātāla situated at the junction of the waist. One should meditate upon them in that manner, extending upwards.
The Bhūrloka is in the middle of the navel, and the Bhuvarloka is situated in the heart;
the Svarloka is to be known in the chest, while the Maharloka is at the throat.
One should contemplate Janaloka in the middle of the palate, Tapoloka on the forehead, and Satyaloka at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra); these are the fourteen worlds.
One should prepare the articles of worship according to the previously stated procedure.
[Then one should recite] the three *mṛtī* seeds, followed by *māninī* originating from the head.
In front of Kūrmarudra, in another color within the hermitage of the sages,
one should extract the seed-syllable beginning with fire (Ra) and place it upon the serpent Ananta in Śivā.
One should visualize Vāsana in front and Samālikha in the middle;
O Great Goddess, Saṃvartaka is situated upon the seat of Mahākātya.
And at the entrance of this [mandala], one should place a lamp in the hell [direction];
and one should place [the deity] seated upon the seat in the northwest, occupying a portion of the *arghya* offering.
O Goddess, the fifth syllable is the *kṣepa*; the name and so forth are at the beginning, followed by the syllables, and then again the three seed-syllables (*bījas*) outside.
Just as this science has been declared, it is considered the five-syllabled Vidyā;
those seed-syllables were extracted by the Rudras in the abode of the Sages.
The great Rudra named Kāla is adorned with the end of Vāmā;
the letters of the elements and the letters of the qualities are as before.
Thus, this Great Vidyā is considered to be the Bhūtākṣarī in that same way,
according to the number, meaning, qualities, and form of the mantras used in all recitations.
Furthermore, O Goddess, by performing three hundred thousand recitations with every effort,
even a man who has killed an embryo, though afflicted by time, is purified.

A Brahmin [is purified] by twelve hundred thousand [recitations], a Kṣatriya by sixteen, and a Vaiśya is said to require twenty; for those of the Śūdra caste, it is according to their respective number of wives.
As before, having sprinkled the calf a thousand times upon the maṇḍala, he was liberated from all sins; and through his own desire, he delighted in the earth.
Among all those of self-restraint, the eldest became superior to the youngest;
in this matter, austerity alone was weightier, and innate disposition was the cause.
Initiation (*dīkṣā*) arises among Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and women through the distinction of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*);
however, it is pure being (*śuddhabhāva*) that is produced, and not dharma as a means of attaining the *liṅga*.
Since the sage Parāśara is the supreme authority, let there be no [claim to] the status of the twice-born;
for Vyāsa was born as a donkey from a donkey, and was the son of a fisherman’s daughter.
Maḍavyomāṇḍakī was born from the womb of a goat, as was Ṛṣiśṛṅga; Vasiṣṭha was born from a courtesan, and the great sage Mātaṅga was likewise born from a low-caste woman.
Bala was born of Hastinī as Avala; Keśava was born of Kauśikī;
Kuśāpa was born of Murā; and the great sage was Kauśika.
Taittirīya was the son of Taittrī; likewise, Ghaṭodbhava was the son of Agastya; Viśvāmitra was born of a Caṇḍālī woman, and Vālmīki was born from a Mleccha.
All the other sages as well were twice-born, distinguished by their various lineages and clans;
yet there was no family among them that had not entered into the lineage of the twice-born.
Even those born of low caste have all attained the status of the twice-born through austerity;
therefore, I do not honor the status of being twice-born based on birth or lineage alone.
A Brahmin does not become a Brahmin merely by being chosen as one, nor does a Śūdra woman’s womb produce a Brahmin;
since [he] is also purified by the morning twilight prayers and other rites, how then could his mother not be a Brāhmaṇī?
Even a Śūdra attains purity, while a Brāhmaṇa may fall to the state of a Caṇḍāla;
for all are purified by sacred rites and cleansed of their taints through austerity.
Therefore, one should perform the ritual procedure with the purificatory rites such as initiation;
that which is devoid of the prescribed rule must not be performed, for it was previously ordained that [the rite] be done according to the rule.
Even for one who has been initiated, that initiation may become corrupted by a fault according to the rules;
devotion is taught to be fourfold through the divisions of Śāmbhava.
In the five locations beginning with the feet, through the two other seeds beginning with Nivṛtti,
the Rudras who pervade the Egg of Brahmā reside within Saṃvartaka.
O Pārvatī, when the realization of reality is divided, there is the path of knowledge (*jñānamaya*) and,
as previously stated, the path of action (*kriyāmaya*), which consists of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the mandala, and the female deities (*putrikā*).
In Caitra, this initiation leads to suffering; in Vaiśākha, it bestows all accomplishments;
in Jyeṣṭha, it would bring death; and in Āṣāḍha, it is the destroyer of obstacles.
In Śrāvaṇa, it bestows prosperity upon men; in Nabhasya, it is considered to bring suffering;
in Āśvina, it leads to the attainment of all perfections; and in Kārttika, it increases one's knowledge.
In Mārgaśīrṣa it is Śubhakṛt; in Pauṣa it is Jñānavināśinī;
in Māgha Medhā shall be increased; and in Phālguna it brings all things under control.
One should place jars made of gold, silver, copper, and so forth, which are beautiful and free from flaws;
outside of those, there may be sixteen, or even thirty-two, or twice that number again.
The svastika, the sarvatobhadra, and the cakrābja have been previously described;
all of these should be encircled with silk cloth by means of a triple-stranded thread.

Having purified [the offerings] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and [perfumes] such as sandalwood paste, one should worship the Cakra according to the rules with eight and sixteen [substances], including gold, jewels, and the like.
From the Bhairava Āgama, one should offer all kinds of foods and edibles, as well as libations, to the thirty-two and sixty-four Bhairavīs.
Having first worshipped Vaikuṇṭha, Paraśambhu, and then Parāparā as well as Īśvarī, with unprecedented offerings according to the available means of ritual service;
Having learned the sequence of the divine and the non-divine from the guru, one should proceed through the stages in succession;
through the perfection of this sequence, the supreme light will become eternally present.
The attainment of the state of nirvāṇa would be extremely difficult to achieve even for the gods.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the venerable Kubjikāmata. || 0 ||
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret known as the *Vidyā-śaṅketa*:
the Rudras who cause agitation within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), as well as those born from Viṣṇu.
Indeed, the Mālinī, consisting of sixty-four knots for its grasping,
is the Mātṛkā from which all vidyās have been extracted, having subdued both asuras and suras.
Through the sequence of the supreme, the non-supreme, and so forth, she becomes manifold in her forms;
before the gods, the Goddess [manifests] as Navātman and Navātmikā.
One should place Śrīkaṇṭha on the head, indeed as the very self of Saṃvarta;
then Amṛtākarṣiṇī, Indrāṇī, Aiśānī, and again Candramas.

Furthermore, one should place the eight goddesses with upward-pointing hair, who are the embodiments of supernatural power and wrath; and then, in the single [direction], the goddess Aiśvaryamokārī, whose nature is medicinal herbs.
One whose self is decayed should not install Ambikā, Akṣayā, Jñānā, Dhātrī, Atimā, Gāyatrī, or Ghaṇṭadhātrī upon his body.
Caṇḍācchāyā on the ground of victory, Kaṅkārī in the form of knowledge; then Ṭaṅkarasrā, Ṭaṅkārī, Ḍāmarī, and again Ṭaṅkāriṇī.
Śākinī, Tāmasī, Sthāsye, Dākṣāyaṇī, and Rātrikā;
Nādā, Pārvatī, Phaṭkārī, and Vaṃghanī.
Bhadrakālī, Mahāmāyā, Yaśasvinī, or likewise by me [is invoked],
as well as Laṃbauṣṭhī, Varadāśrī, Ghaṇṭā, and Sarasvatī.
Tākinī, Daśavatī, and Kṣayā—these are the arts (kalās);
and at the end, O Goddess, there are the goddesses Namā, Vāsā, and Caṇḍikā.
One should thus install the god Bhairava everywhere in reality;
those who have been pressed together should be installed as being like white nectar.
The goddesses hold measures, staffs, and nooses, as well as vidyās, rosaries, and skull-cups;
they have matted locks upon their crests and wear the crescent moon as their head-ornament.
Alternatively, O Goddess, one should perform [the ritual] preceded by each respective name;
thereafter, the elemental syllables [should be placed] in sequence according to their emergence.
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, having understood the thread of the eyes of the Vidyā,
O Goddess, one should inscribe the primordial syllable within the temple of Kailāsa.
The syllable of cruel color (KṢ) placed upon Śiva, ending with VĀM and originating from Bhūti (B),
extending from the beginning of the worlds (L) to the head (M), and ending with Śiva (H), is proclaimed as [the seed-syllable].
On the peak of Anantagandha, one should first extract Śveta;
he is seated upon the central throne on Mount Niṣadha, born from Vada.
One should place this, which arises from the previous verse, upon the head;
one should know it as the circular face, subtle at the tip on Mount Mandara.
In the eleventh [syllable], one should place the fourth [vowel], and at its end, one should place the *graha*.
One should place the end of the world (*lokānta*) upon the head, and [the letter] *krānta* in the right eye.
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should place Trimūrti and Bhautīśa in the left eye,
and Amarīśa together with Manmatha in the right ear.
They know that another [destruction] occurs at the end of the eyebrows, and [another] in the left ear;
these are the locations in successive order for Mātṛkā and Surasundarī.
I shall further proclaim another [account], concerning the elemental origin of the world,
in the temple of Anantārtha, situated before the abode of Makaradhvaja.
Furthermore, for another person, one should practice the subtle-point Bhairava-bindu before [the deity];
thus, as the man practices with devotion day after day, [he attains success].
The flood of sins is destroyed within a year; by its splendor one becomes like the sun, and when cool, one becomes like the moon—the very essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Thus, O Queen of the Gods, hear another eternal secret:
O Goddess, among the gods, that which is the protection and the living being is composed of the elements.
One should place Akrūra upon the head and then place him in the positions of the deities;
likewise, one should again place him in the junctions [of the fingers] like the hand of Acchideva.
O Goddess, the letters of the Vedas constitute your head; from you, the stalk is formed. The five names ending with "valā" are your body, and "haṃsa" is proclaimed as your name.
Make the field a favor, adorned at its head with the *bindu* as its stalk;
this *vidyā* is proclaimed to have twenty thousand divisions.
The young maiden resembles a cochineal insect, has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
is adorned with a garland of skulls reddened by saffron, and possesses uplifted breasts.
Seated upon a white lotus throne on eight desire-lotuses,
one should then install the elemental goddess (Bhautikī) until the end of the Saṃvarta [kalpa].
O Pārvatī, this second reality is indeed here, and the third as well;
this imperishable syllable, whose form is Kāmakalā, is situated at the crown of the head.

O Maheśānī, the seed-syllable of Māyā is before this; it is the Rudra born from the beginning, the Lord of the Elements at the end of the first letter, and Rudra himself in the form of the supreme boon.
Mālinī [placed] Sūkṣmarudra upon the head of the syllable Vaktra;
having extracted the god Umākānta from Mālinī, she placed him in front of that.
O Goddess, within the midst of his control, in hell and in the abode of the sages,
there is the great Rudra named Meṣa, who is an ocean of Rudras among the Śaṅkaras.
Having delineated the end of time within them and the end of the worlds from the innermost region,
Brahmā, Rudra, Durgā, Vāgīśvarī, and the other deities likewise [did so].
One should place the limbs (aṅgas) joined with their respective seed-syllables (bījas), ending with the fifth syllable *phaṭ*;
furthermore, the mantras of the eyes ending with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) should indeed be placed upon the Vaiṣṇava deities.
The Mothers, beginning with Brahmāṇī and ending with Lokāntā, are to be worshipped individually in their proper sequence.
O Goddess, I shall now declare that secret which was previously concealed by me.
Having extracted the seed-syllable *itama* (i-ta-ma), and having attained the *haṃsa*,
one should place that very same *so'ham* upon the head of the first letter, at the top of the *lokādi*.

One should offer the seat ending with Dhruva (the syllable *dhru*) to the goddess Dvirandhabhairavī, the terrifying one, in the hermitage of the sages; [the seat] ends in the region of the letter *va*.
O Goddess, accept this final syllable at the end of the qualities in the hermitage of the sage;
it is the seed-syllable of the Goddess alone, joined with the half-measure (ardhamātrā).
The goddess Vajriṇī, adorned with subtle Rudra-mantras, wards off [obstacles];
she possesses the splendor of a seat in the midst of the liberation [of all beings] within the garland of stars and planets.
Mālinī is the color of a wheel, and Vārāhī is on the red head;
again, in her foreign region, make the head begin with Māyā.
In front of Kāntarudra, the one born of Vāyu should be placed;
she is Mahākālī, preceded by Amarī, seated upon an elephant throne.
The portion of the earth shall become further wealth before the God;
and the power of the planets, O Goddess of Gods, is endowed with the command of Nakulīśa.
Cāmuṇḍā stood in front of the assembly of sages;
indeed, Bindurudra was within [the circle], and Siddhijona was in front of him.
With "Pracodayāt" as its concluding throw, it is thus established;
this Vidyā was born of old from Brahmā.

Furthermore, at the tip of the *āśā* line, one should again draw the essence of essences; having written the *kāla* (time) at the end of the *dhruvā*, one should place that which arises from fragrance before it.
May Pāvanī, who is united with Tejasvarṇa, protect;
she is the essence, the nectar, the third [form] through the manifestation of Brahman; indeed, by name she is Nāmnī.
Indeed, it is the foremost among those who discern the field of Brahman, revealing Brahman itself;
it is difficult to attain even for gods who rejoice in Brahman and the Brahmins.
The deities beginning with Brahmā and ending with Śāntyatītā reside in the five faces;
they are all [unified] within the Self, along with Śakti, in the six limbs beginning with the face.
Those who contemplate reality should place [the letters] from the beginning of the feet up to the middle of the body;
starting from the first letter and ending with *pīta* (the yellow one), they should worship Pitāmaha (Brahmā) with the two feet in this world.
One should worship Viṣṇu, who arises from his own strides, extending from the knees to the private parts;
and one should worship Rudra, who has the luster of Kṛṣṇa, from the heart to the top of the head.
One should meditate on Īśa, who possesses the splendor of Viṣṇu, from the crown of the head down to the heart;
he is white, resembling nectar, and above him is Sadāśiva.
Having propitiated [the deity] right there, they obtained fruits here;
one should place the seeds in the middle corner and the sun (Bhānu) in the dot (bindu).
The feet were equal in number to the principles (tattvas), with a *nimba* tree following;
the elephant was [marked] by the color of a swan, by Viṣṇu himself, and by the *udbhava* [mark].
Everything is enveloped by Rudra; fashion it so that it is adorned by Viṣṇu.
In the midst of that, one should contemplate the Goddess in the form of the thread, consisting of the three Vedas.
It consists of three feet and three syllables, embodying the triple energy of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
in its mouth, arms, thighs, and feet reside the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and others.
She holds the gesture of fearlessness, a blade of kuśa grass, a noose, a skull-cup, and a trident; she possesses a multitude of ornaments, including a conch, a lotus, and a food-vessel.
Śivā, seated upon a lotus, adorned with a crest of matted hair as red as saffron,
possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns and a luster equal to ten million moons.
She has a mass of matted hair bound upon her head with a skull-ornament, released by the Most Fierce One;
she is captivating, with lines of thread-like qualities consisting of the sacrifice of omniscience.
She had a girdle fastened with cords and a waistband of gems tinkling at her hips;
she was likewise adorned with the Tarka, Vedas, and Āgamas, which were like the sweet-sounding anklets of a swan.
With the line of body hair as her vine, lightning, bracelets, armlets, and earrings, she [was seen] by the gods,
asuras, humans, and sages of great luster.

[He saw] the goddess, resplendent, beloved of her husband, circular in form, moving as slowly as a pair [of oxen], her path strewn with kuśa grass other than [the usual] and protected by garlands upon her head.
Upon a mosaic floor inlaid with gold and jewels, stood a great tree resembling a celestial creeper, showering the nectar of a beauty that surpassed the charm of Kama himself.
Having been consecrated by the gaze [of the deity], one should worship Īśānī, seated upon Śambhu, at night;
furthermore, one should worship the Śakti, the garments, and so forth, as well as the sandals of the Blessed Lady.
Obeisance to you, O Śivā, the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), who consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, who abides therein, who bestows liberation, and who is the crest-jewel of boons.
Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and Devī in the directions beginning with the East; Umā, Chāyā, Prabhā, and Nityā are the deities of the group of cognizers.
And the Tāmasī Sarasvatī is called Bhāvakā, Vareṇyā,
Vāmā, Mayā, Śākinī, and Bhadrakālikā.
Gāyatrī, Devakī, Rāmā, Śākinī, and again Rātrikā; Mahākālī, Hiraṇyā, Śrīmahī, and Yaśasvinī.

The forms consisting of yoga, residing in the body, beginning with the letters and preceded by Rudra; those beginning with Nārāyaṇī, those beginning with Prabhāva, and those beginning with Caṇḍa, Dākṣāyaṇī, and Yama.
The Mātṛkās, the seed-syllables of the letters, and the lords of the gods beginning with Brahmā,
[are worshipped] in successive order according to the previously mentioned sequence, starting with Kaṣāphala, Nīma, and so forth.
By reciting the *varṇapūta* mantra one hundred thousand times over *palāśa*, *āragvadha*, *śīrṣapuṣpa*, and *kāśmāna* flowers, one shall obtain everything.
In ancient times, through the power of this knowledge, Viśvāmitra attained the status of a Brahmin; others who were rich in asceticism also attained it by means of their penance.
This [mantra], which destroys all the sins of that person, has been revealed by me in the absence of people.
Now, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a secret; listen with diligence.
One should divide [the mantra] according to the number of principles (tattva) by means of the distinctions of the primordial knowledge (ādividyā).
One should place the second [syllable] at the beginning of the third [part], and so on, up to the eighth syllable.
One should extract the word "Viṣṇu" ending in the suffix -ṅe (dative singular) for the three steps;
for the second [step], one should place "Viṣṇu" and "Rudra" at the beginning, followed by "Ananta."
O Goddess, one should fashion a garland for Viṣṇu and Hara using three verses,
or alternatively, by placing those verses in five locations.
In this very way, indeed, suchness (tathātā) is obtained incessantly from the Guru;
[it is] that which culminates in the Left (vāmānta), is elemental (bhautika), cruel, daily (āhnika), and possesses ten powers.
And before him is Kāmājñāna, with five limbs and a bindu upon her head;
and Mahīnī, and again those two, Māninī and Vāmanetraja.
Having extracted the final letter of the vehicle (yāna), one should place the initial letter situated in the middle upon the head.
The illuminator (dīpanī) should be applied to the crown; [then follow] the vital breath (prāṇa), the life-force (jīva), and the elemental (bhautika).
He [attains] Lokānta, Śirasākrānta, Chagalaṇḍa, and Dīpanī;
furthermore, these two, Vājīśa and Mādana, from all the worlds.
O Goddess, one should place the *kalaśa* on the head and the [deities] beginning with Vāmā on the crown;
O Goddess, in the ninefold [arrangement], Khaḍgīśa and Cāreṇṭa shall be at the end of the corpse.
O Mānava, today in the presence of the bridegroom and the bride, one should first place Caṇḍikā consisting of human syllables,
and at the beginning and the end, one should indeed place the Earth-mantra (pārthiva) along with the two goddesses.
Having placed the words according to the number of groups in the Mātṛkā,
one should place the sixteen limbs on the middle of the arms and the feet.
Having uttered the true description [of the deity], one should always perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Gaṇādhipa at the heart and of Gaṇeśa with the *kutū* syllable upon Śivā.
"O Goddess, let there be a reduction accordingly; it has been proclaimed that Gaṇanātha is his mouth, and this was indeed said once more to Ekadanta."
One should place the five-syllable [mantra] and Laṃbakarṇa in front of the eyes;
for the red-beaked one, the seed-syllables are *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, which is considered the weapon-mantra for the directions.
Having placed the armor of the body, as well as the powers such as Mūrti and Śakti,
and the wheel of fifty [letters] along with the passion (rāga), which possesses a luster equal to the colors of the elements;
There,
in the temple of Puṣpāmada, he was seated upon a lotus, his body nourished by flowers, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
Viṣṇu was seated upon the waters; he held a conch, a discus, an arrow, a trident, a citron, and a tusk, and his head was adorned with lotuses and pebbles.
Having extracted the mace, the lotus, the blue lotus, the sword, the cruel lotus, and the spear, one should install Gaṇapati, beginning with the spear and ending with the spear.
One should install the Gaṇeśas and Śaktis according to the procedure taught by one’s mother;
having worshipped them correctly, one shall obtain the inexhaustible fruit of the vidyās.
In front of the center of his navel, one should draw the Goddess and her seed-syllable before it;
situated beneath the celestial mansion, one should depict the seat for worship.
One should place the seed-syllable of the Unfierce One (Akroḍa), situated at the end of the aeon, upon the head;
the Great Rudra, the Destroyer of the Five, is established in the middle of the forehead.
O Goddess, Maheśānī, the principle of Mahat, accompanied by Gaṇapati,
spoke to Śaṅkara within the sacred field (kṣetra) in the presence of Māninī.
One should know that the red [element] residing in Maṇḍara has ascended to the head;
then, taking that seed which is white and adorned with the letter *sa*.
O Goddess, one should place Dhātrīśa, born of Śiva, before Māninī;
in front of him, on the peak of fragrance, one should place Ananta upon his head.
Having placed the seed-syllables *svā* and the rest in the three locations, with the syllable *vadhū* (*va*) below and *puraḥ* (*pu*) in front,
one should place the three types— *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*, and *namaḥ*— along with *vauṣaṭ* and *vaṣaṭ* in a circular manner.
