One should employ the seed-syllable *caṃḍikārā* in its various respective places.
Now, O Goddess, listen as I shall explain another [mantra] in due order.
Viṣṇu and Rudra are in front; O Goddess of beautiful countenance, cross over the cosmic egg born of Viṣṇu at the end of the stream in the middle of the *ṅo* [vowel], O fair-faced one.
Having again drawn Ambikā with her own garment and teeth as before,
one should draw Sadyojāta ending with Rudra in front of Dharmarudra.
O Maheśanī, the speech is harsh within the house, yet adorned in the midst of the thunderbolt;
furthermore, it is the very origin of the illuminator.
Having gone to the wide middle, one should draw the womb (yoni) above;
and the state of lordship over the earth [is established] upon the head of Mahākāla.
In that same manner, one should place Kāma and the others, as well as Dhātrīśa, who is born of Prāṇa;
accompanied by Guhyaśakti, he [Dhātrīśa] causes Caṇḍikā to bestow [the fruit].
Furthermore, one should extract the two seeds of birth through transposition;
[they are] the armor of Rudra and the blood on Gandhamādana.
Having placed the end of *rut* (the letter *u*) submerged within [the letter *a*], and having established the source of the Sustainer (*dhātṛ*) in two places,
there is the Great Rudra named Sūkṣma, seated upon the throne of Ambikā.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of the burner (RA), one should place Rāga and the others upon the head;
likewise, one should place the goddess Mahākālī from the fire, arising from the cruel.
In the half of Vāruṇī is Tārākṣī; again, that [half] is subtly divided. Rudrāṇī is in the ninth; furthermore, at the end of the thigh is the source of fragrance.
One should draw a red lotus with eight petals;
O Goddess, the drinking [of the nectar] situated within it is declared to be in the reverse order.
Having drawn that with the foremost of dharmas, the center alone is [marked] by Caṇa;
then, its initial seed-syllable is indeed Ananta, born from blood.
O Goddess, one should place the āmoḍī within the milk, the end of the sheep at the end, and the inner skin on the red Rudrāsana; then, one should again install Ananta.
One should extract the white vital breath (prāṇa) mounted upon the seat of the root-staff;
it is of auspicious color, Mahākāla, in the abode of the Rishis of the Rudras.
The Vārāha, Pārthiva, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brāhmaṇa [liṅgas]—
O Goddess, such is the sequence, and likewise the others as before.
O Goddess, first one should place the Heart-mantra for Viṣṇu upon the heart;
then the six-syllabled [mantra] of Śiva should be known, and thereafter the Dharma-mantra likewise.
One should employ the weapon-mantra everywhere; one should arrange ten and one [syllables].
From Brahmā to Āśāśvatī, these are the elements (bhūtārṇas) produced in the past.
The ten elements in their respective places flowed forth from his feet,
appearing like the five elements combined, with a radiance like that of ten thousand suns.
In the eighth [petal], which consists of all sacrifices and is gentle, there are various weapons and various ornaments on the four petals.
When the triangle is fixed, one should place the mantra beginning with "Siṃha" (the Lion) and so forth;
in the sixteenth [triangle], there is the application of the letters of the Mātṛkā, which is indeed the Vaidarbha style.
O Goddess of the Suras, it extends upward from the end of the *varṇas* to the end of the earth;
it has the face of a boar, large eyes, and is situated as far as the mortal world.
One should worship half of that [deity] in the region of the face, Pitāmaha with the two feet, Yogīśvarī in the syllable *ku*, and Prāṇa in the breath.
O Goddess, having worshipped Kaṅkaṭa on the path, as well as Uditā and the two Aśvins;
and having worshipped Mahāviṣṇu in the heart, and the Sun and Moon in the right and left [sides].
In his arms and belly are the Vasus and the Khas; on the tips of his fangs is the Earth.
He is the God who embodies all the gods, the manifest embodiment of Brahman.
[He holds] conchs, shields, swords, nooses, goads, maces, and bows.
Or else, [he is] like the luster of a dark cloud or the sun joined with the sun.
I am on his right side, Brahmā on his left, and Viṣṇu before him— Hari, who is richly adorned with the splendor of white nectar and filled with bliss.
Because Ananta is in the west, one should perform the rites beginning with the limbs starting from Mūrti according to the previously stated procedure, excluding Vasundharā.
Having worshipped the immensely powerful Nārasiṃha with his respective mantra— one who has lotuses and lotus-hand symbols as his seat and who is radiant yellow— [one should proceed].

O Goddess, a person whose self is purified by having conquered the six internal enemies and who is devoted to his own duty [perceives] Śivā situated in the center of the sky, like the straight [meridian line] situated in the middle of the heavens.
Mounted upon Raktabhairava, before him is Vedabhairava,
accompanied by Śubhaśakti, with a serpent at his cruel front.
Having uttered that Mahāviṣṇu, may Tārākṣī, blazing with power before her, protect [me], having pierced through [the obstacle] and mounted upon fat and blood.
One dwells in even greater prosperity upon the head of Sahasrāra;
listen now to what kind of being resides before that fourth [face], Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, O Goddess, there is Nārasiṃha, who is again and again terrifying;
then Kātvamadhya, Dhātrīśa, and Raktarudra with the bindu.
O Goddess, having extracted Mṛtyu from the front, Guṇānta from Meṣa,
and Gandhānta from the middle asterism, one should place them upon Śiva.
Having extracted Mahākāla, he stands upon the central seat;
before him is the seed-syllable of Ambikā, ending with Vāmā, consisting of three seed-syllables.
In this way, other external seed-syllables are [to be arranged] according to how they may be;
by means of thirty-two divisions, in accordance with the sequence of this Goddess.
O Goddess, it must be understood that I shall now speak before you this secret,
which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, nor is there any division or portion of it.
O Goddess, through the various divisions of the primordial Vidyā, there is thus a ninefold [Vidyā];
this thirty-two-syllable Vidyā is joined with the original Prastāva.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter in the venerable Kubjikāmata.
The Goddess said:
I am worthy of worship by the God of gods; my life has become fruitful, for I am that Great Goddess previously described, the cutter of all bonds.
As I know it again and again, this [knowledge] shall never fail him;
it is hidden in all the Āgamas and Tantras, and it grants all desires.
O Lord, [it is found] with effort in the Mārtaṇḍabhairava, likewise in the Tripurārṇava,
in the Sarvasaṃmohana Tantra, and in the Rurubheda.
Now I desire to hear that Vidyā through its traditional transmission—
the Āpūr-apatnī-sāman— which bestows both seen and unseen fruits.
O Lord of Gods, O Master, if you are pleased with me, you should deign to explain in detail,
according to the sequence of the Aghorāstra, the [mantras] for the interior of the house.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Great Goddess, this was well asked; indeed, in former times it was heard by Śravaṇa, as well as by Brahmā, O Lord Vāsava, and by the high-souled Viṣṇu.
O Goddess, that supreme Vidyā, having been perfectly propitiated by Śukra, who is the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśa), spoke it to Viṣṇu.
Now I shall speak; listen, O large-eyed one!
That wise Guru, according to the previously stated sequence, [performs] the venerable Śrīkrama.
Having drawn Mount Meru upon a pure ground with substances such as gorocanā and others,
one should likewise place the Great Goddess Mātṛkā there in union with it.
Having duly arranged the Mātṛkā by means of the conjunction of the five Praṇavas and its extraction,
one should then extract the supreme mantra.
A person should perform the extraction of that [mantra] as previously described, joined with five *praṇavas*,
and having interspersed it with the *navātman* mantra, he should recite it at the time of *japa*.
I bow to the Great Goddess, whose very form is all knowledge,
who moves through the sky, who stands amidst elephants, who is shaped like a womb, the ever-new Mother.
"Shall I not act? O Yoginīs, you who dwell upon the earth and are established in the highest station, I shall extract that Vidyā; listen to it with diligence."
O Goddess, in the temple of Kailāsa, he who is known by the name Śrīkaṇṭha should be understood as the first syllable; let this be so in the Traipura [system].
Beyond that, on Mount Mandara, is the [place] of Krūravarṇa given by Śiva;
it is the fourth among the Bhūtas, where Śaṅkhinī is established.
Having established that [first one], the wise man, endowed with the preceding [qualities],
should then establish the second, O lady of beautiful hips, and after that the third.
O Goddess, on Mount Mandara, in the Ṛṣimālā region, that [state] was previously only Kevala; thereafter, situated in its midst, is Pañcāta where Bhairava resides.
One should know the fourth to be absolute; the fourth belongs to Varuṇa.
It is secret, situated in the center of the bhaga, on Mount Mandara, and conjoined with the subtle.
One should know that as the sixth; now hear the seventh and the eighth:
in three places, the syllables *haṃsa* (with the color of a swan), *tu*, *kāṃbhava*, and the fire (*agni*) with a bindu.
O Goddess of the Gods, in the first syllabic unit (varṇasāṃkalpa) he is adorned with the power of knowledge; in the second syllabic unit (varṇasakala) he is mounted upon a corpse.
Having first extracted the syllable of Karālī as it is situated in the yantra,
one should then join it with the syllables beginning with Dhruva, followed by the ninth and tenth [syllables].
On Mount Mandara, within the Bhūtamālā, [he is] Chāgala, borne by peacocks,
seated upon the center of a Bindu, and joined with Sūkṣmarudra.
Having extracted the color of wrath (K), joined with the anklet (Ū), [one obtains] the eleventh [letter]. O Great Goddess, [the letters] of the color of a swan (H) [are repeated] again and again.
Having extracted [the syllables] from the three locations and adorned them with fierce phonemes,
one should join the first with the letter *ta* and the second with the *mūrti*.
In the third [syllable], however, up to the end of *dhruva*, it is joined with the *dīpanī* in three places;
furthermore, the goddess consists of fifteen syllables, including the name *Śrīkaṇṭha*.
In the midst of the universe, in the abode of Śiva, first on Mount Gandhamādana,
in Rudrava and in Rudramālā, it is endowed with the Gāyatrī.
There resides the goddess Bhujaṅgabhairavī, the Illuminator (Dīpanī),
on Kailāsa in the middle of the left, conjoined with the primordial syllable.
Once again, Maheśānī arises from the word "Ghora";
then, having extracted Śrīkaṇṭha, the sound "Ghorā" follows—of this there is no doubt.
The one named Kāla is indeed Mahārudra, who is situated between the two;
by the conjunction of the letters beginning with Dhruva, he is the twenty-third, without a doubt.
O Goddess, when the syllable *ṭha* is placed in the middle, it becomes twenty-four syllables long;
this is where Chāgalī resides in the eleventh station of the seasons.
Where Dīpanī is situated, mounted upon Bhujaṅgabhairava, there is Anantā joined with Krūra; this is the number of the Tattvas, without a doubt.
Combine the trident (Śūla), the goddess Chāgalī, the lamp (Dīpanī), the subtle bindu,
and the eleventh letter [Na], joined with the goddess Māyā.
Nārāyaṇī, the goddess of mortals, is adorned by Sūkṣmarudra;
this mantra consists of twenty-eight syllables and is embellished by Krodha and Sūkṣma.
Furthermore, the goddess Nārāyaṇī is adorned by the subtle Rudra;
the goddess Vajriṇī is situated there, positioned in the middle of the left.
Make it twofold: joined with Sūkṣmarudra and also unjoined with Rā. O Sureśvarī, on Kailāsa, it is joined with the one preceded by Ṛtu and with Rā.
The Goddess of thirty-two syllables is established in the form of the phonemes.
Thus, O Goddess, have I declared it in the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya) on the further shore.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs, one should thereafter perform the placement on the face;
then, one should perform the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa) upon the body according to the sounds of the Mātṛkā.
The teacher should perform the sixfold breath-control (ṣoḍhānyāsa) for the eight [deities] beginning with the three knowledges (trividyā),
just as the Goddess was previously described in detail by means of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā).
Then the Goddess, having performed the deposition of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa) twenty-seven times in number,
worshipped the Lords of the Śrīkrama together with the series of their sandals (pādukās).
Then, with flowers, perfumes, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth, joined with ritual offerings,
[he should worship] the eight seats and then the eight external [deities] to the Goddess in due order.
Having offered the supreme ear-pendant through the yoga of the conduct of the samaya,
one should form the supportless mudrā and dismiss [the deity], saying, "Forgive me."
Standing properly before her, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand, one hundred and eight times;
having understood this, O lady of excellent limbs, she is to be reached through meditation and is beyond the senses.
Having meditated upon her, whose face is like the full moon, who is adorned with ornaments,
who has five faces and ten arms, and whose breasts are full and elevated;
It is the secret of secrets, the most excellent of things to be hidden;
it is the purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of auspicious things.
Thus it has been spoken according to the sequence of yoga and explained, O Mistress of the Gods.
Now, O Goddess, I shall proclaim another [teaching] that is my own secret and difficult to obtain.
I shall now briefly describe that which is divided by the non-difference of the Vidyās and so forth:
O Goddess, formerly, when the great ocean was being churned by the gods and asuras.
O beloved, the gods, led by Ravi and Śakra, were defeated by the Asuras;
therefore, they all came to where I was staying.
Having prostrated with body and speech,
Indra, trembling and deeply distressed, reported exactly what had occurred along with his preceptor.
Then, with a serene mind, [I beheld] that auspicious one who bestows heroism, glory, and victory;
who grants enjoyment and liberation; and who bestows speech and auspiciousness.

O Goddess, it bestows knowledge and sovereignty; it grants the supernatural powers of the sword and the netherworld, as well as the eightfold lordships, the state of moving through the sky, and the fruits desired for heaven.
O Goddess, what is the use of much speaking? Having reflected upon this many times, [know that it] bestows the fruits of all desires and is composed of the essence of all the gods.
The thirty-two-syllable mantra of Manu is proclaimed in the West in the Kaula tradition;
now the Vidyā known as Mayā, the mistress of the Kṛttikā family, is declared.
That Vidyā which deludes the three worlds, categorized by its higher and lower divisions,
was proclaimed to the preceptor Mahendra by that best of teachers.
The Great Goddess, who has come down through the lineage of succession, is declared to have three divisions;
*pāra* is designated as Śakti, while *pāram* is said here to be Śiva.
O Goddess, the Para-ogha is first, the Divya-ogha follows immediately after that, and the Divyādi is the third; the Guru has arrived from all of these.
One should always worship Brahmā for the sake of purity of body, Janārdana for the sake of purity of speech, and Rudra for the sake of purity of mind; thus one attains triple purity.
The *ulakrama*, the *madhyajyeṣṭha*, and the *śekhara* are to be understood;
I shall explain them correctly for the sake of protecting devotees alone.
Even for one who knows all the scriptures and is devoted to the conduct of the ancients,
one should not cause him to perform a prostration if he has fallen from the *oli* lineage.
I bow to the Great Goddess, who is served by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
as well as by hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, by the Pannagas, and by the gods and Asuras.
One should revere Kulakubjikā, in whom reside the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the universe];
one should thus extract that Vidyā from the center of Meru.
O Goddess, having worshipped the convention (samaya) and the lineage succession (kulakrama) as before,
[worship her] where she is established on Mount Mandara in the Ṛṣimālā.
O Goddess, the first [point] is to be known as the center of the body; the second is the middle of the left;
and the third is situated in the middle of the [left] portion.
The fourth [syllable] is joined with the goddess Māyā and Medarā;
at the end of Vāgīśvarī and Valokā, there are five and five—of this there is no doubt.
One should place Cchāgalī in the middle of the Bhūtas, Śikhinī between the ears,
and Kailāsa on Mount Mandara, O Goddess, together with the eastern direction.
One should know that as the sixth; now hear of the seventh and the eighth.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, having extracted the Navātman, you [should proceed] further.
O Goddess, place the seed-syllable situated in the moon and wine within the station of Ambikā; [place] Trimūrti Bhairava in the eastern abode of Niṣadhā.
O Sovereign of the Gods, when the region of Śiva is conjoined with Kubjikā,
one should divide the syllable *haṃsa* threefold according to the sequence of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Even though it is threefold, it is joined with the beloved vowel, the fire, and the bindu;
Śiva, conjoined with Ananta, is the seed of creation in the middle.
O Goddess, it is first unbroken by the ocean of Niṣadha, and again joined with the end of Dhruva; it consists of ten syllables, without a doubt.
Then, O Goddess, Cāmuṇḍā took Karmarudra alone from the hermitage of the sage and went into the midst of the honeycomb, O beloved.
Mahākāla alone is situated in the center of the letter Bha;
in the eleventh [position], he has the color of wrath, and Kalālī is established there.
O Goddess, [the seed-syllable] joined with the letters beginning with *dhruva* (oṃ), situated within the *bilva*,
and endowed with the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), resides in the jewel-palace of Kailāsa.
O Maheśānī, beginning with Kūrmarudra, it is joined with the five-syllable mantra of the Kula; then again, by means of the method of extraction starting from the beginning.
This [mantra] consists of nineteen syllables; Śrīkaṇṭha is the twentieth here.
In the eleventh [chapter], however, is the one called Ghorā, who was previously on Gandhamādana.
O Pārvatī, where the Gāyatrī is conjoined with Sadyojāta,
there is the trident-staff in hell, and the Bhairava named Bhujaṅga.
O Goddess, on Mount Gandhamādana, Śiva is divided into thirty-two [forms] by Ananta;
furthermore, Mahākāla is established upon the seat beginning with Dhruva.
Taking the syllable situated between the *ṭha* and *va*, which consists of as many letters as there are in the Gāyatrī mantra,
and which is the color of a swan, one should divide it into two according to the distinction between creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and maintenance (*sthiti*).
O Goddess of the gods, the first letter beginning with *dhru* is known by the name Chāgalī;
she is mounted upon the seat of the staff of the trident, possessing infinite limbs on Mount Gandhamādana.
O Sovereign Goddess, on the first day of the Haṃsa month, the head was severed by Akrūra;
on the second, the goddess Cchāgalī [was worshipped] with a trident-staff by Trimūrti.
O Goddess of the Suras, these two syllables bring the three worlds under control;
having extracted the syllable *karāli*, the word *dhruvādī* should follow.
Furthermore, these two syllables are radiant; the one between the *tāra* (oṃ) is subtle.
On Mount Mandara, between the sages, are Cāmuṇḍā and Kūrmabhairava.
O Goddess, on Kailāsa and in the temple of Vāma, one should utter it twice;
it is undoubtedly preceded by the syllable *Ru*, joined with the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
I have declared that which is the most essential of essentials and the secret of secrets;
it is the flow toward purification, occurring both in direct and reverse order.
In the seed-syllable of Śakti, there is likewise the previous birth and the color of a swan;
O Goddess, in the same way, it is within the Mā-bīja, situated below the Haṃsa according to the sequence of yoga.
There, Maṇḍiśa Bhairava is joined with the bindu of the fire of the beloved's fall;
then again, O Goddess of Gods, one should apply the Vāruṇa [element].

Thus, having first performed the placement (nyāsa) by means of various divisions or sequences, or by enclosing [the mantra] with the *mātṛkā* mantra, one should perform the placement of its receptacle (tadgṛhinyāsa) in the upward, eastern, southern, and western directions.
Then one should place the northern face and the half-syllable;
worship and meditation are prescribed just as before, without a doubt.
Through the practice of yoga for six months, the practitioner shall become equal to me;
he [subdues] this fire, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Viśvaga, and Śaśin.
One should worship Īśāna in the center, and then the seven groups of eight goddesses;
[one should worship] from Dharma up to the Pretas, according to the division of five times five.
Furthermore, by means of the sequence of twenty-eight, which is divided sixfold,
the *liṅga* situated in the center of the *yoni* is encased within the *yoni*, O God.
In the midst of that, one should repeatedly perceive the form of Vāmana;
indeed, in the center, by means of the churning yoga, it blazes like the fire of time (kālāgni).
From their union, O Goddess, the power of Śiva arises, and from that bliss is born;
consequently, there occurs the state of immobility of both Śiva and Śakti.
One should contemplate oneself being bathed by that nectar;
for this is supreme, divine, and characterized by the highest bliss.
This secret of Maṇipūra has been revealed to you;
though it was hidden within the mantras, it is now disclosed as equal to Lakṣmī herself.
Even for one who has attained the path of accomplishment, [success] is difficult to obtain; how much more so for others?
Success is inevitably achieved within the stated time, provided that one does not disregard these words.
But rather, one should salute that Śāmbhavī Māyā, which has the form of a garland of light and resides in the center of the path of the wheel,
or [salute] the Great Goddess of the Vratas.
Because it bestows manifest results through the states of devotion and love,
and because it does not contradict any of the scriptures, I do not consider the *Yoginī-mahā* to be eternal.
When the Bhairavī Tantra is active, all castes are twice-born;
when the Bhairavī Tantra has ceased, all castes remain distinct.
Thus, O Queen of the Gods, this secret has been revealed;
O daughter of Nanda, you who are endowed with devotion, it must be imparted by you everywhere.
Since the recitation (*japa*) consists of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*), the rite of oblation (*huta-kriyā*) is half of that;
[the worship] of the Lord of the Mind (*mano-vīśvara*) is superior, O Vasudeva... [and so forth].
O Supreme Goddess, this Vidyā is the source of all desires in this world;
by [reciting] three hundred thousand [times] of the goddess who consists of seventy million [syllables], one shall attain perfection.
Svāhā, Sañjita on the head, Ṅe Vāhasaṃkṣreṃ Hrīṃ Hrāṃ; this Vidyā named Juhūtejasaṃkarṣaṇī bestows all fruits together.
Hā svāmanāṃ kraṭokṣu vopracohaṃkaṃ hrīṃ oṃ ai& juḥ saḥ havīśvanayetva manākaśīrṣakaṃ svaḥ yanohaṃsaṃ hrīṃ ruḥ svaṃ u || 0 ||
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter in the venerable Kubjikāmata. || 0 ||
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, cause of the causes of the universe;
that which has been taught in the Kubjikāmata in its extent of ninety million verses—
My consciousness has arisen, bestowing the attainment of the state of Nirvana; today, through you, I have been liberated from the manifold impressions known as latent tendencies.
I ask again concerning that knowledge which leads to eternal liberation;
it has emerged from the Śaiva tradition, not from the Ākulika, and is derived from the Pañcakalpa, the Vedas, and other sources.
The final doctrine of the Pañcarātra and other systems is supreme knowledge that bestows liberation;
yet those who attained the state of Brahman through austerity were not [merely] "rich in austerity" (tapodhana).
In this matter, I shall show you that which has been extracted from those [scriptures],
which even the gods do not know, let alone other people.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'ha', up to Sadāśiva, upon the locations of the body;
it is said that the letter 'ha' is Śiva, while the syllable *oṃ* is called Śakti.

Likewise, one should place the syllable *U*, which consists of the *bindu* and *nāda* and has the *bindu* at its head, followed by Śrīkaṇṭha; then the deities beginning with *Asya* and ending with *Anta*.
One should place the end of the left [hand] upon the head; Mālinī originates from the head. Then one should place that middle [finger], and again the first [finger] as Māninī.
O Goddess, from the region at the end of Śrīkaṇṭha,
in front of Dīpta, and before Merurudra, there is that which originates from fragrance, ending with the sound "ru."
Having raised up the depressed middle, this shall be her seat;
it is the color of a god, bestowed by Śiva, with its center marked and provided with fat.
Then, O Goddess, one should offer meat mixed with an abundance of perfumes to that Rūpin; listen now to what follows after this.
Ānanda is indeed the groundless state, while Prāṇarudra is the absolute;
Medorudra, the Great Rudra, is endowed with auspicious devotion.
The blood of the Rudras, situated upon the seat of the Red Rudra,
should be offered upon their heads on Mount Mandara, arising from the subtle source.
O Goddess, they know the letter *tā* alone when situated between two *bhā*s as *Tārākṣī*;
and again, the white *ka*, *la*, *vā*, and *pa* when situated between two *si*s.
And O Goddess, one should place Jñāna in front, red upon the blood;
O Pārvatī, one should place it situated upon Sūkṣmarudra above Śakra.
One should worship Dhātrīśa in the center of the beloved ones, and Kāla above the left [breast];
being a celibate student, having conquered anger, and endowed with the practice of vows.
Pure, wearing pure garments, adorned with garlands, eating at the proper time, and firm in his vows,
he should practice meditation in the three places within the extensive white [meditation].
This is Śiva, the God of gods and teacher of the world, who possesses the luster of cow’s urine and jasmine flowers,
and whose single waistband is fastened by Ananta.
I wear a crown of matted hair and am resplendent with the autumnal moon;
on my left side is a most beautiful water-pot encircled by the serpent Ananta.
On the right, he fashioned a row of letters composed of various garlands,
which was indeed an infinite lotus-thread, the end of the lotus-skin.
One should meditate upon Śiva, the peaceful Lord who sits upon a lotus and moves according to His own will;
here, by means of the thread [of meditation], one should contemplate the six limbs and the six steps as previously described by oneself.
O Goddess, one should place the thirty-two syllables within the center of the *piḍa*:
Umā, Durgā, Prabhā, Satī, Cāmuṇḍā, Haṃsī, and Pāsinī.
Vijayā, Virajā, Viśvā, Jayā, and Sumukheśvarī;
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Ambikā, Icchā, and Bhayapradā.
Dākṣāyaṇī, Surānandā, Bhadrakālī, Kulāṅganā,
Kulaśobhā, Mahādevī, Hṛllekhā, and Gaganāsatī.
Furthermore, Raktākarālikā is Mahāsūkṣmā Sarasvatī;
he who is seated upon the great seat of Kāla is named Saṃhāra.
Joined with half of Pāvaka and well-endowed with the force of Vāyu,
and endowed with Anugraha and Śiva, he himself moves between the east and the west.

O Goddess of the Gods, one should place those seed-syllables of knowledge in their respective locations; O Sovereign of the Gods, one should arrange the remainder as previously described for the five-syllable mantra.
O Goddess, O Śivā, one should draw the most excellent [mandala] of the planets in the terrible celestial palace within oneself, in front of the Lord of the Dūtīs.
One should place the bindu upon the head; that which arises from the thighs of Māninī is white and situated in the middle of the heart, while its foremost part is the middle section.
One should visualize Vāgīśa as the seat and place Akrūra upon the head; O Goddess, one should likewise meditate upon the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, and Kṛṣṇa himself.
Furthermore, [place] the letter *pa* in the center, the *śuṣma* (the letter *ra*) upon the head of the *krūra* (the letter *kha*),
the *śivā* (the letter *i*) in the middle of the *vila* (the letter *la*), and the *bhairava* (the letter *ba*) with a *bindu* at its forefront.
Having performed the *dhruva-anta* at the center of the *kāla*, there should be the mounting upon the *dhenu*;
then, one should mount the *khaṇḍapāvaka* while holding a *vetasa* staff in the hand.
One should establish the subtle Rudras within the supreme wheel of Māninī;
first, they are situated upon their seats ending with Dhruva in the ninefold [array] previously described.
In the temple of the Rudras, one should first write "sadyaḥ" before it;
having extracted the letter of the navel (na), one should place it in the middle along with the bindu (ṃ).
One should extract the bracelet for Viśvarūpa, Vajriṇī, and Bhautika;
indeed, one should utter the salutation and the first seed-syllable according to the prescribed sequence.

O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, [the mantra] consists of the syllables *aghora*, *vasu*, *narda*, the worship (*pūjā*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the seed-syllables (*bīja*), and the letters of the elements (*bhūtavarṇa*), joined with the four.
We worship the Goddess; may we be released from death and increase [our merit].
Having come together with the seed, the peaceful, the infinite, and the meditated upon.
One should cause everything to increase for the virtuous and likewise uplift them once more;
[one should employ] this seed-syllable beginning with Amarīśa, conjoined with Sthāṇu, Rudra, and the others.
Having extracted that [syllable] from its beginning and placed it before her,
one should extract those [syllables] from the three locations and place them in their own positions with six syllables.
The slayer of Rākṣasas, the slayer of Vala, the one with a gracious countenance, the one whose form is Time;
the Victorious, the Conqueror, the All-conquering, and to the one who has transcended the mind, to Bala.
Having worshipped the form with the syllables of the *bhūta-śakti* and with words such as "Saṃkrandana" and others, one who is firm in his vow should then recite the *Rudra-lakṣa*.
O Goddess, this mantra, which bestows desired fruits, is the playful sport of Death;
it is formed by extracting the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu (M), placing 'Ru' at the end, and adding 'Ha' before it.
The world also [worships] the third Ekarudra, who is stepped upon by the head;
he resides within the space of Mount Mandara, beginning with the Self, resembling a bindu.
One should diligently install Śiva, who is born from half of her [Pārvatī],
and Rudra as the third [deity] of Māninī, whose color is like that of a cloud.
One should provide a seat for Dhātrīśa situated between the sages;
and in the practice of accomplishment, one should draw Dīpanī in the southern region.
Furthermore, O Goddess, at the tip of the nose there is the unstable Rudrāsana;
at the end, when the thousandfold rays flash forth, it extends from the middle of the heart to the end of the fixed point (dhruva).
The great Rudras are named Kāka; they are the illuminators, subtle, and moving upward.
One should duly place the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ga* in front of the eleven [Rudras].
The fourth [state] is in the midst of the elements, while the beloved [Vajra] is in the center of Vairocana;
as the seat of Mahākālī, he is embraced on Gandhamādana.
O Goddess, let there be prostrations for the sake of the body to other vegetables; know yourself to be united with the Supreme State, as previously described.
That which is called the "unoriginated nature" has, from the perspective of ultimate reality, arisen;
furthermore, these are the seeds of Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
And Nārāyaṇa, ending with Caurī, as well as Navātmā situated in front;
likewise, the four [deities] with the Vasus of the gods, and Vahni with his own Bhūtas.
O Queen of the Gods, one should place [the deity] within the center of the body according to the prescribed method;
[one should meditate on] the Lord as Ardhanārīśvara, adorned with ornaments all over his body.

He praised the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, who is as beautiful as the moon, the sun, and fire, who is enchanting with various ornaments, and who is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great being.
In the left and right [hands], he holds a noose and a goad; [in the others] a rosary and a human skull-cup.
He resembles molten gold and is as red as vermilion.
O Goddess, one should satisfy the lions on the Viṣṭi day as before;
the lotus is to be worshipped in the west, and the arrow is located in the direction of Kubera (the north).
One should worship Rudra, Ākhaṇḍaleya, and Īśvara, who resembles the sun, in the four directions starting from the east; and furthermore, Hṛllekhā and Gadā.
They praised the red-hued goddess Karālikā, the great and subtle Maheśvara,
while they themselves, adorned with braided hair and holding blue lotuses, offered their salutations.

One should worship the six types [of deities] beginning with the eight *pūrva*s, the Vasus, and the ninth, Cara; one should worship the Lord of Speech (Brahmā) in the southeast, the Lord of Fire (Agni) in the south, the Lord of Cows (Indra) in the east, and the Lord of Water (Varuṇa) in the west.
In the sacrifice, one should diligently honor the sixty-four [deities] beginning with Brāhmaṇī, according to the prescribed ritual, in the northeast corner of the Atri-born [Atri’s lineage].
O King, the fire sacrifice (homa) was performed in the southern sacrificial pit with parched grain, sesame seeds, rice,
self-blossomed flowers, and also with the wood of the Bilva tree.

Having first recited the mantra five hundred thousand times while it is mixed with camphor and musk and saturated with jaggery, honey, and ghee, one should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa).
Furthermore, he should offer refreshing drinks that are new, fragrant, and pleasing;
eating sparingly in three portions, he remains devoted to the practice of his vow.
Then, when they have been satisfied by the dogs, the two supreme lords shall bestow everything desired, including the state of moving through the air and the attainment of the eightfold perfections.
Having leveled a portion of ground and smeared it with sandalwood and agallochum,
one should fashion there a mandala consisting of four petals and three yonis.
Then, one should gradually arrange the letters on the outside; beginning with *ā* and ending with *ī*, one should place them as the Mistress of the World (*jagadīśvarī*).
Having meditated upon his form there in the heart-lotus as before,
the yogi revolves with his mind for as long as Brahmā lives.
O Goddess, Hari holds Hara on his left and Hari on his right;
likewise, the Lord Śiva holds the trident and the conch, while Hari holds the discus.
The goddess should first place the syllable *tāra* (oṃ) with the bindu, which is a firebrand for the heart, upon the heart;
then she should likewise place the word *sarvānta* (the end of all), followed by *meṣa* (ram), upon the head.
At the end of Maholka, [he worships] Nityatṛptā, Vīra, and Vīrolka;
at the crest-lock (śikhā), he worships Anādibodha and the third, Parameśvarī.
Indeed, at the end of the third letter of the first group, "svā" and "taṃ" were spoken;
then, suddenly, by the scent of wine, he [uttered] everything again, including the fifth [vowel].
One should place Praśakti at the tips of the nose for the protection of the eyes;
Vāgīśa at the Sahasrārka, and Anantaśakti at the Kaṇṭaka.
One should worship with devotion as before, without creating a distinction between difference and non-difference;
for one whose mind is full of doubt perishes, attaining neither happiness nor the supreme goal.
One should place supreme trust in dharma; one should never trust in adharma.
For by means of dharma, even through a sacrifice, the deities are nourished.
Therefore, they know the world to consist of mantra and dharma to consist of mantra;
having conquered the earth through dharma, [they travel] by means of divine, mind-captivating vehicles.
Even today, gods and those whose wealth is asceticism are seen sporting;
yet for those whose wisdom does not abide in this mantra which is the very soul of dharma,
there is neither heaven nor liberation, neither in this world nor in the next.
Both the north and the south—these two [are the paths] for all embodied beings.
Those two paths having been lost, unrighteousness increases;
indeed, one is threatened by births such as those of the *darddharī*, the *daṃśūka*, and other venomous creatures.
In those [hells], many sufferings arising from misery are experienced;
there is not even a trace of happiness there—alas, O Supreme Goddess!
Afflicted by the suffering of dwelling in the womb, deluded by ignorance in childhood,
fallen into the objects of the senses in youth, and facing death in old age;
The birth of one who has died is like the turning of a water-wheel;
therefore, the people of the world are restrained by the words of the Vedas.
One should place the middle [part] by avoiding the defects of the beginning and so forth;
like tanned leather, it attains great softness through the removal of its impurities.
Therefore, O Goddess, a wise person who knows the mantras, having applied himself according to the prescribed rule and procedure as previously described within this difficult-to-traverse yantra,
becomes the sovereign lord of the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as Khecarī and the rest.
Now I shall proclaim another [method], which is most secret and difficult to find even on this earth.
By the mere non-recognition of which the three worlds are agitated;
the Goddess is the two seed-syllables, and at the end, the Goddess again comes as the pair.
One should know that which is situated on the ground of the *āṣāḍhī* in the garland of syllables as the third; and that which is at the end of the barley (*yava*) is the fourth.
The drop (bindu) of that syllable, situated below the two lines of the letter *i*,
is the facial syllable of Mālinī, residing within the nine-petaled lotus.
In the Tārākṣī-grahamālā, one should place the head ending with *vaṃ oṃ*;
at its end, upon the peak of fragrance, is Ananta, conjoined with the cruel [syllable].
Nārāyaṇa should be joined with Sani; Kāma should have a red seat.
Up to Rudra, there is Krūraśikhara, and Pinākin is above him.
In the eleventh position of the sages is Arghīśa, who is above him.
Furthermore, its beginning is situated in the letter Ra, endowed with fragrance and a sprout.
Having extracted the syllable *na*, which is the first letter, from the root of the right [hand], that is the staff;
the seat for it is the *mālinī* born from the mouth.
Having placed *ru* at the end in front, and likewise *vi* in the middle;
they know that the great Rudra named *medas* is situated alone above.
Furthermore, O Śivā, one should place the subtle Rudra upon Mālinī, which is of the same color as this [Rudra] and joined with the tree, by means of its being the seat of the red Rudra.
The first seed-syllable of Mālinī is conjoined with Jhaṇṭīśa;
it is Saṃvartaka, Mahārudra, and Bhava situated upon Astirudra.
It is red, Rudanta, Akrūra, Prāṇa, and then Meṣa.
And in its own eleventh position, it is of whatever color [it may be], with a bindu at its head.
And in front of this is Phetkārī, accompanied by Khaṇḍasomeśvara;
thus, this is the supreme secret, purifying, and the granter of all desires.
O Goddess, by the mere remembrance of him, even the most heroic Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas flee away like deer terrified by a lion.
Through the recitation and fire-offerings of this [mantra], enjoyment and liberation are placed in the hand;
Hari himself accomplishes one's own goal when it is recited for women and for the acquisition of knowledge.
One should not harbor enmity toward them even for hundreds of offenses.
One should draw a square [mandala] provided with streets and gates.
The lotus of the throat, the supreme goad facing in all directions,
endowed with sixteen spokes and the digits [of the moon] through the sequential application of the phonemes.
One should place the thirty-two syllables in the center of the circle of letters;
furthermore, outside the four consonants, there is an eight-petaled lotus.
Having likewise arranged the phonemes, the Lord of the Classes (Vargiṇ) spoke the six-syllable mantra;
in all the coverings of the elements, the deities are Brahmā and Ananta.
Furthermore, O lady of excellent complexion, one should establish the Nārasiṃha [mantra] conjoined with Śiva within the fire; having inscribed it there, one should accomplish all tasks.
O Pārvatī, having placed there the great lion of the Sudarśana,
which has tawny eyes, fangs, a terrifying appearance, a magnificent body, and is exceedingly difficult to conquer;
Therein, [he holds] a conch, a sword, a shield, and again a javelin and a mallet;
as well as a noose and a goad, a lotus, and a bow with an arrow.
[He saw] the god of gods, the teacher of the world, who bestows boons, holds a lotus-stalk and fire,
is clothed in silk garments, and is adorned with red ornaments.
His gaze and his single face possess a splendor equal to the sun;
I am situated within his mouth, and he stands upon the two feet of Brahmā.
He is remembered as having Siṃhikā’s mouth and the goddess Kuśā within his belly.
The fires in the eyes are difficult to endure, as are those in the solar orb of Śakra.
At the beginning and end of words such as "omniscient" (sarvajña) and so forth, there is first a group of seven syllables;
the second [group] consists of six syllables, and the second [syllable] shall be accompanied by the goad (aṅkuśa).
Having placed the seed-syllable of the Goddess in the supreme [position], one should place the armor with nine syllables;
O Goddess, the eye-mantra is then applied again to the words.
To Viṣṇu, to Īśvara, to Amoda, to Gagana, to Vasu, to Tapa, to Ananta, to Nārāyaṇa, to Rāma, to Yama, to Yajñapuruṣa, to Sarvakriya, to Hara, to the one whose beloved is the joy of all women,
to Yajana, to Lakṣmīśvara, to Varuṇa, to Nṛsiṃha, to Skanda, to Halin, and to Nanda.

To Hayagrīva, to Nandaka, to Oṃkāra, to Phaṭkāra, Svāhāpati, and to Hari-Hara; the primary forms and images— [bearing] the conch, discus, noose, goad, arrow, and bow— are established within the center of the *piṇḍa*.
Through the sequential application of the vowels to the seed-syllables (bīja), the All-pervading Lord [is manifested];
these are the other Śaktis, the Jinas, who are celebrated as these very forms (mūrti).
She is Ramā, Rākā, Prabhā, Satyā, Citrakṣaumī,
Hiraṇyagā, Dhāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Surā, Raudrī, Umā, Saṃdhyā, and Niśā.
Śivā, Vijayā, Sarvadā, Nityā, Sarvāṇī, Sarvamaṅgalā,
Lakṣmī, Śrī, Rati, Kānti, Medhā, Prajñā, and Sarasvatī.
Āhlādinī, Bhagānandā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā—
these should be worshipped in front, duly depicted within the yantra according to the prescribed ritual.
One should place Keśava and the others in the position of the vowels on the eight petals of the Śakti-form;
one should assign the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) to the corners and the deities of Viṣṭi and the rest to the petals.
In the center, within the corners of the triangle, I am Brahmā and Hari himself,
seated upon the expansive seat known as Anantabhogāsana, the yogic seat.
In the west, it shines like the sun; wherever its hoods spread,
it is joyfully served by ṛṣis and hosts of siddhas.
The lords of the gods, adorned with their own ornaments, had their hair tied in braids;
some were embraced by their beloveds, while others held nooses, goads, and skull-cups.
O Goddess, in secluded places upon the earth, those firm in their vows perform two hundred thousand oblations, or half of that, with *kiṃśuka* blossoms.
With lotus-milk, parched grain, sesame, rice, and bilva—
when this is performed, one becomes Īśvara himself, Brahmā himself, and Hari himself.
I cannot turn away from this; what use have I for other trivial accomplishments?
Even if Mount Meru were to move from its place, or if the sun were to deviate from its station.
O God, O one endowed with divine color, that which you have declared regarding the center of the earth shall certainly not be false; it is certain concerning Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Manmatha.
Beginning with the seed-syllable of Śiva and so forth, one should write sixteen [syllables];
or else, the seed-syllable of Śūdrī and the seed-syllable of Ramā within the two A-manmathas.

Or, having placed the mantra in the three locations, one should join it with the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrī) at the end of the sixteen [vowels] in reverse order; the elemental letters (bhūtavarṇas) are situated in the hands.
The gentle one, bearing a mass of hair, is non-dual with Śukra, the conch, and the skull;
he resembles molten gold and is seated upon the command of Lakṣmīśa.
On the ocean of milk, in the middle of a shining golden island,
there is a lotus with eight petals, its stalk reaching to the hands of the Youthful One (Viṣṇu),
encircled by coiled serpents, and possessing a pericarp as vast as the earth, strewn with the soles of the feet of the gods.
Having meditated upon him according to the previously mentioned method, one attains perfect success;
listen, O Goddess, to another supreme [method] concerning Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Pitāmaha.
One should cause the vowel *a*, which is not a means [of derivation], to be preceded by the letter *ś* (śa);
one should place the final consonant *t* at the beginning, and one should place the word "world" (*loka*) at the head.

O Goddess, [one should meditate on] the beloved one seated upon a red throne, with the two [syllables] "u" and "oṃ" at the middle and the end; O Goddess, [the mantra] should be recited in the abode of the sages with the nasalized "ṅo" and the upward-stretching "vu" in the middle.
When the seed-syllable of Ūrddhacakriṇī is at the end of the Āṣāḍhī conjunction, it should be placed upon his head;
the end of the sound [is to be placed] in the left temple.
Having extracted the triad of Vidyās, one should erase Bhautīśa at the top;
likewise, the bindu on the head of the letter of the Veda and Dhātrīśa [should be erased]. O Goddess, the syllable Kumaṃta is situated on the seat at the tip of the nose.
It is joined with the beloved situated above the *minarudra* and united with that *gandhāna*.
And the third [is] in the abode of the Ṛṣi, adorned by Ekarudra and others;
there resides the goddess Navādīpanī, seated upon the throne of Āṣāḍhīśa.
Vāgīśī, known as Bhairavī, resides at the end of the left-hand [channel] in the mouth;
at its end is the hell-tattva, which is merely consumed along with the food.
Before this is the seed-syllable of Ambikā; next is Yāma situated in the middle seat;
then Medhā, then again Prayatna, and then the two seed-syllables of the Dūtīs.
The end of the world (la) with the head (ha) above it, joined with the second vowel (i),
followed by two seed-syllables of birth (sū), and then the Lord of Beings (bhau) from the midst of fire (ra).
The syllables of the goddess are established in their proper order before it;
furthermore, Mādana (the letter *ka*) appears again before Śukra (the letter *śa*), joined with the end of the world (the letter *la*).
At its end are the letters of fire (ra), another vital breath (ha) with a bindu;
at the end of that are the letters of water (va), to which one should join the principle of Śukla (the letter la).
Having extracted the syllables from *bhūta* up to the end of the letters of the seasons (*ṛtu-varṇa*), one should join them to the head;
then, starting from the name and ending at the head, one should apply them to the northwest (*vāyavya*).
In front of the syllable *haṃsa*, that seed-syllable joined with speech (*vāc*) [is placed];
as before, there are those numbering the seasons (six), and likewise at the end of the *navātman* mantra.
One should install the Goddess within the Navātman [mandala], beginning from Meṣa-rudra;
this was diligently accomplished by Brahmā and Vāsava.

The seed-syllables beginning with the Hayabīja (Hrīṃ) should be deposited according to the prescribed method upon the five faces starting from the left, along with their respective portions and words in due order.

The heart-mantra should consist of the syllables of the elements; Śiva may also be the six-syllabled mantra. With two seed-syllables, one forms the crest-lock (śikhā), and likewise the body-armor (tanucchada).
O Goddess, for the protection of the eyes, the syllables of the planets are again declared in front [of them],
along with the syllables of the elements according to their respective directions in due order.
She is Vāgīśvarī, Mahāmāyā, Śivadūtī, and the consort of Śiva;
she alone is the bliss of Śiva to be propitiated, the command of Śiva, and the very form of Śiva.
One should worship Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī;
then Vairiñca, Adhokṣaja, Rudra, and Vahni, again in pairs.
In the middle corner are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī,
while Sarasvatī is in front of Śivā, reciting [the scriptures] and possessing a luster like the fat of a beast.
She is ruddy, auspicious, slender, with a smiling face and beautiful luster;
she resembles the white of a cow’s eye and her feet are like saffron.
In his two hands he holds two jars of the nectar of the Vedas, a ritual mudrā, and a rosary;
indeed, he is resplendent with his head adorned by many coiled serpents.
The God who wears a crescent moon, who has a serpent as his sacred thread,
who is clothed in a garment of deer-skin, seated upon a lotus throne provided with a wish-fulfilling tree.
Having commenced the practice of sitting upon a serpent-seat and moving about with one arm tucked under the armpit,
one who is firm in his vow should meditate upon and worship the Lord one hundred thousand times.
O Queen of the Gods, by offering one hundred thousand *vija* flowers along with auspicious sesame seeds for three years, one becomes a master of speech (*vāgīśa*) on earth, and no other.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the *Nava-koṭi-saṃhitā* according to the *Śrī-kubjikāmata*.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Queen of the Gods, I shall speak at length of this most secret of secrets:
the armor of the body is to be placed either in the village or even within the body itself.
In the great forest of the host of spirits, in the assemblies of the Saṃgha-less, and in the realms of the pretas,
he is seen as if amidst grass, amidst the wicked throngs of yakṣas and rākṣasas.
The waters [are located] in front of Śrīkaṇṭha; Rudra is at the end of the bindu, Bhairava is in the middle of the *oja*, and they recite it upon his head, conjoined with the cruel [syllables].
One should indeed first write the seed-syllables of Yama and Īśa; then one should place the letters representing the elements upon the head and likewise upon the deity.
The second [is joined] with the second, forming a half of six;
the fourth [is joined] with the fourth, forming a half of ten.
Likewise, O Goddess, one should know that the seventh [syllable] is in the seventh [position];
the eighth [syllable] of the Vidyā should be joined as the eighth, and one should duly place the fifty [syllables] in the half [of the wheel].
The collection of sounds (the alphabet) should be diligently installed within the six limbs;
as it has been said: "Just as knowledge [is conveyed] by fire, so too is the five-syllabled Vidyā."
Listen, O Goddess, to the ritual procedure which is indeed difficult even for the gods to obtain;
by the mere performance of which, every single bond is severed.
Even one who possesses every possible fault, whether he be a vulgar man, a fool, or a rogue,
suddenly becomes powerful on this earth like the lord of the gods.
O Śivasaṃbhavā, the goddess Keśavī is before you; she stands upon the calf of Dakṣa, who is full of pride, ending with Rudra and adorned with a bindu.
Having extracted the Yavamadhyam [tune], which possesses the Nāvarṇa and the Carma-bhairava,
and which rises above Mīna and Rudra, from it was born the Māninī-kṣīra.
Furthermore, O Goddess, the middle of the *vecu* is the *prāṇarudra* conjoined with Śiva;
indeed, the third from that, ending in *loka*, is situated at the head.
One should place that seed-syllable in front through the conjunction with the first letter *ru*;
one should place Merubhairava above and Lokādi on the head.
In this way, this is the Great Vidyā; before it is Bhakṣiṇī again, having extracted those seed-syllables (bījas), and then the mantra of Nārāyaṇa.
This knowledge, preceded by *natipūrva*, accomplishes all aims;
it resides in the midst of the syllables of mercury and earth, originating from the head of Māninī.
One should extract that thread situated in the middle of the barley-grain, which is joined with the infinite Nārāyaṇa,
as the Haṃsa from the front of Vāgīśa in reverse order.
Having extracted the center of the navel, the one named Vyāhṛti, who is infinite,
[is placed] before Prāṇarudra, accompanied by the *śulva* and the letter *repha*.

One should extract the heart-mantra from the left [side] at the end of the nine-fold staff, joined with the *haṃpharṇa* (the sound *haṃ*), and ending with the bow (*varmaṇā*)— this is the charming [mantra].
Then, in sequence, the consonants and so forth, together with the deities situated in the center,
are joined with words such as "kruddha" and the like, as well as the syllable of the *tāra* (om) and the *śakti*.

O beautiful goddess, by means of the oral instructions from the Guru, the letters and *kalās* of the twice-born classes [are to be assigned] in sequence through all the *ājñā* and other stages, as previously described.
One should first draw the wheel with the Vāgbhava syllable by means of the Vāgbhava;
in its center is the Goddess Śaktigā, consisting of eight syllables and accompanied by the King (the letter *r*).
Having again enveloped the letters situated within the *tāra* with the *haṃsa-śakti*,
one should draw the eightfold power (*śaktyaṣṭaka*) on the rim, which is designated as the culmination of the Vedas (*vedānta*).
When there are sixteen [squares] in each of the other eight [sections],
Hari is in the middle of that corner, and Dhruva arises in the north.
In the midst of that, one should contemplate the Sun, possessing the luster of a rain-cloud,
endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, and emitting light from his eight rays.
Endowed with a conch, discus, mace, lotus, noose, and goad,
resembling white nectar and possessing a luster like a red lotus.
Having fashioned the goddess Vidyā with an axle-string and a four-armed discus,
one should worship the god Śara-ikṣu-puṇḍraka, who is endowed with a noose and a goad.
Then I saw her seated upon a couch, her face like the full moon,
with her lover embracing her from the right, while another man stood firmly by her side holding a lotus.
Resembling molten gold, adorned with every ornament,
she is the supreme goddess Manmatha, the left-hand illusion who possesses thorns.
That seed-syllable is the king of mantras, white and terrifyingly red;
one should place it upon the heads of those two, as the syllable situated between the *kāma* (the letter *ka*) and the end (*ra*).
O Śivā, having extracted the white [syllable] of Mālinī and the white-and-red [syllable] differentiated by Vāmā and the others, [place it] alone in the heart of Mālinī.
O Goddess, Mālinī is above Śiva, seated upon the throne of Kūrma and the others; O Goddess, Khaṇḍāsāṭhī is at the head of the gods and in front.
Indeed, the seed-syllable beginning with *ṛṣimālā* is joined with *svastikāt* and so forth,
followed by *vijaye*, O Great Goddess, and the words *prasīda*.
Having extracted those very seeds from the midst of the sages and elsewhere,
one should offer the infinite seat (anantāsana) extending as far as the region of Ekarudra.
They [should place] meat above in the narakas, but only that [meat] before them;
starting from the eleventh seed-syllable, it should be offered while standing in front.
Having placed Karālī in front with the Bhautika [mantra],
and Vāgīśa with the Guṇonta [mantra] alone, she is established upon her seat by means of the Kālīśa [mantra].
O Sovereign of the Gods, the Lakṣmī-vidyā is remembered as bestowing manifold enjoyments;
it grants longevity, radiance, fame, renown, prosperity, and good fortune.
By the recitation and fire-oblation of this, one attains the eternal state.
The fire-offering (argha) with its causal basis is "Oṃ namo māṃ tu maṇḍala."
Having worshipped and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should meditate upon the fruit of nectar;
recollecting the root mantra, [one visualizes] the white [deity] streaming with white nectar.
With a well-concentrated mind, he should sprinkle himself and the sacrificial materials;
O beautiful one, he should worship constantly with the Vidyā according to the path previously described.
Victorious, steadfast, reaching the hearts of the deities— thus devoted to right conduct, peaceful, truthful, and firm in his vows,
he subsisted on alms, or ate only at night, or consumed milk, parched grain, and fruits.
And having sat upon a seat made of cloth in a clean place, endowed with excellence,
one should offer one's own *piṇḍa* a hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform oblations with nyagrodha, pippala, plakṣa, and udumbara wood, as well as sesame seeds,
rice, lotuses, and gems, twenty-one times each.
One who fears the terrors of saṃsāra should perform oblations with the *brahmavṛkṣa* (palāśa) wood;
likewise, one should perform various rites both in the direct and reverse orders.
Through recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, one shall become the lord of the siddhis;
O Goddess, the triad of form and power, as well as the limb-worship, are designated by name.
If it falls on the eastern petal, there is fire; if on the southern, a passionate woman;
if on the southwest, it is charming; and if in the water [petal], one becomes Viśvatanu.
Having strung the two bows, Vimalā and Cāpa, upon the northern petal, one should worship Hari;
and on the northeastern [petal], Bhadrā, with the limbs as before, starting from the east.
Whatever one constantly desires, whether in heaven, among mortals, or as a serpent, that too one obtains perfectly; this is the truth, the absolute truth, and not otherwise.
Beyond that, I shall fully describe another, the most excellent Śambhu, who is difficult to attain;
by the mere remembrance of whom, O Goddess, one may destroy the darkness of worldly existence.
Having extracted Dhruvasūti, Kṣe, Anta, Ambikā, and Śiva;
[then] the first seed-syllable of Mālinī and the third in the abode of the Sage.
O Goddess, one should draw Navakeśavaka twice above the head of Sūkṣmeśa,
and in front of Mālinīraktabīja, one should draw Ananta.
In front of Dharmarudra is Haṃsa; from its reverse order, joined with Vahnidūtī, is the three-seeded [mantra]. Hari is in the ninth square.
One should extract the syllable *śiva* ending with *eṣa rudraḥ*, with the letter *nṛ* (*na*) situated between them;
likewise, one should extract another *śiva* at the end of *haṃsa*.
Having raised up the center of the navel, Vālinī is auspicious at the forefront;
from the midst of the sages arises the corpse, and above the object of destruction is that which is born of the subtle.
At the end of Khaḍgīśa Bhairava, on Mount Gandhamādana,
at the peak situated on the left arm, there is indeed Haṃsa, which arises from the hair (lomataḥ).
And on the Mandara half of Arghīśa, one is adorned by Kāla and Lokānta;
those seed-syllables (bījas) should be placed before [the name], at the end of Dhruva, or otherwise.
At the end of Ambika and at the end of Kṣema,
as well as at the beginning, there shall be two Navātman deities, Dhruva and Pate, O Goddess.
Listen further to those [elements] which have been declared together with Caṇḍikā;
O beautiful one, listen to the eightfold essence of the temple.
First, having performed the *āmiṣṭa* [offering], one should visualize the Wind above the Blood,
with the *Lokādi* [syllable] pressing down upon the head, destroying the white Bhairava.
One should know that Dhātrīśa is Śiva conjoined with Gandha;
indeed, he is attained first, and you go to the middle, which is Māruta.
The syllable *anugraha* (anu-gra-ha), joined with the nasal bindu and adorned above;
this is the second deity to be extracted, ending with *śivāya*.
The third [mantra] ends with the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu, followed by "to Maheśvara";
the fourth is the fierce one, ending with "svāhā," followed by "to Śiva."
O Goddess, know that this mantra, consisting of Gaurī and Śiva, which has been recited at the end, is Śiva himself in human form; understand that everything present before you is he.
O Goddess, in the abode of Kailāsa, they know Śrīkaṇṭha as the first; Viṣṇu, Rudra, Dhruva, and Haṃsa are likewise known, while Vijña is considered to be for Dhruva.
The mantras concern ancient events and do not depend on distinctions such as lineage;
they describe Śiva, who resembles pure crystal and possesses ten arms.
The Goddess beheld him who bears five faces, endowed with five forms,
seated upon a lotus throne, radiant and blazing with splendor.
Wearing a crown of matted locks, peaceful, adorned with all ornaments,
imperishable, endowed with the ten [perfections], and graced with a garland.
The god, wearing divine garments, possessing a vehicle of knowledge, and resplendent, holds a multitude of axes,
[bestows] fearlessness, and is the protector of the field.
In his left hands he holds a bell, a serpent, and fire, as well as a noose and a goad;
his shanks, thighs, and feet are symmetrical, having surpassed the tortoise in grace.
Having meditated thus, one should constantly worship the deity Ardhanārīśvara;
the support and the seat are declared to be water, and [the deity] is Supreme Śiva.
That which is called Lāṅgalika is known as the Bindupīṭha;
there is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there a Śiva devoid of Śakti.
Power is to be known as being in flowers like fragrance, and likewise in sesame seeds like oil;
it is in the body like the vital breath (prāṇa). Therefore, one should worship power.
Śakti alone is declared to be the seat (āsana), consisting in sequence of Pañca, Ananta, and so forth,
as well as the terrestrial egg (pārthivāṇḍa), the pedestal (avaskaṃdha), the stalk (nāla), and the binding (bandhana).
First is the *tanonatyāsana*, the second is the *siṃhāsana*,
the third is the *yogāsana*, and the fourth is the *padmāsana*.
And the fifth is named Vimala, consisting of the five elements;
it is circular in shape and possesses the splendor of ten million suns.
One should fashion four feet in the form of lions at the corners;
they have faces terrible with fangs, three eyes, and fearsome forms.
Each [of these] is filled with assemblies numbering in the millions;
in the corners, in their true forms, are those beginning with Pāda, Kṛta, and Yuga.
One should meditate on the white, red, yellow, and black [forms] in the shape of a lion;
these four are the Unmanifest (avyakta), Necessity (niyati), the Fruit (phala), and Time (kāla).

The light of Niyati has the luster of unmanifest crystal; the light of Kāla has the brilliance of collyrium; the light of Janaprabhā has the hue of pomegranate flowers, yet she is inseparable from Kāla.
Thus has yoga posture been described; after this, the lotus posture (padmāsana) follows.
The principle of Māyā is circular, adorned with the thread of the knot of Vidyā;
it has the petals of the Vidyeśvaras as its parasol and is endowed with the filaments of Śakti.
The reality of knowledge (vidyā-tattva) is conceived as being equal to the reality of the beloved’s body;
its seed-syllable has the luster of the primary color, and its sprout has the brilliance of silver.
Its stalk is indeed silver-colored, and its thorns are reddish-brown;
the tips of its petals are conch-white, while its roots are known to be like lotus leaves.
In the pericarp, there should be blue and yellow filaments in the center;
within those, nine seed-syllables, and in their midst, a drop (bindu) with the luster of gold, in sequence.
O Goddess, one should assign the powers beginning with Vāmā to the filaments;
from Indra up to Īśāna, and one should place Manonmanī in the center.
One should place the principle of the Self (Ātmatattva) in front, in the gentle [position] corresponding to the letters of that Vidyā;
the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva) on the right, and the principle of the Universal Self (Sarvātmatattva) in the center.

Thus the lotus posture (padmāsana) is described; above that is the stainless seat (vimalāsana). Herein, the three mandalas are likewise established according to the ritual manual as the stainless seat.
Having worshipped oneself and the four [deities], the remainder is as previously stated;
[one should worship] either in the center of the *liṅga*-maṇḍala or within the interior of the pericarp.
There, one should recite the mantras for the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, along with their respective times;
and by means of the eight groups of digits (kalās), the eight petals of the eightfold mantra should be formed.
In the center of the *bhūta-yantra*, one should place the four [syllables] beginning with *satya*;
these are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara, joined with the long vowels beginning with *ā*.
One should worship [the deity] endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics using ritual offerings;
one should meditate upon the Lord Īśāna, the eternal, auspicious, and immutable.
Resembling a crown of matted locks, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
the omnipresent Lord mounted upon the bull-bannered vehicle accompanied by Bhavānī.
Performing the worship of the powers beginning with Vāmā while seated upon a lotus seat—
he is declared to be the Lord (Īśvara), the cause of all causes.
To the right of Īśvara, Brahmā arises from Viṣṇu;
to the left side of Īśvara, Viṣṇu arises from Śiva.
The Sun is in her right eye, and the Moon is indeed in her left eye;
Jātavedas (Fire) is in the eye of her forehead, and the Vedas are born from her mouth.
The wind has arisen in the nose; he who is born from all directions is in the ear.
Gaṇeśa is born from the hosts; he who is born from the six-faced one is in the heart.
In his navel are indeed the twelve Ādityas, and the entire world is born from his belly;
and all the eleven Rudras are manifested in his lower parts.
The Vasus were born from the regions of the hips, Prajāpati from the penis;
the Aśvins were born from the thighs, and likewise Gandharva from the feet.
The gods, yakṣas, mandarās, siddhas, vidyādharas, and others—
all the gandharvas and apsarases— have their origin at the soles of his feet.
Twenty-eight crores of deities have arisen from all his pores;
likewise, there are crores upon crores of forms produced from his body hairs.
Such is Mahādeva, the Lord, the sovereign of the thirty gods;
[he is joined by] Bhavānī, who has the luster of the color of gold, two eyes, and is endowed with two arms.
The goddess has her right hip and hand extended, endowed with a single hand;
O Goddess, she is supported by the root of Saumya, with a face slightly smiling.
The goddess is complete with all ornaments, adorned with a crown and other finery,
clothed in fine silk garments, and possessed of full thighs, hips, and breasts.
One should thus meditate upon Gaurī as the supreme primordial power (Parā-śakti), possessing the luster of the lunar disc and a wheel, who resides in the left portion of all forms.
Everything in the masculine gender is Īśāna; everything in the feminine gender is beloved of the Blessed One.
All progeny, both stationary and moving, are born from Umā and Rudra.
Lakṣmī, Dhātrī, Mahādhātrī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī,
and Gāyatrī— these goddesses, joined with their seed-syllables (bījas), are situated in the corners of the rasa [mandala].
Durgādevī, Mahādevī, Yoginī, and again Ḍākinī—
these are the supreme powers (parāśakti) of Jyeṣṭhā, originating from the merit and solar energy (saura) [of the sun].
O Goddess, I have previously determined this secret among the unmanifest extremes; it is the essence, the supreme secret—listen as I speak it to you.
That which abides in the body, that which resides within the body, that which is manifested by means of the body,
that which is condensed by means of the body— that body one should deposit within all bodies.
Having condensed it by means of the *piṇḍa*, it is declared to be in the form of a *piṇḍa*.
The wise know this *piṇḍa* to be composed of Śiva and composed of all the *tattvas*.
Having worshipped Umā and the others at the tips of the eight petals ending with the direction of Kubera,
according to the prescribed rite, one should worship Sadāśiva with these mantras.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Śiva.
Oṃ, salutation to the embodiment of the Great Auspicious One.
Oṃ hauṃ, homage to the body of knowledge.
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva.
One should assign the syllables of the *bhūta-mantra* individually according to the number of seasons (six),
or else, O Goddess, one should arrange eight parts using the eight-syllable mantra.

Each [element] is associated with its respective syllable and likewise with the eight-syllable [mantras]: Ether, Air, Fire, Water, Earth, Space, the Immobile, and the Essence of Nectar; and [the lords] Caṇḍeśa, Durgā, Śunī, the Directions, the Nose, the Moon, and the Army, as well as Vṛṣabha, follow in sequence.
One should worship according to the path of consumption with the Lords of the World, Vajra, and so forth;
thereafter, one should perform the vajra-body ritual in the sacrificial pits and upon the petals in due order.
One should dig a hole in the ground measuring one cubit in depth and an equal width;
it must be made according to the measurement of a finger-breadth (mānāṅgula), and one should not have it done otherwise.
One should place a grass mat (viṣṭara) all around with a measurement of one finger-breadth;
outside of that, the girdle (mekhalā) should be nine finger-breadths in width.
The lower girdle-band (mekhalā) is ten finger-breadths in width;
its height should be known to be equal to that, and the middle girdle-band is one finger-breadth [in height].
Its height and width are indeed three finger-breadths each;
above that, it is four finger-breadths in width, with its height being equal to that.
The base (yoni) should be known as five finger-breadths in measure, and its circumference should be eight finger-breadths;
one should smear it with cow dung and sprinkle it with arghya water.
One should draw a six-angled figure (ṣaṭkoṇa) ending with six lines,
which is a source of power (yoni), born from the churning of fire and originating from all the Atharvaṇa texts.
One should perform the purificatory rites within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) by means of initiation, sprinkling, and so forth;
the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) for the fire should be performed separately with the Aghora mantra.
Having thus meditated upon the fire according to the rules with a self that is free from pride, the place is first established from the west; Śiva is said to be above.
It is proclaimed that [the syllable] is located on the right and left arms, on the sides, in the eyes, in the ears,
in the middle of the face, and on the tip of the tongue.
Where the *kāṣṭhās* are, there the *śrotras* are; from that, the *bhūmis* are the leaders.
From the *kāṣṭhā*s comes fire, which is the flame; it resides in the eyes and the head—of this there is no doubt.
If someone has committed a stain upon the region of the head, it perishes;
likewise, one should perform the rite for increasing the blazing fire and the sacrificial flame.

For one of the Śāṇḍilya gotra, Jamadagni is the ṛṣi, Jātavedas Agni is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the metre. One should invoke the seven tongues— Kālī, Karālī, Mano-javā, Lohitī, Śvetī, Dhūmrā, and Piṅgā— as well as the mother Aruṇā, the father Varuṇa, and the one named Pāvaka.
Having a single heart, two wheels, two nostrils, three girdles, and three feet, it is adorned with seven tongues;
it is mounted upon a ram, possesses four horns, and is embellished with a crown of matted hair.
On the right there are four hands, and on the left side three hands;
likewise, there is a set of eight spears, and in the right hand a *śruk* and *śruva* ladle.
In his left hands he holds a spear and a fan, and especially a vessel of clarified butter;
he has a brilliantly radiant golden body and victorious tawny eyes.
Having thus meditated upon this form, which accomplishes all desires and aims,
one should worship the fire according to the rules and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the fire-mantra.
Through the frequent recitation of the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the word "svāhā," and through water-libations and burnt offerings (*japa-homa*), the Fire-god is perpetually gratified.
One may offer one thousand and eight, or half of that, or even one hundred and eight oblations of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *śamī*, sesame, *rājī*, *havī* grass, and barley.
Whatever the practitioner desires shall indeed be obtained, though perhaps after some time;
O Goddess, three methods for the accomplishment of mantras have been proclaimed.
For one who recites [the mantra], there may arise a deficiency in the fruit of the worship due to a lack of meditative concentration;
however, when the wise one is propitiated, there is grace for all embodied beings.
O Lord of all, listen now to how the individual soul (jīva) is like Gaurī;
they say her qualities are before the Haṃsa, while the intellect (mati) is behind.
A slayer of a Brahmin is constantly purified by means of recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth;
for one who bows [to this], no evil deed whatsoever remains—thus it is declared by the Lord at the time of initiation.

Having first performed the meditation as previously described, one should place the syllables beginning with *dhruva*, the colors of the seasons, and the words of omniscience within the six locations.
The knowledge of Śiva consists of four ends; at the end of the remainder is Kālabhairava.
The supreme mantra begins with Dhruva and is fixed upon the vital breath (prāṇa), ending with the syllable *Ru*.
The syllable ending with *dhruva* (the letter *u*), conjoined with *bindubhairava* (*ha*) and placed within *śivā* (*i*);
then *māninī* (*ī*), the letter of *śiva* (*ha*), and the seed-syllable beginning with the middle of the sages (*ṛ*).
Next, I shall proclaim another [mantra] for the front of the center of the universe:
having extracted the seed-syllable of the Goddess, one should place Dharmabhairava at the end of the boat (nau).
The third [is] in the Garland of Planets (grahamālā), at Anantagandhamādana;
it is exclusively the middle watch of the night, not far to the west of Viṣṇu.
The previously mentioned mantra, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals,
contains the essence of the flavors situated in the center, along with the fish, Rudra, the goal, and the bindu.

The word "Nārāyaṇa" ending in the dative case, followed by the seed-syllable of the Goddess; then the word "Loka" ending in the locative case, surmounted by the "Head" (Śiras), ending with the "Guna," and joined with "Kālasena."
Know this supreme truth: it is indeed thus at the corners of the eyes;
likewise, O Lord, so too are the others, for this is the truth regarding the origin of the worlds and all else.
The syllable JÑĀ is a red seat with a severed head and the Bhairava of the Bindu;
before it are pure letters, or it may consist of seven syllables.
Therefore, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa because he is the leader (nayanam) of men;
and because there is bowing (natiḥ) to that Goddess, he is certainly I-hamsa.
The universe is composed of the five elements, and the body is made of these five elements; Śiva is said to be composed of that very same essence—one should contemplate, "I am Śiva."
Therefore, O fair-faced one, it is the truth, the absolute truth,
that having extracted Viṣṇu from the eternal [state], fire itself is the means of attainment.
Whatever color field-marks (kṣetrabindu) appear before Ekanetra,
one should seek to conquer Śiva at his front, in the presence of Āṣāḍhī-Sāmaga.
In the house of the sages (the fifth house), place the head of a water-pot (culuka) and so forth;
furthermore, in the half of the house of love (the seventh house), one should install the cintāmaṇi jewel.
These seeds are placed before [the name] as proclaimed by Saṃkarāyaṇa;
likewise, O Goddess, there are eight syllables. Now hear from me that which ends with the twelfth.
The seed-syllables are further joined with the word "bhagavat" for that purpose; above which is the syllable of breath (praṇava), ending with the sage (ṛṣi) and originating from fragrance (gandha).
Place Pūtanā above him, and perform the seating starting from Dhruva; place Kātyā on his middle head, and Vāmā and the others on the crown of the head.
To the left, in front of the central [deity], one should draw the breasts of Māninī;
and in front of Vāgīśabhairava, the Rudras born from the sages.
By means of the application of the colors starting with Kūrma and so forth, and by the reversal of the seed-syllables (bījas),
there is the sequence of the twelve forms beginning with Keśava according to their divisions.
Through the distinction between Āditya and Ravi, there are twelve forms of Gāyatrī in sequence;
and by means of the union with Gāyatrī through the distinction between Āditya and Ravi.
One should perform the nyāsa, limb-mantras, and form-mantras, along with recitation, worship, and libations,
according to the previously mentioned procedure, preceded by the yoga of the self.
Having smeared the ground and made it level, he should place the two [seats] of Dharma and Adharma;
there he should meditate upon Acyuta, who is the end of the Mātṛkās and possesses Śakti.
The Kaumodakī mace, the discus, the conch adorned with lotuses,
the two earrings, and the forest garland— all beautifully decorated according to every ritual prescription.
Having entered [the mandala] with Lavaṅga and performed the rites of sitting and so forth, he was instructed on the offerings and other matters;
then [he worshipped] Keśava and the others on the tips of the petals, as well as Vāyu, Deva, and the Vasus.
In the subtle, void, and pointless (bindu-less) regulation of the trunk (kabaṃdha-niyama),
which is without support, one should contemplate the deity, having entered the root.
By that, one shall go to the state of liberation, where there is no further birth in a womb.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the venerable Kubjikāmata. || 0 ||
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, I shall speak of that which is an absolute secret and extremely difficult to obtain here;
even the gods do not know it, let alone human beings and others.
One should strive to accomplish [the goal] through recitation, worship, libations, and so forth.
