Before the goddess situated in the center of the navel is the seed-syllable together with its weapon.
Śukra is mounted upon a red seat; before him is the elephant-gesture (gajabindu).
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Karālī, he himself is red and possesses the bindu.
One should place the *śirasi-ikādi* upon the head of Kṣīravarṇa;
before this is the *mādana* seed-syllable, ending with *vāmā* and having *krūra* at its head.
One should draw a blow in front of the cruel-colored [deity] of the proud woman;
one should cause the world of Indra and so forth to be made below, and place it upon the head.
Then [one should worship] Nityakālī, Dhātrīśa, and again that red seat;
then the middle of the arrow, at its end Dharma, and indeed Vastukaṇṭhaka.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu and again [extracted] his beloved,
she who brings all beings to auspiciousness quickly led away this Vidyā.
O Great Goddess, this Vidyā bestows all prosperity, fame, chariots, heaven, and the attainment of the divine hosts; she appears as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa according to their respective distinctions.
The seed-syllable of Śakti, established even without words such as "omniscient" (sarvajña) and so forth,
should have the name "madadravā" joined before it, O Supreme Goddess.
The Goddess, resembling an indragopa insect and like the color of cow’s milk,
stands upon a lotus, bears a crescent moon on her crest, and holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Oṃkārī, Hrīṃ, Phetkārī, Sarvānandā, Aṅkuśā, Pāpāśā, Hrīṃkārarūpā, Aiṃkārī, and Vajrarūpiṇī.
One should worship the sixteen [deities] beginning with Nidrā, Cakrā, Bhayā, Abhīti, Madā, Dākṣāyaṇī, Harā, Vedā, and Bahukṛtī.
In the middle group of six, beginning with the letter *ṭa*, and in the first group of eight beginning with *brahmā*,
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times before an enemy, using *palāśa* wood.
Having offered the libations, he should say, "One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with [the substance] born of the Bindu";
and with flowers, one should perform the oblation in the fires beginning with Oṃkāra, which are known as the Brahmajānis.
In three years, one who has conquered the self shall become the lord of the Siddhas;
[the mantra] consists of the Goddess, the Seed-syllable, Purata, Dhruva, Indu, and Caturānana.
Again, having extracted that seed-syllable together with its preceding vowel and its final phoneme,
one should likewise place Viṣṇu and Rudra before it, along with the Moon and the syllable *hasa*.
Heṣaya-dvitaya, Dharma, Trailokya, and Padam;
Nāśinī in the form of a lion, and Nimekam—make these threefold. At the end, the external color as before, and Dharmāgni twice, making three.
This is that one named Siṃhikā, occurring at the end of a lion [sign] for ten degrees.
Or else, O Goddess, one should perform the previously mentioned Siṃha-ananta recitation;
having performed the previously stated nyāsa, including the placement on the joints and so forth, according to the proper sequence.
By means of the recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*) of this [mantra], one shall attain the aforementioned accomplishments.
One should place Sāvitrī, Viṣṇu, and Rudra in sequence in front [of oneself].
Below that, one should cause to be made the red Bhairava, who is red and possesses a dot;
he is preceded by the letter *ḷ*, has the color of the god, and is the infinite one (*ananta*) with a dot of light.
While Devavarṇa was writing, with the letter *ḷ* preceding *na* at the beginning,
the Goddess appeared with red sandalwood paste, and the four-faced Brahmā entered his vital breaths.
The letter *da* with *ha* and joined with the upward stroke (*ūrdhvarepha*) is between the breasts;
it is the color of the navel and reaches the head from the front.
The seed-syllable *prāṇa* is Viṣṇu, and the seed-syllable *mā* is Satya with the Bindu;
she is renowned as Lakṣmī, whose nature is bliss, and who bestows many enjoyments at the conclusion.
O Goddess, Kāmadeva himself, reflecting upon Soma and Bhāskara,
assumed a human form so that he might roam the earth.
Having worshipped the fire, which possesses the colors of the seasons and is endowed with qualities both double and single,
like the Lord of Tripura, while being fully integrated with the yoga of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having first worshipped the wheel, he made a jar filled with water;
then, firm in his vow, he performed the libation for one month according to the prescribed method.
One should recite the vidyā for a day and night and perform oblations with lotus stalks or sesame seeds soaked in honey; in every way, one obtains wealth.
The seed-syllable situated in the letter *kha* is established upon the seat of Pūtanā;
it has the root-staff beginning with *na* and ending with *ru*, preceded by *maḷ*.
This is Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, Gaṇeśa, or Sarasvatī;
or else, O Goddess Śivā, one may again perform the recitation of the Vedic syllables.
The messenger of the unprecedented nectar (Amṛtadūtī) is established with the true phonemes;
having extracted the fixed wealth, she does not pass beyond the piṇḍa in the west.
Furthermore, O Goddess, there is the true form, the seed-syllable of power, and the collection;
the final letter of the seed-syllable *mā*—listen now to the next syllable.
In front of the seed-syllable of Dhṛti, Karālī is stationed there;
her head reaches the end of the world, and she is the seed-syllable of Rudra joined with Śakti.
One should write two *piṇḍas* for the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, preceded by Puruṣa-Viṣṇu;
then, O Maheśānī, the [next] seed-syllable is adorned with the *piṇḍa* of the Vedas.
Alternatively, within the established doctrine, one should draw the ground conjoined with the Siddhānta;
in front of the seed-syllable of the *dūtī*, one should draw the world covered by hair.

O Goddess of the gods, these are considered the seed-syllables (bījas), described according to their seasonal colors: the syllable *mā* preceded by *śakti* (the letter *i*), conjoined with *bhūti* (the letter *ha*).
One should draw the *piṇḍa* situated in the middle of the eye, and at the end of the *dhruva*, one should write the *śakti*;
first [placing] Ananta, O Goddess, accompanied by Sudarśana and the gods.
One should again place the *vicakra* joined with *śivā* (Ś) and followed by the dative suffix *ṅe* (ai),
as well as the *sucakra* joined with *svasā* (Svā), O Goddess, situated at the vital point (*marman*) in the three worlds.
Furthermore, one should place the wheel accompanied by the Astra-Śiva-mantra, which brings an end to the Śiva-asuras;
having performed the placement of the limbs (aṅgas), either separately or as distinct phonemes.
Adorned with a fresh garland of tinkling clusters of small bells,
residing within a blue lotus, and possessing eyes like red lotuses.
One should worship with fresh butter and milk-rice prepared by cowherd women with their own hands,
according to the prescribed method, performing a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma) along with the libation (tarpaṇa).
He possesses a hundred thousand marks equal to those of Indra and is his equal in prowess;
furthermore, I shall describe another, namely Tāraśakti and Mādana.
O Goddess, first [there is] the proud one;
first there should be Viṣṇu, O Blessed One, ending in the suffix -ṅe, [and] Raktarudra, located at Dhruva and the other [points].
One should draw the subtle [mandala] consisting of marrow and so forth, or the region of the middle;
then the wheel, the pair of months, the mass of light, and immediately after that, the messenger (dūtī).
The seed-syllables are the heart, the goddess, and the seasonal syllable conjoined with Śiva;
among these, the friend is the discolored [syllable] within the interval between pairs of letters.

And [one should place] Rukmiṇī on the tips of the petals; Vāsudeva and the others, beginning with Vāsava, are situated upon the seats of the shoulders of the enemy, standing within the center of the lotus which is as red as the dawn.
It was filled with a multitude of people, resembling a mass of golden clubs and other weapons;
at its edge stood the beloved woman, her limbs languid with the intoxication of passion.
One should perform ten thousand or one hundred thousand oblations with the flowers of the *daśavidyāpārijāta*;
having extracted the *dūtīrudra* from the end of the *ṛṣimālā*.
Then, the lunar disc (māsacakra), permeated by that primordial fragrance and endowed with qualities,
situated within the mouth of the Unborn (Aja), subtle and extended, is pierced by the shanks.
With the *aṃgulīdakṣamālinī* [mudrā], perform the seat (*āsana*) starting from nine;
[place] Vāgīśa with the left ear and Ananta with the cruel head.
In the center of the Grandfather (Brahmā), one should draw Vasu and Rudra;
one should place Dhātrīśa and Bidugandha upon a subtle seat made of fragrant paste.
O Goddess, one should first offer the Rudrānta seat before Śivām;
then the Piṇḍa, Varma, and Rudra, situated in Kānta, which originate from fragrance.
Having extracted the eleventh [letter] and so forth, it is divided by half of space;
the god is red, with a bindu, possessing the *mādana* [letter], and situated on the circle of the tamed.
O Goddess, the seed-syllable of the Goddess must be extracted with effort;
it is Kṛṣṇa himself, the crusher of the Daityas, who establishes the stability of the worlds.
When the destruction of Dharma occurs in the world, O Supreme Goddess,
she creates a net of illusion and many forms as well.
He who acts according to his own will, the unborn, the true, the eternal—
[he is] the four Vedic castes at the foremost position within the fivefold abode.
One should place five or six limbs upon the five cakras;
likewise, the previously mentioned groups of eight and eight, as well as Rukmiṇī and the others, and the Vasus.
She possesses the power of the primordial female energies beginning with Keśavā,
and her hair is as dark blue as a peacock’s tail, bound together with a crest of peacock feathers.
With a face graced by a gentle smile, adorned with a red crescent moon,
endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great being, all-pervading, and possessing a radiance that reaches everywhere.
Hari, resplendent with various ornaments, bearing the discus, conch,
and excellent flute, wearing yellow garments that shimmer upon his rounded hips.
Shining with the splendor of the earth, adorned with the Śrīvatsa and other marks,
his two feet were marked with the signs of the banner, the discus, the lotus, the conch, and the svastika.
Indeed, it was surrounded by multitudes of gods and celestial nymphs, as well as by Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and others, and by the cowherds and cowherdesses who had sought refuge [in Him].
Having thus reflected with a concentrated mind, one should worship Vāsudeva and the others— who are without beginning or end— by means of their own powers through the forms of Keśava and the rest.
One should offer curd, fresh butter, and the like, ending with *kṛśara*, combined with meat and vegetables,
according to the sequence previously described.
O Goddess, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, preceded by their respective seed-syllables, [should be worshipped] along with Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī in the southeast corner.

In this manner, one should perform four hundred thousand oblations, with a tenth part [of that] as the concluding portion; the offering should consist of well-prepared lotus flowers, lotus stalks, or sesame seeds with milk-rice (pāyasa).
O Queen of the Gods, through recitation, libations, and fire-offerings for three years—
by these three means, He becomes gracious by His own command.
O beautiful one, listen as I shall further describe that which is free from rebirth;
O Great Goddess, it is the seed-syllable of the Goddess, residing subtly within the center of the Bindu.
That very [Kālacakra] should be joined with fragrance;
he should place it in the middle of the body like a staff, situated in the midst of the planets, extending from the tip of the nose to the subtle [aperture].
And first, the root of the punishment for the proud woman is right there before her;
then, that which was initially divided [into parts] becomes white again, and finally, it becomes that alone.
One should fashion the space from the end of the eleven [fingers] at the front to the middle of the thighs;
and the staff-like arm should extend upward from the elbow, joined with that [space].
O Goddess, the word *māṃsa-rūpa* refers to the servant who is dark as a rain-cloud;
O Lord Viṣṇu, he possesses a moving tongue and a beautiful command.

Having again stood in the *uttarākta* [position], one should place the syllables ending with *māyā* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*), preceded by the *lokādi-śiras* (the *praṇava*, *oṃ*), before the beloved Śivā.
The limbs [of the mantra] are formed by the syllables experienced in sequence, three by three;
in the apertures, there are as many syllables as there are letters, numbering six and ten in the ten locations.
One should employ the *prāṇeśamana* (the pacification of the vital breath) consisting of five verses [beginning with] "tāpikaṃ bhāskaraṃ devaṃ," which is adorned with necklaces and other ornaments.
Adorned with an ornament of peacock feathers that are smooth and excellent like a net of rays,
wearing yellow silk garments, and graced by a gentle smile.
Or else, with jeweled sandals set upon his feet,
he stood with his left foot placed beneath the breast of his beloved, who was clinging to him.
By this, the animal sacrifice, the protection of the worlds,
and the mantra— which, when worshipped, honored, and offered as before, grants its own perfection— are accomplished.
Adorned with white garlands and unguents, dressed in white garments and ornaments,
seated upon a white lotus, he remains silent, his mind fixed on the distant earth.
Having prepared white ritual substances and being seated upon a deer-skin spread,
one should daily contemplate the deity Dhanada.
O fair-faced one, it is indeed true that one attains the state of absolute liberation through the application of the Mātṛkā-weapon,
which is the established conclusion of all mantras.
While the mantras are being recited,
one who is intent on devotion should perform various vows, remaining disciplined and self-controlled.
O Goddess, for a man devoid of devotion, even abundant oblations are like offerings poured upon ashes.
Now, O beautiful one, out of affection for you, I shall speak of another matter.
All cruel men delude one another;
this knowledge must not be disclosed, for it is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Immortals, Dānavas, humans, and those whose wealth is asceticism,
by the power of the Soma-vidyā, roam the earth according to their own will.
The entire world of moving and non-moving beings trembles at its incomparable power;
having offered libations in due order, one should recite it a thousand times every day.
Having initiated the pure disciple, the teacher alone should impart the Vidyā to him;
therein, he should perform the extraction (*uddhāra*) within this most beautiful Meru.
O Goddess, one should draw Rudra in human form, with Kailāsa and Mandara at his left side, a cruel head, and his mouth wide open.
One should draw the seat, the upper wheel, and the illuminator, along with the cruel [deity];
on Niṣadha, which consists of four syllables, one should cause it to be marked by Śiva.
Having united Śiva and Śakti, she who recites the mantra situated between the letters *kṣa* and *ja* is the illuminator of the seed-syllable of Bhairava through its essence.
One should burn the Āmanam, beginning with Vāgiśa at the midpoint of Yāma and ending with Dhruva;
then one should place Lokādi on the head, conjoined with the eleventh [vowel].
O Bhadrā, O best of heroes, this imperishable [mantra] which effects both creation and withdrawal is located within the cluster of the fingers of Dakṣa, O Bhairavānanā.
Then, O Goddess, one should cause the seed-syllable (bīja) to be joined with its respective region;
likewise, O Great Goddess, [one should place] Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha.
Having undertaken the knowledge of the *soma*, which bestows immediate praise,
one is liberated from great poverty, misfortune, and the darkness [of ignorance].
Having worshipped the wheel according to the prescribed rite, one shall attain freedom from old age and death.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus in the center, surrounded by the circle of wealth.
One should place the form of the *piṇḍa* upon the pericarp of the *kāla*-lotus;
first, one should place the sixteen digits (*kalās*) with their bindu upon the sixteen-spoked wheel.
The second is located at the heart, the third is toward each petal,
the fourth is on the third [ring], and [the fifth] is on the row of the fourth petals.
In the fifth syllable, one should place *lāṃgalī* with *medarudra* and the bindu;
having placed the white [syllable] in the sixth, *ambikā* shall be in the seventh.
One should place the syllables outside that [circle], beginning with *kāmakrūra* at the head,
followed by sixteen circles joined with the bindu.
On its petals, one should write the Lord beginning with *nṛ* (Nṛsiṃha) within the eightfold circle;
at the tips of the petals, one should write *Śaśijvāla* (Moon-flame) conjoined with the *sudhā* (nectar) seed-syllable.
Having thus written this great wheel, one should worship Soma and Īśvarī on a level portion of ground, free from depressions and elevations.
On a pure ground smeared with cow-dung, resembling the surface of a mirror,
adorned with a canopy rich in white splendor, and beautifully decorated with chowries and other ornaments;
On the full moon day of the month of Puṣpa, at an auspicious moment, the practitioner, having anointed himself with fragrant sandalwood paste and adorned with Mālatī flowers, [should proceed].
Having received initiation from the Guru, the practitioner, with a restrained mind,
should prepare a mandala of water and draw a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) in its center.
Again, he should draw a mandala as before using four-cornered dice;
having inscribed a wheel within it, he should fashion a very beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the center.
One should take one hundred thousand firm and pure *arka* flowers, wrap them three times around [the vessel],
place nine gems inside, and fill it with a *droṇa* of water.
Two horse-prints (hayādvī) [are the measure] for the limbs, and eight āḍhakas of water for the outer [enclosure]; twelve niṣkas are measured for the circular [boundary].
With sixteen [vessels] numbering half of that half, one should place an image fashioned from silver into the central pitcher within the outer mandala.
Having sequentially cast nine gems into the various jars,
one should wrap them with pairs of fine silk cloths and then wash them there in due order.
Having consecrated all the flowers with unbroken grains (akṣata), fragrant substances, and so forth,
one should invoke Soma into the central pitcher and worship him with devotion.
Having remembered [the deity], one should recite the vidyā over the water-jar (kumbha) one thousand or one hundred and eight times;
and having established the mantra-fire in all four soma-vessels (somakuṇḍa).
There, four officiating priests (ṛtvij) should likewise cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be recited;
having completed the worship of the fire (śikhin), one should offer oblations with [substances] smeared with honey.
O Goddess, the libation is performed with ghee, milk-rice, śāli rice, and sesame seeds; it is accompanied by pure people in equal measure.
Having first performed the three-fold nyāsa, one should visualize oneself as the embodiment of the mantra,
and likewise the body of the disciple, as a mass of light filling the lotus of space.
Having dissolved [the deity] with the [mantras of] emanation and so forth, one should instruct the mantra for the sake of purification;
having performed the consecration according to the rule, one should then recite the mantra a hundred times.
Or, having performed one thousand and eight recitations even if the chanting was involuntary,
[one should offer] *mālatī*, jasmine, *punnāga*, and *rājāpadma* flowers moistened with honey.
When this has been performed, this Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) becomes accomplished within a year;
by practicing for three months, one shall attain all perfections (sarvasiddhi).
For the group of gurus is indeed to be attained, as are the deities and the collections of mantras;
therefore, the gurus who have bestowed these should be worshipped with great effort.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter in the illustrious Kubjikāmata. || 0 ||
